Yichen stood nearby holding the gift bag. And once again, he looked at Xiaoran and lost his train of thought. It kept happening all evening—the way she smiled politely at older relatives, the way she laughed, the way the warm light caught her earrings.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He blinked. Teacher Su smiled knowingly.

“You’ve been staring at Xiaoran all evening.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped her tea. The other students choked trying not to laugh. Even Meilin looked delighted. Outwardly, Yichen stayed calm. Inwardly, not at all. The tips of his ears gave him away. Teacher Su continued smiling warmly.

“You two are very cute together.”

Xiaoran buried her face in her hands.

“This wedding is attacking me personally.”

Yichen looked away, the corner of his mouth lifting, which only made everything worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, as the guests began to leave, a light rain started outside the hotel entrance—soft enough not to matter. The others waited for their rides while Xiaoran and Yichen stood a little apart under the decorative lights by the garden path. A quiet moment. Warm night air. Everything felt softer. Xiaoran looked down at her shoes.

“…Do I really look beautiful?”

Yichen glanced at her.

“What kind of question is that.”

“You kept staring.”

Silence.

“Because you do.”

Xiaoran looked away fast. Why did simple compliments from him feel so dangerous? Yichen stepped closer, close enough that his suit jacket brushed her sleeve. He looked unfair tonight too. Black formalwear should be banned for teenage boys. Especially Zhou Yichen.

“I think everyone noticed,” Xiaoran mumbled.

“What?”

“That you kept looking at me.”

“It’s hard not to.”

Silence. Was he trying to kill her tonight? Yichen looked thoughtful, like he wanted to say something else. Then, very quietly—

“You know what scared me earlier? When you came downstairs.”

“…Why?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Because for one second,” he admitted softly, “I genuinely forgot how to talk.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

chapters.desc: One secondhand poetry book. One very dramatic girlfriend. One week nobody at school will ever forget.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Became a Poetry Menace
chapters.epigraph: “Even ordinary afternoons become literature.”
chapters.content:
It started because Lin Xiaoran bought one old poetry book at a secondhand bookstore. One book. That was all it took to destroy the peace.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It smells intellectual.”

Tang Meilin stared at the dusty hardcover in horror. The four of them were at a café on Saturday while Xiaoran proudly showed off her purchase: an old, faded hardcover of translated classical poetry and romantic prose. She already looked like a changed woman.

“It’s vintage,” she corrected seriously.

“It smells like someone’s grandfather.”

“That’s called history.”

Yichen glanced at it, stirring his iced coffee.

“Do you even like poetry?”

“I’m evolving.”

Yuhao looked suspicious.

“Last month you said philosophy was fake.”

“That was before literature entered my soul.”

Meilin sighed.

“We’re doomed.”

Unfortunately, she was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Monday morning, Lin Xiaoran was unbearable. Not normal unbearable. Poetic unbearable, which was worse. She leaned against her desk in the morning sun.

“Some people,” she sighed, “are like moonlight reflected across water.”

Silence. Meilin looked up from her homework.

“…What.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Beautiful but impossible to hold.”

Yuhao stared. Zhou Yichen stopped writing and slowly looked at her. Where was this coming from? Then, calmly—

“Good morning to you too.”

Xiaoran nodded wisely.

“The moon also rises gently.”

“I hate this already,” Meilin muttered.

It got worse. Much worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch, Yuhao stole a dumpling off Xiaoran’s plate. Instead of yelling like a normal person, she narrowed her eyes and whispered:

“Greed is a fire that consumes friendship.”

Yuhao froze.

“…What.”

“Ancient wisdom.”

“That was a threat.”

“That dumpling had meaning.”

Yichen nearly smiled into his drink. Watching Xiaoran weaponize poetry all day was getting more entertaining by the hour, especially because she so clearly felt intelligent now. Then she turned to him. Danger.

“What,” Yichen said.

Xiaoran pointed her chopsticks at him.

“You know,” she murmured, “there’s a phrase here that reminds me of you.”

Silence. Yichen leaned back.

“Hm?”

“‘The pine tree does not bend easily before winter winds.’”

Meilin gagged. Yuhao looked horrified. Xiaoran went on proudly—

“It means someone calm and steadfast.”

“I know what pine trees symbolize,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Oh.”

“But thank you.”

He said it simply, gently, and it got to Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. Zhou Yichen always took her nonsense seriously. Even poetic nonsense.

“You’re not making fun of me?”

“Should I?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

Meilin watched the interaction with dead eyes.

“I’m dropping out of school.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem started on Wednesday, because Xiaoran had memorized too many lines. Way too many. Now she ambushed people with them all day. At PE class—

“The wind today feels lonely.”

During math—

“Numbers are humanity’s attempt to organize chaos.”

While eating crackers—

“Crisp sounds remind us life is fragile.”

Yuhao finally snapped.

“WHO GAVE HER THIS BOOK.”

In afternoon study hall, Yichen sat beside Xiaoran while she copied poetry into a notebook—concentrating hard, a tiny frown on her face, completely serious. Dangerously cute. Then, without looking up—

“Yichen, if I died young, would you compare me to flowers?”

Silence. Yichen slowly turned toward her.

“…What kind of sentence is that.”

“It’s literary.”

“It’s creepy.”

Xiaoran finally looked up.

“In poetry, beautiful people always die tragically.”

“You’re not dying.”

Xiaoran smiled—small and soft, like that answer pleased her far too much. Yichen noticed, and that tiny expression got to him too.

“What would you compare me to then?” she asked.

Yichen thought about it for a second, while nearby Meilin and Yuhao braced for emotional damage.

“You remind me of sunlight.”

No teasing, no hesitation. Just honest. Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…That was way too romantic.”

“You asked.”

“But you answered TOO well.”

Yuhao grabbed Meilin’s arm.

“I can’t survive this.”

Yichen went back to his notes like he hadn’t just destroyed everyone. After a moment, he added—

“Sunlight’s noisy too.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“And she’s back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Friday, the poetry phase should have been over. Instead, it evolved. Xiaoran started leaving tiny folded notes in Yichen’s notebooks. Not love letters, exactly. Just random lines—some romantic, some threatening, some completely incomprehensible. For example:

“The stars tonight resemble your emotional unavailability.”

“Even mountains erode eventually, unlike your stubbornness.”

And:

“If abandoned, I will haunt you artistically.”

In chemistry, Yichen opened his notebook and found another one. He unfolded it calmly.

“When I look at you, even ordinary afternoons become literature.”

Slowly, the corner of his mouth lifted. Across the room, Xiaoran saw it and hid behind her textbook. Writing the lines had been fine. Watching him read them was embarrassing. Beside her, Meilin looked spiritually exhausted.

“You’re both becoming worse.”

“No we’re becoming cultured.”

“You’re becoming insane.”

Fair criticism. Then a folded note landed on Xiaoran’s desk. She opened it. Inside, in Zhou Yichen’s neat, slightly slanted handwriting:

“You should keep reading poetry.”

And below that, one more line:

“Because you sound cute when you talk like this.”

Xiaoran put her forehead down on the desk with a thunk. Across the room, Zhou Yichen smiled a little and went back to work, completely unaffected. On the outside. Terrible man.

chapters.desc: His first game back after the injury. Scouts in the stands. Lin Xiaoran, holding nothing.
chapters.title: The Game the Scouts Came to See
chapters.epigraph: “Some people worry with their whole body.”
chapters.content:
The invitational was on a Saturday, and Lin Xiaoran had not slept properly since Wednesday. It wasn’t the scouts. Everyone at school had been talking about the scouts for two weeks—how many were coming, which universities, whether one of them was from Beijing. Yuhao had a theory that one of them was secretly a former national team player. Nobody knew where he’d heard it. Xiaoran didn’t care about any of that.

She cared about his ankle.

“It’s fine,” Yichen said on Friday, for what had to be the fortieth time.

“Show me.”

“We’re in a convenience store.”

“Show me anyway.”

He sighed, put down the onigiri, and rolled his ankle slowly in a full circle, right there between the drinks fridge and the instant noodles. The cashier watched them over the counter with open interest.

“See?”

“It made a noise.”

“That was my shoe.”

“Shoes don’t make noises.”

“These are basketball shoes. They squeak.” He picked the onigiri back up. “Coach Wang cleared me. The physio cleared me. I’ve practiced for ten days.”

Xiaoran tugged her sleeves down over her hands and said nothing.

Yichen looked at her for a moment. Then he bought her a strawberry milk she hadn’t asked for, stuck the straw in for her, and said more quietly, “I won’t do anything stupid.”

“You said that last time.”

“Last time someone pushed me.”

“What if someone pushes you again?”

“Then I’ll fall better.”

That was not the reassurance he thought it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gym on Saturday was louder than the semifinal had been. Students from four schools packed the bleachers, and someone had hung a hand-painted banner for their team that spelled “invitational” with two Ls. Near the scorer’s table, three adults in plain jackets sat with clipboards, not cheering for anyone. Everyone kept looking at them. Xiaoran sat between Meilin and Yuhao, gripping nothing this time. She’d decided that on the way in. No jacket to strangle, no water bottle to wring. If she held something, she would only hold it harder.

“You’re very calm,” Meilin said.

“I am extremely calm.”

“Your knee is bouncing.”

Xiaoran put a hand on her knee to stop it. Down on the court, the teams were warming up. Yichen moved through the layup line like he always did—easy, unhurried, a little bored-looking, which Xiaoran had learned meant he was concentrating. Then, on his way back to the end of the line, he glanced up at the bleachers, found her, and tapped the tape on his left ankle twice with two fingers.

It took her a second to understand. See? Fine.

“Oh my god,” Yuhao said. “Did he just send you a signal?”

“No.”

“He did. He sent a signal.”

“It was a cramp.”

“In his fingers?”

Two rows behind them, a pair of girls had gone quiet. Xiaoran recognized one of their voices before she recognized the face—the storage-room voice. She’s honestly holding him back. The girl looked away the second their eyes met. Xiaoran turned back to the court and found, to her own surprise, that she didn’t care what the girl thought anymore. She had a much more important job today, which was not passing out.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first quarter, Yichen played carefully. Too carefully. He passed when he could have driven. He landed on both feet every time, like someone stepping off a curb. Xiaoran noticed, and so did the other team, and by the end of the quarter they were down by six. At the break, Coach Wang said something to him that nobody in the stands could hear. Yichen nodded once, wiped his face on his shirt, and walked back on.

Then he stopped being careful. It wasn’t reckless—Xiaoran knew reckless now; reckless was the semifinal, cold and angry and going straight through people. This was different. He looked like himself again. He read a pass before it happened and took it the length of the floor. He pulled up for a jumper with a defender in his face and didn’t even watch it go in. When a player from the other team bumped him on a drive, he stumbled, caught himself, and kept going, and Xiaoran forgot to breathe for that entire second and remembered all at once when he scored.

“He’s okay,” Meilin said, very quietly, like she knew.

“I know,” Xiaoran said, and her voice came out wobbly.

By the fourth quarter, the three adults by the scorer’s table had stopped writing and started just watching. They won by eleven. Yichen played the whole second half and didn’t limp once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward, the gym emptied slowly. Xiaoran waited by the side door with Meilin and Yuhao, which was where she always waited, except today it took much longer than usual, because Yichen was talking to one of the men in plain jackets. Then to a second one. Coach Wang stood beside him the whole time with his arms folded and the expression of a man trying very hard not to look proud.

“That’s Beijing,” Yuhao whispered. “I’m almost sure that one’s Beijing.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I have a feeling.”

When Yichen finally came over, he had two business cards in his hand and his hair was still damp from the showers.

“Well?” Yuhao demanded. “Were they impressed? Did they cry?”

“Nobody cried.”

“Did they say ‘generational talent’?”

“No.”

“Did they say anything?”

Yichen thought about it. “One of them asked about my grades.”

Yuhao looked personally betrayed by higher education. Meilin dragged him off to buy drinks, which was the most obvious exit Xiaoran had ever seen, and suddenly it was just the two of them by the side door, the evening coming in cool around them. Xiaoran looked at his ankle. Yichen looked at her looking at his ankle.

“Still fine,” he said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You were going to.”

She was. She bit her lip instead. Then, because there was no point pretending, she said, “You were really good today.”

“Hm.”

“Not normal good. Scary good.”

“You noticed the first quarter.”

“You were scared,” she said. “I saw.”

He didn’t deny it. That surprised her more than anything else. Zhou Yichen, who said “I’m fine” about everything, turned the business cards over in his fingers and said, “A little.”

“What changed?”

He looked at her for a moment, like he was deciding how much to say.

“Coach told me to stop playing like I was afraid of getting hurt,” he said. “And I looked up, and you weren’t holding anything.”

Xiaoran blinked. “What?”

“Last time you held my jacket so hard you stretched the sleeve.” The corner of his mouth lifted. “Today your hands were empty. So I figured you weren’t that worried.”

“I was VERY worried.”

“I know that now.”

“I was worried with my whole body. I just didn’t hold anything.”

He laughed, quietly, and took her hand—the empty one—and laced his fingers through hers.

“Then thank you,” he said, “for worrying without strangling anything.”

She leaned her forehead against his arm and let out a breath she felt like she’d been holding since Wednesday. A few weeks later, the first recruitment letter arrived. By the end of the month there were four, spread across his desk in a neat, terrifying row, and Xiaoran started to understand that the future everyone kept talking about had an address now. But that came later.

That evening, they just walked home slowly, at his pace for once, while she told him in great detail every moment of the game she had almost died during. He listened to all of it.

chapters.desc: University offers are arriving for Zhou Yichen. Lin Xiaoran is quietly terrified of where they might take him.
chapters.title: Which Future Includes You?
chapters.epigraph: “Plans change. People stay.”
chapters.content:
Choosing universities should have been exciting. Lin Xiaoran treated it like impending doom.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re staring at the same page.”

Tang Meilin looked up from her laptop. Xiaoran hadn’t moved in a while. University brochures covered the whole café table—prestigious schools, scholarship pamphlets, department rankings. And in the middle of it all, Zhou Yichen’s basketball recruitment letters. Apparently being tall, smart, and athletic wasn’t enough. Universities wanted him too. Annoying, honestly.

“I hate higher education,” Xiaoran muttered.

“That’s because applications started.”

“No.” She slumped across the table. “It’s because adulthood is scary.”

Meilin sighed. Fair. Lately everyone talked about the future constantly—majors, dorms, career plans, cities. It scared Xiaoran more than exams did. Not because she didn’t have dreams. Because for the first time, she realized dreams could pull people in different directions. And Zhou Yichen had so many options, while she still changed her mind about careers every three weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem had started yesterday, when Xiaoran overheard teachers talking about Yichen after basketball practice.

“He could definitely enter Beijing.”

“Or Shanghai.”

“His coach said sports universities are contacting him too.”

“He has a strong future.”

Strong future. The words lodged in her chest. Suddenly the future wasn’t abstract anymore. It was real, and terrifyingly far away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen noticed the change right away, because Lin Xiaoran physically could not hide her feelings. At lunch she sat beside him, poking at her rice. Quiet. Too quiet.

“You failed a test?” Yichen asked.

“No.”

“You lost something?”

“Yes.”

Yichen paused.

“What.”

“My peace.”

“You’ve been weird since yesterday.”

“I’m reflecting on life.”

Across from them, Yuhao was eating noodles peacefully. Then he decided to get involved.

“She’s probably thinking about universities.”

Silence. Traitor. Xiaoran glared.

“How do YOU know?”

“You’ve been reposting sad quotes.”

Meilin nodded from beside him.

“One literally said ‘distance turns even stars into strangers.’”

Yichen blinked, then slowly turned to Xiaoran. Now he understood. Xiaoran immediately regretted existing. Out loud, it sounded dramatically pathetic.

“Forget I ever spoke,” she muttered.

But Zhou Yichen looked thoughtful now, which only made her more nervous.

“Come with me after school.”

“Where.”

“You’ll see.”

“Every time someone says that in a drama, something terrible happens.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After school, Yichen took her to the old outdoor court behind campus, the quiet one that was usually empty in the evenings. The sky was cloudy, the wind cool. Peaceful. Xiaoran sat beside him on the bench, bracing for devastation. What if he really wanted a university far away? What if he left? What if—

“What university do YOU want?”

His question cut her spiral short.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“What do you want?”

Silence. Nobody had asked her that yet. Everyone asked about scores, options, being practical. Not what she wanted.

“I don’t know yet.”

“That’s okay.”

“But you do. You already have plans.”

Yichen leaned back against the bench.

“Not really.”

“You literally have recruitment offers.”

“That’s basketball.”

“That’s your future.”

He glanced at her, then said calmly—

“You’re part of my future too.”

He said it so naturally, like it was obvious, like there had never been another possibility. Xiaoran’s chest ached.

“But what if your best opportunity is somewhere far?”

Yichen didn’t answer right away. He looked out at the empty court for a moment.

“Do you know why I haven’t accepted anything yet?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Why?”

“Because I’m waiting for your applications first.”

Silence.

“WHAT.”

He said it so calmly, like it wasn’t a completely insane boyfriend thing to say. Xiaoran stared at him in horror.

“You can’t make life decisions around me!”

“I can.”

“That’s unhealthy.”

Finally, Yichen laughed—warm and quiet—while Xiaoran kept short-circuiting beside him. Then he looked at her again.

“I’m serious. I’ll choose the place that makes the most sense for both of us.”

That scared Xiaoran more than distance did. Because suddenly she understood that Zhou Yichen loved her in frighteningly serious ways. Not loud. Not dramatic. Just steady. Real. Shaped like a future.

“What if I don’t get into good schools?”

“You will.”

“But WHAT IF.”

“Then we’ll figure it out.”

Simple again. It always was with him, like nothing was frightening if they faced it together.

“I don’t need everything perfectly planned right now, Xiaoran.”

The wind moved through his hair as the evening light faded behind the court, and somehow he looked older. Not in age. Just steadier. Then he added quietly—

“I just know I don’t want a future without you in it.”

Silence. Then the tears came, because Lin Xiaoran always cried when she was overwhelmed.

“Why are you crying?” Yichen sighed.

“You said things.”

Even crying, she shifted closer until her shoulder pressed against his arm. After a moment, very quietly—

“What if we fight more in university?”

“We will.”

“What if we get busy?”

“We will.”

“What if you meet prettier girls?”

Yichen looked deeply unimpressed.

“Seriously?”

“I’m planning ahead.”

“You’ll still be annoying there too.”

“Oh.”

“And I’ll still love you there too.”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“This conversation is a personal attack.”

Yichen smiled and gently pulled her hands away from her face. Then, softly—

“Stop being scared alone.”

Somehow, that comforted her most of all. Maybe the future really was uncertain. Maybe university would change things. Maybe growing up would be messy. But sitting beside Zhou Yichen, his hand warm around hers under the evening sky, the future didn’t feel quite so frightening anymore.

chapters.desc: One internet question. One very serious girlfriend. Zhou Yichen was not prepared.
chapters.title: Would You Still Love Me If I Was a Capybara?
chapters.epigraph: “Real love answers ridiculous questions sincerely.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen should have known peace never lasted long around Lin Xiaoran, especially when she went quiet. Quiet usually meant one of three things: she wanted something, she had done something, or she had discovered internet nonsense. Today, it was the third one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen was doing homework at Xiaoran’s house while she lay upside down across the bed beside him, scrolling through videos. A normal, safe afternoon. Or so he thought.

“Yichen, would you still love me if I was a capybara?”

Yichen’s pencil slowed to a stop. What kind of question was that? Xiaoran was watching him from upside down, waiting. Completely serious.

“…A capybara.”

“Yes.”

Yichen blinked. Twice.

“…The giant rodent?”

“Don’t call me that.”

“I’m asking for clarification.”

Xiaoran sat up.

“You’re stalling. That means hesitation.”

“There SHOULD be hesitation.”

Across the room, Tang Meilin looked up from her phone with dead eyes.

“Oh no.”

Yichen set his pencil down. Experience had taught him that this kind of conversation could get dangerous. Then, calmly—

“Why specifically a capybara?”

“They’re calm.”

“You’re not calm.”

“They’re cute.”

“Hm.”

“And they sit in hot springs with oranges.”

“Important trait.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen looked at her for a moment. Then—

“Yes.”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…Really?”

“You asked.”

Meilin groaned.

“You people are impossible.”

But Xiaoran wasn’t finished.

“What if I was an ugly capybara?”

Yichen sighed.

“There’s no such thing.”

“Wrong answer. Some capybaras definitely look unemployed.”

“That’s oddly judgmental.”

“I’m asking seriously.”

Yichen leaned back in his chair. Then, calmly—

“You’d still be Xiaoran.”

Simple and warm, and Xiaoran’s whole face softened. Disaster. Zhou Yichen always answered ridiculous questions sincerely.

“What if I couldn’t talk anymore because I was a capybara?”

“You already say nonsense half the time.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Meilin nearly collapsed laughing. Yichen finally smiled a little. Then he added—

“You’d still follow me around.”

“That’s true.”

“And steal my food.”

“ALSO TRUE.”

“See?”

Xiaoran stared at him suspiciously now.

“…You’ve thought about this too comfortably.”

“I adapted quickly.”

Meilin cut in tiredly—

“Can I ask why this conversation exists.”

Xiaoran grabbed her phone and shoved a video at them. On screen, a capybara sat peacefully while tiny ducklings climbed onto its head. Yichen watched.

“…Okay.”

“LOOK AT THEM.”

“Hm.”

“They look so calm.”

Fair. Even Yichen had to admit the capybara looked weirdly at peace. Then Xiaoran pointed accusingly.

“See? If I became one, you’d live a calmer life.”

“No.”

“No?”

“You’d still create problems somehow.”

Silence.

“…That’s true.”

Meilin nodded.

“You’d become the first capybara banned from libraries.”

“Why specifically libraries.”

“You’d chew the books.”

“That’s species discrimination.”

Yichen went back to his homework. Conversation over, probably. Unfortunately, Lin Xiaoran still had thoughts. Too many thoughts.

“Would you pet me?”

The pencil stopped again.

Meilin got up and headed for the kitchen. “I need water.” Coward.

Yichen looked back at Xiaoran, who was now sitting cross-legged, hugging a pillow, waiting seriously. Then, calmly—

“Yes.”

“…Really?”

“Hm.”

“How.”

Yichen considered it. Then he reached over and patted the top of her head. Once. Twice.

“Like that,” he answered quietly.

Silence. Xiaoran completely malfunctioned. Why did the simplest affection from him always hit harder than expected? Yichen looked suspiciously amused.

Xiaoran crawled over until her head was resting on his shoulder. Very capybara behavior, somehow. Yichen glanced down.

“What now.”

“I’m testing if you’d still cuddle me.”

“You’re already doing that.”

“Oh.”

“Would you still date me publicly?”

“Yes.”

“What if society judged you.”

“I already date you now.”

“ZHOU YICHEN?!”

Meanwhile Meilin shouted from the kitchen—

“HE GOT YOU THERE.”

chapters.desc: Lunch at Zhou Yichen’s house, with both his parents home. Lin Xiaoran is not emotionally prepared.
chapters.title: I’m Invited to Zhou Yichen’s House?
chapters.epigraph: “You learn the most about someone from the people who raised them.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran knew something was wrong the moment Zhou Yichen casually said—

“Come over tomorrow.”

Silence.

“…Where.”

“My house.”

A longer silence. Excuse her? His house? While his parents were HOME?

✦ ✦ ✦

That Friday night, Xiaoran sat frozen on her bed while Tang Meilin watched her spiral.

“He invited me casually.”

“Hm.”

“CASUALLY.”

Meilin looked up from her phone.

“You’ve already met his parents before.”

“That was different.”

Technically true. The first time Xiaoran met the Zhou family was the airport goodbye before their trip. The second was the ride home when Yichen came back. Both times were short, sweet, and polite. Mrs. Zhou smiled warmly. Mr. Zhou seemed calm and gentle. Nobody asked serious relationship questions. It had almost felt like they saw her as just a cute high school girlfriend. Young. Temporary, maybe. Which had actually made her less nervous.

But now he had invited her over on a Saturday, with both his parents home. Then Xiaoran sat bolt upright.

“Oh my god.”

“What now.”

“What if this is evaluation day.”

“…Evaluation day.”

“What if his mother secretly observes whether I can become a daughter-in-law.”

Meilin stared at her.

“You’ve watched too many dramas.”

“YOU DON’T KNOW RICH FAMILY CULTURE.”

“The Zhou family is literally normal.”

“That’s what makes them scarier.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came too fast, and Lin Xiaoran spent TWO HOURS choosing clothes. Not too pretty—suspicious. Not too casual—lazy. Not too cute—impossible.

Meanwhile Zhou Yichen received seventeen messages during basketball practice.

Xiaoran: Does your mother prefer elegant girls or cheerful girls

Yichen: Normal girls.

Xiaoran: That didn’t help.

Then later—

Xiaoran: What if your father hates me

Yichen: He won’t.

Xiaoran: How do you know

Yichen: Because you’re cute.

Xiaoran lost focus for the next fifteen minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Yichen met her at his front gate that afternoon, Lin Xiaoran looked one small inconvenience away from collapse. She was holding a cake box awkwardly—hair carefully done, white top, soft pink skirt. Yichen almost smiled. She had clearly tried very hard.

“You’re nervous.”

“No I’m not.”

“You nearly walked into the mailbox.”

“…It came out of nowhere.”

Before Yichen could answer, the front door swung open and Mrs. Zhou appeared.

“Oh, Xiaoran’s here!”

Warm smile, gentle voice, no scary mother-in-law aura whatsoever. Which somehow made Xiaoran MORE nervous.

“Hello, Auntie,” she said quickly, with a small bow. “I brought cake.”

“You’re so polite,” Mrs. Zhou laughed softly. “Come inside quickly.”

In the living room, Mr. Zhou looked up from his newspaper.

“Yichen finally stopped hiding his girlfriend from us.”

Xiaoran froze. Yichen sighed.

“Dad.”

Mrs. Zhou laughed, and the air softened a little.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Zhou house felt exactly like Yichen. Clean, comfortable, quiet but warm. Neatly organized bookshelves. Basketball photos along the hallway, including one of a gap-toothed little Yichen holding a ball almost as big as he was. Soft music coming from the kitchen. Seeing him in his own home got to Xiaoran more than she expected. This was his real space. The place he grew up. The place he became himself.

“Xiaoran, sit beside me,” Mrs. Zhou said warmly from the sofa.

“Oh.”

Yichen looked suspiciously amused. Traitor boyfriend. So Xiaoran sat down carefully beside Mrs. Zhou while Yichen disappeared into the kitchen. Abandoned.

“He talks about you a lot.”

Silence. Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…He does?”

Mrs. Zhou smiled knowingly.

“Hm.”

“Oh.”

Her ears went pink. Zhou Yichen talked about her at home? What did he say? Had he mentioned the time she cried over math homework?

“You don’t need to be nervous around us.”

Her voice was soft, like she really meant it.

“We already met you before,” she continued. “You’re exactly what I expected.”

Silence. Somehow that made Xiaoran even more nervous.

“…Good expected?”

Mrs. Zhou laughed lightly.

“Very cute expected.”

Yichen came back from the kitchen with drinks just in time to see Xiaoran quietly malfunctioning beside his mother. It almost made him laugh. Lin Xiaoran, who talked nonstop around everyone else, was sitting perfectly upright with both hands in her lap, trying desperately to behave. Then Mr. Zhou spoke from across the room.

“So.”

Oh no. Xiaoran sat up straighter.

“Does Yichen bully you at school?”

“Yes.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“He judges my math.”

“You failed two quizzes.”

“See? Bullying.”

Unexpectedly, Mr. Zhou laughed. Actually laughed. And the whole room relaxed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was easier after that. Not because Xiaoran stopped being nervous, but because the Zhou family was surprisingly normal. Mrs. Zhou kept putting food in her bowl. Mr. Zhou calmly asked about university plans. Nobody interrogated her. Nobody acted weird. At one point, Mrs. Zhou sighed fondly, watching Yichen peel shrimp for Xiaoran without even thinking about it.

“He really likes you.”

Yichen paused. Xiaoran nearly dropped her chopsticks. Adults really just SAID things.

“He spoils her too much,” Mr. Zhou added.

“That’s true,” Mrs. Zhou agreed.

Yichen finally looked a little helpless.

“You’re both making her nervous.”

“We’re telling the truth,” his mother replied calmly.

Then she turned toward Xiaoran again.

“He’s been calmer since dating you.”

Xiaoran blinked, holding her bowl.

“…Calmer?”

Mrs. Zhou smiled softly.

“Hm. Yichen used to stay in his room a lot more.”

Across the table, Yichen paused—a tiny pause, almost invisible. But Xiaoran noticed. Mrs. Zhou went on—

“He was always a good child. Responsible. Quiet. Never caused trouble.”

“That sounds accurate,” Xiaoran nodded automatically.

“But sometimes,” Mrs. Zhou added softly, “he carried things by himself too much.”

The table went quiet, and Xiaoran was suddenly curious. She knew Zhou Yichen at school—basketball captain Zhou Yichen, calm boyfriend Zhou Yichen, the boy who spoiled her endlessly while staying perfectly composed. But what had he been like here, before her? Before she could stop herself—

“What was Yichen like at home?”

Yichen looked up slowly.

“…Xiaoran.”

Too late. Mrs. Zhou was already smiling.

“Oh, he was very serious.”

“Mom.”

“He’d come home, finish homework, practice basketball, study again.”

“That still sounds like him.”

“Hm, but now he laughs more.”

Yichen actually looked a little embarrassed. A rare sight. Xiaoran stared at him.

“…You didn’t laugh before?”

“I laughed.”

Both his parents looked unconvinced.

“Not often,” Mr. Zhou corrected calmly.

“Oh my god.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“You were a robot.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“It’s TRUE.”

Yichen sighed while Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“He laughs a lot when he talks to you at home.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…At home?”

“Hm,” Mrs. Zhou nodded casually. “Sometimes we hear him on calls with you.”

Across the table, Yichen closed his eyes. Complete defeat. Xiaoran’s ears went pink.

“WAIT.”

“He’d be sitting there looking normal,” Mrs. Zhou continued gently, “then suddenly smiling at his phone.”

“Mom.”

“And once,” she added thoughtfully, “he laughed so hard because of you that his father thought something happened.”

Mr. Zhou nodded once.

“I was concerned.”

Xiaoran turned slowly to Yichen, who looked deeply resigned.

“…You laugh like that because of me?”

“You say stupid things constantly.”

“That’s not the important part.”

Xiaoran’s chest went painfully soft. Picturing Zhou Yichen alone at home, smiling at her messages, got to her more than she expected—especially because at school he always looked so composed. Apparently he carried little pieces of her into his private world too.

“What else does he do?”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“No, I want to know.”

Mrs. Zhou nearly laughed again. Mr. Zhou added calmly—

“He checks his phone more now.”

“Oh my god,” Xiaoran whispered.

Yichen looked exhausted.

“You’re all enjoying this too much.”

It felt unfair. At school, Zhou Yichen had dignity. Respect. Control. Meanwhile his parents were casually revealing that yes, he smiled at her texts alone. Yes, he waited for her calls. Yes, he was happier now. Mrs. Zhou looked at Xiaoran warmly.

“Thank you for taking care of him.”

That made Xiaoran go still. Nobody had ever put it that way. People always talked about how much Yichen took care of HER—protected her, spoiled her, loved her patiently. But his mother was thanking her, like she mattered just as much in his life.

“I don’t think I do much,” Xiaoran admitted honestly.

Across the table, Yichen looked at her, and before anyone else could speak—

“You do.”

Xiaoran’s heart stumbled. Then, holding her gaze—

“You make things lighter.”

Mrs. Zhou smiled. Mr. Zhou looked unsurprised. Xiaoran forgot how to breathe. He’d said it in front of his parents, so naturally. No teasing. No joking. Just honest. Under the table, her fingers found his hand. And this time, Yichen held on first.

chapters.desc: For her first birthday as his girlfriend, Zhou Yichen plans everything—and remembers something she forgot.
chapters.title: The Birthday Where Zhou Yichen Lost Financial Control
chapters.epigraph: “He remembered the things she forgot she wanted.”
chapters.content:
Three days before Lin Xiaoran’s birthday, Chen Yuhao noticed something suspicious.

“…Why are there shopping bags in your locker.”

Zhou Yichen closed the locker calmly.

“Nothing.”

“Those are luxury brand bags.”

“Basketball-related.”

“Are basketballs sold in jewelry stores now?”

Nearby, Tang Meilin looked exhausted.

“He’s gone.”

“What.”

“He entered rich devoted boyfriend territory.”

Zhou Yichen had been acting strange all week—checking his phone constantly, leaving practice early, ignoring his teammates. At one point he’d turned down basketball plans because he had “important things to prepare.” Terrifying. Finally, Yuhao cornered him at break.

“What did you buy her.”

“Nothing excessive.”

Silence.

“…That answer means it’s excessive.”

Yichen looked away. A tiny pause. A bad sign.

“She mentioned wanting it once.”

“Oh no.”

“And forgot about it afterward.”

“Oh NO.”

Yuhao clutched his chest.

“This man is too far gone.”

“Stop being weird.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Xiaoran had no idea, mostly because she’d spent the whole week invested in one question: would Zhou Yichen do something romantic? Not expensive. Not huge. Just… romantic. It was their first birthday together. Then, on Friday night, she got a message.

Yichen: Tomorrow morning. Wear something comfortable.

Xiaoran screamed into her pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday arrived with suspiciously perfect weather—warm sun, a soft breeze, a bright blue sky. Romantic conditions. Xiaoran spent ninety minutes choosing an outfit. Not too obvious. Not too plain. Cute but effortless, which took tremendous effort. She settled on a pale blue dress with tiny ribbons at the sleeves. Soft. Pretty. Very girlfriend. Then the doorbell rang, and the second Xiaoran opened the door, her heartbeat betrayed her. Zhou Yichen looked unfair today. Black long-sleeve shirt. Relaxed jeans. Hair a little messy from the wind, one hand in his pocket. And the way his eyes went soft the second he saw her.

Yichen blinked.

“…You dressed up.”

“You noticed too fast.”

“You’re pretty.”

Xiaoran turned around.

“No. Restart the greeting.”

Yichen laughed softly near the doorway.

“Okay. Take two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first half of the date was surprisingly normal: lunch, wandering downtown, holding hands, stealing each other’s drinks. At one point Xiaoran dragged him into a stationery shop and judged notebooks for twenty minutes.

“This one looks smart.”

“It’s paper.”

“You don’t understand aesthetics.”

Later, they wandered through crowded shopping streets, sunlight bouncing off the shop windows, a comfortable quiet between them. Until Yichen stopped walking.

“Hm?”

“Wait here.”

Before she could investigate, he disappeared into a nearby store and came back a few minutes later with another shopping bag.

“…What’s that.”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a boyfriend lie.”

“It’s your birthday.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

Yichen just smiled and kept walking, which only made her more curious.

✦ ✦ ✦

As evening came, Yichen took her to the riverside—golden sunset on the water, street musicians playing, warm lights coming on along the walkway. Beautiful. Dangerously romantic. Then Xiaoran noticed a small cake box on a reserved table by the river. Beside it, her favorite flowers.

“…You planned this?”

“Hm.”

“By yourself?”

“I had help.”

“From who.”

“Unfortunately Yuhao.”

Xiaoran sat down, staring at it all. Nothing extravagant. Warm lights, a pretty view, a small cake, the exact desserts she liked. Somehow that made it feel even more sincere.

“This is really pretty.”

Yichen relaxed a little. He’d spent two weeks planning this—not because Xiaoran demanded grand gestures, but because she deserved the effort.

“Oh wait.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes suspiciously.

“…What’s inside the shopping bag.”

Silence. Yichen looked away. Another bad sign.

“Open it later.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“NOW.”

With visible resignation, Zhou Yichen handed over the bag, and Xiaoran froze. Inside was the necklace she’d pointed at MONTHS ago while window shopping—a delicate silver chain with a tiny star charm. She’d looked at it quietly and said—

“Way too expensive.”

And then she’d forgotten all about it. Apparently, Zhou Yichen hadn’t.

“You remembered?”

Yichen looked oddly calm, which usually meant he was nervous.

“You liked it.”

“That was months ago.”

He shrugged. But his heart was already racing. He’d worried about this gift too much—too romantic, maybe, too serious. The moment Xiaoran touched the necklace and her eyes went soft, relief hit him all at once.

“I wanted your first birthday gift from me to be something you’d keep for a long time.”

Silence. Xiaoran’s eyes went suspiciously watery.

“Oh no,” Yichen sighed immediately. “Don’t cry.”

“I’m NOT crying.”

“You literally are.”

“It’s because you’re acting too much like a husband.”

“…That’s your complaint?”

“Yes.”

Yichen laughed despite himself, and that familiar laugh made the evening warmer.

“Come here.”

Xiaoran leaned closer. Carefully, Yichen lifted the necklace and fastened it around her neck himself—warm fingers brushing her skin, close enough that she could smell his cologne, close enough to hear him breathe. Her heart started racing too. Then, near her ear—

“Pretty.”

That one word was too much. The necklace mattered less than the way he looked at her wearing it, like she was precious long before the gift was.

“Do you like it?”

Xiaoran looked at him for a long second—the boy who remembered things she forgot herself, who planned quietly, who spoiled her endlessly without ever making it feel heavy. Her chest felt too full. Before Yichen could say anything else, Xiaoran stood up and hugged him tight. No warning. No speech. Just her arms around him and her face pressed against his shoulder. Yichen froze for a second. Then his arms closed around her waist, holding her steady. The riverside lights shimmered around them while music drifted through the evening air.

“I really like it,” Xiaoran mumbled against his shoulder.

Yichen smiled softly near her hair.

“Hm.”

“You’re too good at this boyfriend thing. My heart can’t take it.”

He laughed quietly—the soft laugh only she ever heard this close. Xiaoran pulled back a little, hands still loosely gripping his sleeves, eyes suspiciously emotional. Then she rose on her toes and kissed his cheek. Soft. Quick. Enough to make Zhou Yichen go completely still. Lin Xiaoran almost never started things this directly. Usually she got shy halfway through. But maybe it was the lights, or her birthday, or just loving him too much—she kissed him first anyway. Then her face went red.

“…Oh no.”

Yichen looked at her, very quietly. Something in his eyes had changed—softer, darker, more focused. And Xiaoran realized that kissing her boyfriend out of nowhere beside a romantic river might have been a tactical error.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“How am I looking at you.”

“Like you’re planning crimes.”

Yichen laughed under his breath before pulling her back closer lightly by the waist again.

“Too late.”

“Zhou Yichen, this is MY birthday. You’re supposed to behave.”

“No one told me that rule.”

Xiaoran hid her burning face against his chest again while Yichen held her there. With the necklace resting against her skin and his heartbeat steady under her ear, Lin Xiaoran felt dangerously happy. Too happy. Which usually meant Zhou Yichen was about to make things worse. She was right. After a few quiet seconds, Yichen tilted her chin up, slow and careful.

“…What?” she whispered.

Yichen just looked at her. The riverside lights caught in his eyes, the night breeze moved around them, and he looked unbearably handsome again.

“You kissed me first.”

“That was a mistake.”

“You should forget it happened.”

“I don’t think I will.”

Xiaoran’s ears went even redder. The way he was looking at her felt unfair—focused, warm, like she was the only thing worth paying attention to tonight.

“Can I kiss you back?”

He usually just kissed her by now—her forehead, quick kisses, small affections. Asking like this felt much more dangerous. Much more intimate. Xiaoran forgot how speaking worked.

“…You’re asking?”

“I’m being polite.”

“That’s somehow worse.”

Yichen laughed softly under his breath.

“Hm?”

That stupid calm hm, the one that always made her surrender. So, very weakly—

“…Okay.”

Yichen’s whole face softened. Then he leaned down slowly—enough time for Xiaoran to panic, for her fingers to tighten on his sleeves, for her heartbeat to become completely ridiculous. His lips met hers—warm, gentle, unhurried, like he wanted the moment to last. That made it worse. Zhou Yichen kissed exactly the way he loved her. Patiently. Carefully. Completely. Xiaoran melted, eyes closing, his hand resting light and steady at her waist. The city lights blurred behind them, music drifted from somewhere by the river, and for a few quiet seconds nothing else existed but him.

Then he kissed her again, a little deeper. Still gentle. Still controlled. But enough to make Xiaoran’s knees feel unreliable. He pulled back slowly, their foreheads almost touching, both of them breathing quieter now. Xiaoran immediately hid her face against his chest again. Total failure.

“…I can’t survive this birthday,” she mumbled.

Yichen laughed softly while holding her closer.

“You started it.”

“I was being affectionate.”

He smiled against her hair.

“Happy birthday, Xiaoran.”

Hearing him say it like that, still holding her by the glowing river, felt more special than every gift combined.

chapters.desc: Xiaoran wants to follow him to university. Yichen says no. Their first real fight about the future.
chapters.title: Somewhere Between Your Dream and Mine
chapters.epigraph: “Love isn’t following someone. It’s finding the place where both of you can grow.”
chapters.content:
The fight started because they both loved each other too much, which felt deeply unfair.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I said I can follow you.”

“And I said no.”

Lin Xiaoran stood in the empty classroom after school, glaring at Zhou Yichen. Outside, the evening sun stretched across the desks. Inside, it was war. University applications were real now. Painfully real. And the closer the deadlines got, the more careful Zhou Yichen became around her. Too careful. The kind of careful that got on Xiaoran’s nerves.

“I don’t understand why you’re acting difficult,” she complained.

“I’m not.”

“You literally ARE.”

“No, I’m thinking realistically.”

“And realistically,” Xiaoran crossed her arms stubbornly, “I can just apply wherever you go.”

Silence.

“No.”

Too fast. Too firm. Xiaoran’s chest tightened. That hurt more than she expected.

“…Why not.”

Yichen sighed and pressed his fingers to his temple. This conversation scared him too—more than basketball, more than entrance exams—because their future suddenly felt fragile in ways neither of them understood yet.

“Because I don’t want you choosing your future around me.”

“But you literally said you were considering MY applications.”

“That’s different.”

“How is that different?!”

Good question. Terrible question. The real answer was simple: Zhou Yichen trusted himself to give things up for her. He didn’t want her giving things up for him. Not this young. Not before she’d even figured herself out. Xiaoran looked upset now. Not dramatic upset. Hurt. Yichen immediately regretted his tone.

“I’m not saying I don’t want us together.”

“But that’s what it sounds like.”

“It’s not.”

“Then explain properly.”

For a moment, neither of them spoke. Somewhere outside, a basketball thudded against the court. Then Yichen sat down in one of the chairs by the window, tired and thoughtful. After a second, Xiaoran sat beside him. Still upset. But closer anyway. Always closer anyway.

“When I think about university,” Yichen admitted quietly, “I get scared too.”

Xiaoran blinked. Zhou Yichen almost never admitted to being afraid. Especially not this calmly. Then he continued—

“What if basketball stops working out. What if classes become too hard. What if we fight more. What if we grow differently.”

His voice was steady, but she could hear the uncertainty underneath. Her anger softened. He wasn’t pushing her away. He was scared of failing both their futures somehow.

“I don’t even know what dream I want yet,” she admitted.

It was embarrassing to admit. Everyone else seemed so sure—medicine, business, law, engineering. Xiaoran changed interests depending on her mood and whatever drama she was watching. Last month it was interior design. Before that, psychology. Before THAT, she’d nearly decided to open a café because the aesthetic felt healing.

“I just know I want you there.”

It made Yichen’s chest ache, because he wanted the same thing. More than anything. After a moment, he took her hand carefully between both of his.

“Okay,” he murmured. “Then let’s think about this differently.”

Xiaoran looked at him quietly.

“How.”

“We stop choosing FOR each other.”

Silence.

“And instead?”

“We choose somewhere both of us can grow.”

Not sacrifice. Not a painful compromise. Something gentler. Something shared. Then Yichen pulled a folded brochure from his bag. Xiaoran blinked in confusion.

“…What’s this.”

“A university halfway between our options.”

She looked down at it. A strong school. Good academics. A decent basketball program. Not the farthest, not the closest. Balanced. Then Xiaoran looked back up.

“You researched this already?”

“Hm.”

“When?”

“Last week.”

He really had been thinking about it seriously. Not avoiding it. Trying to solve it quietly on his own.

“You idiot,” she whispered.

“Hm.”

“You made me think we were breaking up.”

“We were discussing universities.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen laughed quietly under his breath.

“It doesn’t have to be this exact place.”

“But…”

“I just wanted us to find a middle ground together,” Yichen said.

That sentence fixed something in Xiaoran. Suddenly the future didn’t feel like losing or following. It felt shared—something they’d build slowly, together.

“What if we both get rejected.”

“We’ll cry. Then we apply somewhere else.”

“What if we become long distance anyway?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Then we try.”

He said it so simply. Not because life was simple, but because loving her wasn’t something he ever questioned first.

“I don’t care if we end up in different cities temporarily,” he admitted. “I just don’t want either of us regretting our choices later.”

Silence. Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder. Warm evening light filled the classroom, and for the first time in weeks, the future stopped feeling like something trying to pull them apart.

“You know what’s annoying?”

“Hm?”

“You sound mature today. It’s annoying.”

Yichen smiled slightly.

Meanwhile Xiaoran looked down at the brochure again before mumbling—

“…I like this school.”

Yichen’s fingers tightened gently around hers.

“Me too.”

Then after a second—very casually—

“If we go there together,” Xiaoran added thoughtfully, “you’ll still buy me snacks, right?”

Yichen looked deeply unimpressed.

“This is your priority?”

“Yes.”

“…Then yes.”

Immediate satisfaction.

“Okay.” Xiaoran nodded seriously. “Now I feel ready for adulthood.”

chapters.desc: The gaokao: two exam venues across the city, one fraction question, and a taxi that took thirty-one minutes.
chapters.title: Two Days in June
chapters.epigraph: “You always know the first step. Write that.”
chapters.content:
The night before the gaokao, Lin Xiaoran packed her exam bag four times. Admission ticket. ID card. Two black pens, two spare black pens, two pencils, an eraser shaped like a strawberry that she had been told was not technically allowed and was bringing anyway for morale. A clear plastic pencil case, because the rules said clear. A watch without a screen, because the rules said no screens. She unpacked it all, checked it, and packed it again.

At 9:30 her phone lit up.

Yichen: Stop repacking your bag.

Xiaoran: how do you know

Yichen: Because it’s 9:30.

Xiaoran: that’s not evidence

Yichen: Call me.

She called. He picked up on the first ring, sitting at his desk with his study glasses pushed up into his hair, a single lamp on behind him. He didn’t look nervous. He never looked nervous. It was one of the most irritating things about him.

“What if I forget how fractions work,” she said, instead of hello.

“You won’t.”

“They’re arrogant. I told you. They think they’re better than whole numbers.”

“You scored a hundred on the final.”

“That was a different me. That me had you sitting beside her for three weeks.”

He was quiet for a second.

“That me is still you,” he said. “I didn’t do the test.”

She pulled her knees up to her chest and didn’t answer, because there was a lump in her throat that had appeared out of nowhere. They weren’t even going to be in the same building tomorrow. The exam venues were assigned by student number: Xiaoran at the middle school on the east side, Yichen across the city near the river. She had looked it up on the map three times. Forty minutes by car.

“You’ll be fine,” he said.

“You can’t know that.”

“I know you.” Then, after a pause: “Go to sleep. Don’t look at notes.”

“I already put the notes away.”

“Where?”

“…Under my pillow.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She moved them to her desk while he watched, then lay down with the phone on the pillow beside her. Neither of them hung up. At some point she fell asleep listening to him turn pages, and when she woke at six the call had ended at 11:52 and there was one message.

Yichen: Eat breakfast. I’ll see you after math.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother drove her to the exam site herself. Mrs. Lin was not a soft woman. She was an accountant, and she approached the gaokao the way she approached the end of the tax year: with a checklist, a thermos, and no patience for nonsense. On the way she quizzed Xiaoran on the contents of her bag without once looking away from the road.

“Admission ticket.”

“Yes.”

“ID.”

“Yes.”

“Pens.”

“Four.”

“Why four?”

“In case three stop working.”

Her mother sighed through her nose, which in Mrs. Lin meant she was trying not to laugh. Xiaoran’s father had not come, because her father cried at things like this, and her mother had decided that crying outside an exam gate was bad for morale. Instead he had sent fourteen messages since six a.m., most of them stickers of cartoon rabbits holding banners. The street outside the school was already full. Parents three deep along the barrier. Police directing traffic. A row of mothers in red qipao for luck, a few fathers holding sunflowers. Someone had set up a tent handing out free water. When the gates opened, the students went in one by one past the ID check, and the parents stayed outside, holding thermoses, not talking much.

Before Xiaoran got out of the car, her mother reached over and straightened the collar of her shirt. It was the only soft thing she did all morning.

“Don’t leave anything blank,” Mrs. Lin said. “Even if you don’t know. Write something.”

“I know.”

“And don’t look at the clock every two minutes. You do that.”

“I don’t do that.”

Her mother just looked at her. Xiaoran got out of the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chinese in the morning was fine. Better than fine—the essay prompt was about a small thing that had changed how you saw someone, and Xiaoran wrote eight hundred words about a boy at an arcade who won a stuffed bunny out of a claw machine on the first try and then pretended it had been luck. She changed his name and the setting. She did not change the bunny. Math in the afternoon was a war.

She hit the first fraction question twenty minutes in and froze completely. Her mind went blank and white like a fresh page. The girl at the next desk was writing fast. The clock on the wall said 3:21. Don’t look at the clock every two minutes. She put her pen down. Closed her eyes for one breath. Then she heard it, absurdly clearly—a calm voice across a study table, three weeks before the final, pushing a sheet of paper back toward her: Slow down. You always know the first step. Write that.

She wrote the first step. Then the second. She didn’t finish every question. There was one near the end she only half understood, and she wrote everything she knew about it anyway, because her mother had said to, and because leaving it blank felt like giving up out loud. When the bell rang at five, her hand ached and her shirt was stuck to her back and she had no idea how it had gone.

She walked out into the sunlight with two hundred other students, and the crowd of parents outside surged against the barrier, and somewhere in the middle of all of it—Zhou Yichen was standing by the tent with the free water, holding a strawberry milk. Xiaoran stopped dead. He was not supposed to be here. His exam had ended at the same time as hers, forty minutes away, across the river.

“How,” she said, when she reached him.

“Taxi.”

“You can’t have—it’s forty minutes—”

“Thirty-one. The driver was motivated.” He put the strawberry milk in her hands and studied her face. “How was it?”

She opened her mouth to say terrible, and what came out instead was:

“I didn’t leave anything blank.”

Something in his expression went very soft.

“Good,” he said.

Behind him, Mrs. Lin was getting out of the car. She looked at Yichen. She looked at the strawberry milk. She looked at her daughter, who was very obviously about to cry in public. Then she got back in the car and waited, and for once didn’t honk.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second day passed in a blur of English and science, and by the time the last bell rang on the evening of the eighth, Xiaoran didn’t feel happy or sad or relieved. She just felt empty, like someone had carefully poured everything out of her and set her down.

That night the four of them met at the noodle shop near school, because none of them could think of anywhere better. Yuhao ate three bowls and announced he would never read a book again. Meilin, who had already worked out her expected score to within five points, refused to tell anyone the number. Xiaoran fell asleep against Yichen’s shoulder halfway through her noodles and woke up to Yuhao filming her.

Afterward, Yichen walked her home. The streets smelled like rain that hadn’t come yet.

“It’s done,” she said, at her building’s gate.

“Hm.”

“Whatever happens, it’s done.”

“It is.”

She looked up at him. He had come straight from his own exam, crossed a city in a taxi, and stood outside a school gate in June heat with a strawberry milk going warm in his hand. He had never once told her he was nervous for himself.

“Were you scared?” she asked. “Today?”

He thought about it honestly, which was one of the things she loved about him.

“During my exam, no,” he said. “Waiting outside your gate, a little.”

“Why?”

“Because if it went badly, you’d have walked out alone.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she hugged him, hard, right there at the gate, where her father could absolutely see from the fourth-floor window and was absolutely watching.

“Thank you for the taxi,” she mumbled into his shirt.

“Thank the driver.”

“I’m thanking you.”

He rested his chin on top of her head.

“Then you’re welcome,” he said. “Now go inside. Your dad is waving.”

chapters.desc: Applications are in, results are coming, and four friends are refreshing their portals in the same hour.
chapters.title: The Day Our Futures Arrived
chapters.epigraph: “Some futures arrive all at once.”
chapters.content:
Application season turned their whole class a little unhinged. Some students got motivational. Some got religious. Some got frighteningly competitive. Lin Xiaoran got dramatic. Naturally.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I think I’m going to faint.”

“You said that yesterday too.”

“This is a CONTINUOUS faint.”

Xiaoran was lying across the cafeteria table while Tang Meilin calmly worked through practice questions beside her. All around them, people were talking about applications—interviews, scholarships, majors, cities. The future was everywhere now, and it exhausted Xiaoran. She still couldn’t believe they were old enough for this. Then Zhou Yichen walked over with drinks—tall, calm, unfairly reliable-looking—and Xiaoran sat up a little, like a flower turning toward the sun. Embarrassing, honestly.

Yichen handed over her usual drink without a word and sat down beside her.

“You ate lunch?”

“Yes.”

“She ate fries,” Meilin corrected.

“Fries are a vegetable.”

“They are not,” Meilin said.

Yichen sighed, opened the lunchbox beside her, and put the chopsticks in her hand.

“Eat properly.”

Watching him do that without thinking made Xiaoran’s chest ache a little these days. University meant that one day, this wouldn’t happen every afternoon anymore. Yuhao dropped into the seat across from them.

“I’ve decided.”

“Hm?”

“If university life doesn’t give me romance, I’m suing society.”

Meilin didn’t even look up.

“You’d lose the case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After weeks of discussions, tears, arguments, and spiraling, Xiaoran and Yichen had finally chosen their universities. Together. Not sacrificing. Not blindly following. Together. Zhou Yichen applied mostly to universities with strong business programs and good basketball teams. Basketball mattered to him, but he thought realistically about the future too—something Xiaoran quietly admired, even if she teased him for being “too mature.” Xiaoran chose media and communication studies, which surprised nobody. Lin Xiaoran physically could not stop talking. But more than that, she loved stories, people, ideas. Even her random obsessions somehow fit.

When she told Yichen, he didn’t look surprised at all.

“You were always going to choose something people-related.”

“What does THAT mean.”

“You make strangers tell you their life stories in cafés.”

“That’s charisma.”

“That’s weird.”

Still, he smiled afterward—soft and proud—and that meant more than any compliment. In the end, they both applied to Huaining University in Shanghai: a respected school with strong programs and a competitive basketball team. Not the highest-ranked school Yichen could have chased. Not the closest, most comfortable option either. Just the place that felt right. The middle ground they’d found together. They both applied to backup schools too, because unlike romance dramas, real life required common sense.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then results day arrived, and peace died immediately.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I can’t open it.”

“You literally have to.”

“I’d rather disappear.”

Xiaoran sat frozen in Yichen’s bedroom, staring at her laptop like it might bite. Yichen sat beside her, much too calm.

“How are you not nervous?” she demanded.

“I am nervous.”

“No you’re not. Your face looks normal.”

“My heart rate is elevated.”

“That’s not normal.”

Across the room, Yuhao was pacing and Meilin had gone pale, because somehow all four of them were getting results within the same hour. Terrible planning by the universe. Yuhao screamed.

“I GOT IN.”

Immediate chaos. Meilin grabbed his laptop.

“YOU ACTUALLY DID.”

“I’M EDUCATED.”

Xiaoran’s anxiety went up about five hundred percent.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen reached over and squeezed her hand.

“Open it with me.”

It made breathing a little easier. Slowly, Xiaoran clicked into the portal. Loading. Loading. Loading—silence. Dead silence. Yichen leaned closer.

“What.”

Xiaoran blinked. Twice. Then she covered her mouth, because there it was. Admission confirmed. Huaining University. Media and Communication Studies. For a full second, she couldn’t process it.

“OH MY GOD.”

Screaming. Tears. Total collapse. Yichen caught her when she launched herself at him.

“I GOT IN.”

“I know.”

“YICHEN I GOT IN.”

His arms tightened around her while she nearly cried into his shoulder from relief. Then she froze. Wait.

“…Your results.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t check yours yet.”

Silence.

“Oh no.”

Now they were both nervous. Yuhao and Meilin watched like sports commentators.

“This relationship controls my blood pressure,” Yuhao whispered.

Then Yichen opened his own portal. Quiet room. One second. Two. Three— Accepted. Business Administration. Huaining University. Xiaoran started crying again.

“Why are you crying more than me?” Yichen laughed.

“BECAUSE THIS IS CINEMATIC.”

Xiaoran grabbed his face with both hands.

“We’re going together.”

“Hm.”

“ZHOU YICHEN WE’RE GOING TO UNIVERSITY TOGETHER.”

His eyes went soft at the happiness all over her face. And quietly—

“So we are.”

It felt bigger than anything. Suddenly the future wasn’t blurry anymore. Dorms. Classes. A new city. Adult life. Together. Xiaoran looked at him again.

“We survived.”

“Application season, yes.”

“No.” She smiled shakily through tears. “The future.”

And for the first time, Zhou Yichen let himself believe that maybe they really would make it there together.

chapters.desc: One summer gap, one campus in Shanghai, and a café they’ve already decided is theirs.
chapters.title: Practicing Our Future
chapters.epigraph: “Practice makes the future less frightening.”
chapters.content:
After results came out, something strange happened. Everyone suddenly had nothing to do. School was technically over, but graduation hadn’t happened yet, and university hadn’t started. They were stuck in a weird one-month gap where life felt paused. No uniforms. No exams. No schedules. Just waiting. Lin Xiaoran loved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“This feels wrong.”

They had taken the train into Shanghai for the day, and Xiaoran was walking beside Zhou Yichen near Huaining University’s main gate, iced coffee in hand. The summer air was warm and breezy, sunlight glinting off glass buildings and tree-lined paths. Students wandered past with laptops, skateboards, books. Adult-looking people. Terrifying, honestly.

Yichen glanced down at her. “What feels wrong?”

“We’re here without homework.”

“That’s called freedom.”

“I don’t trust it.”

It was their third unofficial “future practice date”: visiting the campus, exploring nearby streets, pretending they already belonged here. Xiaoran was enjoying it far more than she’d expected. The more familiar the campus became, the less frightening adulthood felt. Then she stopped walking.

“Oh.”

“What.”

Xiaoran pointed at a café across the road: floor-to-ceiling windows, warm lighting, bookshelves along the walls, soft music drifting outside. And, most importantly, cute desserts.

“That’s OUR café.”

Silence. Yichen followed her gaze.

“…You decided that in three seconds.”

“Yes.”

“Based on what criteria.”

“The vibe.”

“That’s not a system.”

Ten minutes later, they went in anyway, because Zhou Yichen indulged her too much.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside smelled like coffee and vanilla—warm, comfortable, very university. Students typed quietly on laptops while couples shared desserts by the windows. Xiaoran was immediately moved.

“Oh my god.”

“What now.”

“We’re becoming adults aesthetically.”

She grabbed a menu and sat down across from him.

“No matter what happens,” she announced seriously, “this is our meeting spot.”

“Hm.”

“After classes.”

“Hm.”

“If we fight, you still have to come here.”

“You’re planning future arguments already?”

“I’m realistic.”

Yichen watched her over the menu. Hearing her talk so easily about their future got to him more than he expected. Months ago, she’d cried over applications. Now she was casually planning which café they’d go to after lectures. Growth. Very cute growth.

“What if the drinks are bad?” Yichen asked.

Xiaoran froze. Oh. Good point.

“This relationship depends entirely on beverage quality.”

“Thought so.”

So, naturally, they ordered far too much: two drinks, three desserts, and a sandwich neither of them planned to share and both of them did. About fifteen minutes later, Xiaoran put both hands flat on the table.

“It’s perfect. The strawberry cake is perfect.”

Yichen looked around the café—sunlight through the windows, Xiaoran across from him talking happily about nothing—and the future suddenly felt very close. Real, not abstract anymore.

“You’re excited,” he observed.

Xiaoran blinked, then smiled a little.

“…I think I am.”

It made Yichen smile too. For weeks he’d worried that all the university talk only stressed her out. Now she looked genuinely happy imagining what came next. Xiaoran leaned forward.

“We should choose more places.”

“What places.”

“Important relationship infrastructure.”

“…Infrastructure.”

“Yes.”

So that was the rest of the afternoon: future practice.

✦ ✦ ✦

They started with a bookstore, where Xiaoran found the communication shelves and immediately started judging textbook covers.

“This one looks arrogant.”

“It’s a grammar book.”

“Exactly.”

Then Yichen dragged her to the sports center—huge courts, training rooms, bright indoor gyms. Watching him there made Xiaoran pause. He already fit here somehow. Tall under the university banners, confident, comfortable, like the future had been waiting for him. Then he turned around.

“What.”

Oops. Caught staring again.

“…Nothing.”

“You’re staring again.”

Then he reached over and fixed the twisted strap of her bag. A small, automatic thing. Xiaoran’s chest went painfully soft. Adulthood might change a lot of things, but she couldn’t imagine him ever stopping these tiny ways of caring.

“You know what’s weird? I used to think university would feel super romantic.”

“And now?”

“It mostly feels expensive.”

Yichen laughed quietly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, the sky turned orange above the campus while they sat by the lake behind the library, drinks half-finished beside them, a warm summer wind moving through the trees. Xiaoran rested her head on Yichen’s shoulder. Not dramatically, this time. Just comfortably. And after a moment—

“Do you think we’ll change a lot?”

Silence. Yichen looked out at the water.

“…Probably.”

“Oh.”

“But I don’t think that’s bad.”

Somewhere nearby, students were laughing.

“My mom said people change after university.”

“They do.”

“What if you become too cool for me.”

Yichen looked unimpressed.

“You ask strange questions.”

“I’m serious.”

“No matter what university does to me,” he said, “you’ll still be the first person I call when something happens.”

Xiaoran groaned into his shoulder.

“Why are you suddenly romantic again.”

“You started it.”

She looked around slowly—at the paths they’d walk, the café they’d chosen, the buildings waiting for them—and instead of scared, she felt warm. Like this future already held little pieces of them.

“We’re really growing up.”

“Hm.”

“Still,” Xiaoran added thoughtfully, “we should try every dessert here before the semester starts.”

“Obviously.”

chapters.desc: On graduation day, Lin Xiaoran accidentally asks Zhou Yichen to marry her. His answer is worse.
chapters.title: Yichen, Will You Marry Me?
chapters.epigraph: “Some questions are asked too early. Some answers are not.”
chapters.content:
Graduation day felt strange. Too loud. Too emotional. Too bright, somehow. The school grounds were full of students taking pictures while teachers pretended not to cry. Uniforms for the last time. Classrooms for the last time. High school ending quietly under the summer sun. Lin Xiaoran did not handle emotional transitions well.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Don’t cry before photos.”

“I’m NOT crying.”

“Your eyes say otherwise.”

Tang Meilin was fixing Xiaoran’s graduation ribbon while Xiaoran blinked through suspiciously shiny eyes. Nearby, Yuhao took about fifty group selfies nobody had asked for. Across the courtyard, Zhou Yichen was talking with a few teachers outside the basketball building. Tall in the afternoon sun. Calm. Steady. Still exactly Zhou Yichen, even today. And Xiaoran got emotional all over again. They had really survived high school. Meilin noticed her staring.

“…There she goes again.”

“What.”

“You’re doing the boyfriend-staring thing.”

Yuhao zoomed in with his phone camera.

“Look at her face.”

“DELETE THAT.”

“You look like a wife seeing her husband return from war.”

“That’s literally just graduation.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony was emotional chaos: teachers giving speeches, students crying, parents taking far too many photos, and one boy confessing publicly and getting rejected on the spot. A historic disaster. Xiaoran spent most of it leaning sleepily against Yichen, because it was too warm. At some point, without thinking, she found his hand under the sleeve of her gown, and his fingers closed around hers right away. Everything softened—the noise, the crowd, the fear of growing up—because Zhou Yichen still felt exactly the same beside her.

“We’re graduating.”

“Hm.”

“That sounds fake.”

“A little.”

“What if university secretly sucks.”

“We’ll survive.”

After the ceremony, everyone scattered across campus for photos—classrooms, hallways, the basketball courts, the old staircase behind the library. Ordinary places turning into memories much too fast. Xiaoran and Yichen walked slowly along the empty sports field as the evening light turned gold, their gowns loose around their shoulders, a warm wind moving through the trees. Then Xiaoran stopped walking. Yichen looked back at her.

She looked at him for a second. He looked really handsome today. Not just physically. Older, maybe. More certain. Like the future already suited him. And before her brain caught up—

“Will you marry me?”

Silence. Even the wind seemed to go quiet. That had come out WAY too naturally. Xiaoran froze.

“…Wait.”

Zhou Yichen was looking at her very calmly. Not shocked, exactly. Just deeply focused.

“Is this a proposal.”

“No.”

“You asked me to marry you.”

“I didn’t mean NOW.”

“Hm.”

“Oh my god.”

Xiaoran covered her face. What kind of graduation sentence was that?

“I meant… someday. Maybe. In theory.”

“That clarified nothing.”

And, very unfortunately, Yuhao and Meilin showed up at exactly the wrong moment.

“What clarified nothing?” Yuhao asked immediately.

Dead silence. Xiaoran’s survival instincts kicked in.

“NOTHING.”

Too late. Yichen turned to them calmly.

“Xiaoran asked me to marry her.”

“WHAT?!” Yuhao yelled.

“LIN XIAORAN,” Meilin said.

“YOU PROPOSED BEFORE UNIVERSITY STARTED?” Yuhao went on.

Xiaoran slumped against the fence in embarrassment.

“I HATE EVERYONE.”

Yuhao looked revived.

“This graduation just became incredible.”

Meilin stared at Xiaoran in disappointment.

“You couldn’t even wait until adulthood.”

“It wasn’t serious!”

Then Yichen said quietly—

“I’d say yes though.”

Everyone froze, Xiaoran included. Slowly, she turned to him.

“…What.”

Yichen looked completely, suspiciously calm.

“If you asked seriously later,” he continued casually, “I’d probably say yes.”

Yuhao screamed loud enough to scare the birds out of the trees. Meilin grabbed Xiaoran’s arm before she could slide down the fence. Xiaoran stared at Yichen like he had personally destroyed her future.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“What.”

“YOU CAN’T SAY THINGS LIKE THAT CASUALLY.”

“You proposed first.”

“I WAS JOKING.”

“Hm.”

That hm again—the terrible, calm hm that meant he was secretly enjoying this. Yichen reached over and straightened her crooked graduation ribbon. Small. Careful. Somehow it felt more intimate than the entire accidental proposal.

“Still,” he murmured, “you’d look good marrying me.”

Xiaoran covered her face again while Meilin nearly collapsed laughing beside her.

“This relationship is ridiculous,” Meilin declared.

Yuhao wiped away fake tears.

“Young love survived graduation.”

And while Xiaoran malfunctioned beside him, Zhou Yichen smiled quietly at the sunset-lit campus. The future didn’t feel far away at all anymore.

chapters.desc: The graduation-day question, from the side of the boy who heard it.
chapters.title: Will You Marry Me? — Zhou Yichen’s Side
chapters.epigraph: “He stayed calm on the outside. He always did.”
chapters.content:
The problem with loving Lin Xiaoran for this long was that she said terrifying things casually and expected him to survive them normally. Which was impossible.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Will you marry me?”

For one second, Zhou Yichen forgot how to breathe. Not visibly. Never visibly. Years of basketball, exams, responsibility, and Xiaoran’s personality had trained him to stay calm on the outside. Inside, it was a complete disaster. It came so suddenly. So naturally. Like she really could imagine a future with him that far ahead. Marriage. Her. Him. Together. The picture hit his chest before logic could, and his heart reacted first. Fast. Much too fast.

He looked at her in the evening light—her gown, her hair moving in the wind, her eyes still wide from realizing what she’d said. She looked younger and older at the same time. Still his dramatic Xiaoran. But not just a high school girl anymore. Someone standing at the edge of adulthood with him. His heart beat even harder. Because the first thing he wanted to do wasn’t laugh, or tease her. He wanted to pull her close. He wanted to hear her ask again, properly. He wanted to kiss her stupid forehead and ask—

“Do you even understand what you just said to me?”

But he didn’t, because Lin Xiaoran would combust on the spot. So he stayed calm. He always stayed calm first.

“Hm,” he answered quietly. “Is this a proposal?”

Outwardly relaxed. Inwardly, not even slightly. Because part of him wished it was real. That surprised him. Not because marriage sounded impossible—but because with Xiaoran, he could imagine it far too easily.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran panicked.

“No. I didn’t mean NOW.”

Yichen watched her—the flustered face, the embarrassed eyes, the way she wouldn’t look at him when she was overwhelmed. His chest tightened. This girl trusted him with her future so naturally already. Even as a joke.

Then Yuhao and Meilin arrived and chaos broke out. Yichen barely heard half of it. His mind was stuck on one thing. Will you marry me? Such a ridiculous sentence. Such a dangerous one. Especially today, when the future had suddenly become real. Then Xiaoran shouted—

“It wasn’t serious!”

Yichen looked at her, and before he could think too carefully—

“I’d say yes though.”

Silence. The moment he said it, he knew he meant it. Completely. Not joking. Not half-joking. That scared him a little. Zhou Yichen wasn’t impulsive. He thought things through. Planned. Protected. But with Xiaoran, the truth sometimes got out before he could stop it. And the truth was simple: if Lin Xiaoran ever seriously asked him someday, he could not imagine saying no. Xiaoran looked at him in total horror.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

His heart sped up again. She looked devastatingly cute when she was flustered, especially with the graduation sunlight on her face.

“You can’t say things like that casually.”

Yichen almost smiled. The irony was unbelievable. This girl had accidentally proposed first—and now SHE was overwhelmed? But instead of teasing her, he looked at her for another second. Really looked. At the girl who cried easily. Who got lost constantly. Who annoyed him every day. Who loved him loudly without realizing how deeply. And a frighteningly soft thought settled in his chest: I really could spend my whole life with her.

It didn’t feel dramatic. It felt calm. Certain. Like something he’d known for a long time. Then Xiaoran complained weakly—

“I was joking.”

Yichen stepped closer and straightened her crooked graduation ribbon, slow and careful—something to do with his hands so she wouldn’t notice his heart still hadn’t calmed down. If he held her hand right now, he might not want to let go.

“You’d look good marrying me.”

There it was again—the tiny sharp breath, the flustered face, the look of someone who couldn’t decide whether to hit him or hug him. Yichen finally smiled to himself. Maybe she didn’t know yet. Maybe she really had been joking. But Zhou Yichen knew one thing very clearly now: someday, if Lin Xiaoran ever asked him again for real, he would probably say yes before she finished the sentence.

chapters.desc: Tang Meilin has been hiding something for three months. Lin Xiaoran is a professional investigator.
chapters.title: Tang Meilin Had a Boyfriend?!
chapters.epigraph: “The quiet ones always have the best secrets.”
chapters.content:
They found out by accident, which somehow made it worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Wait.”

Lin Xiaoran lowered her spoon and narrowed her eyes across the café table. It was one of their usual summer-break afternoons. Normal. Peaceful. Until—

“Why are you smiling at your phone.”

Tang Meilin froze for half a second. Almost invisible. Unfortunately, Lin Xiaoran was a professional at detecting suspicious behavior.

“…I always smile.”

“No you don’t.”

“She literally doesn’t,” Yuhao added.

Meilin glared at both of them. Xiaoran leaned forward.

“WHO IS IT.”

“There’s no one.”

“You looked happy. You’re never happy.”

Yichen sipped his drink and watched. When Xiaoran went into investigation mode, survival rates dropped sharply. Meilin’s phone buzzed again, and Xiaoran saw the preview. [Did you eat already?]

“OH MY GOD.”

Several customers looked over. Yuhao nearly choked on his drink. Meilin looked like she wanted to disappear.

“Lower your voice.”

“YOU HAVE A BOYFRIEND?”

“No.”

“Then why does someone text like a husband.”

“Maybe they’re polite.”

“NO ONE SAYS ‘did you eat already’ POLITELY.”

Even Yichen looked mildly interested now.
