“…Who is it.”

Meilin stared at all three of them with betrayal.

“This is why I keep secrets.”

“You kept THIS secret?” Xiaoran gasped dramatically. “From ME?”

“Yes.”

“Betrayal.”

Yuhao nodded seriously.

“She’s right.”

“You’re both insane.”

Another notification appeared: [Call me later.] And under it, a heart emoji. Silence. Xiaoran grabbed Meilin’s arm.

“TANG MEILIN.”

“STOP SHAKING ME.”

Even Yichen was smiling now—a small, rare smile—which only encouraged Xiaoran.

“How long has this been happening?!”

“…Three months.”

“THREE MONTHS?!”

Yuhao looked genuinely wounded.

“You hid a whole man.”

“It wasn’t serious yet.”

“THERE ARE HEART EMOJIS.”

Meilin finally sighed and put her phone down. Escape was impossible.

“Fine.”

All three of them leaned in. Nosy vultures.

“We met during volunteer tutoring last semester.”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“THAT quiet guy?”

“Hm.”

“The tall one with glasses?”

“Hm.”

“The one who looked like he paid taxes already?”

“…That description feels disrespectful.”

Yuhao snapped his fingers. “Wait, I know him. Shen Zixu, right?”

Meilin nodded once. Xiaoran stared. Tang Meilin—the stable one, the friend who judged everyone else’s romantic decisions—had secretly been dating someone for THREE MONTHS. This was historically significant.

“You held hands before telling us?”

Meilin looked exhausted.

“Yes.”

“Kissed?”

“Xiaoran.”

“ANSWER THE COURT.”

Yichen covered his mouth, very clearly hiding a laugh. Traitor boyfriend. Then Meilin crossed her arms defensively.

“At least I’m normal about relationships.”

Silence. Then all three looked at her together.

“…What.”

“You hid a whole boyfriend for three months,” Yuhao said. “That’s not normal.”

Meilin glared harder.

“At least I don’t ask people if they’d still love me as capybaras.”

Xiaoran immediately pointed at Yichen.

“He answered yes.”

“That’s not helping your case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Once Xiaoran had information, she was impossible. The interrogation went on for TWO HOURS.

“How did he confess.”

“He didn’t.”

Dead silence.

“What.”

“I confessed first.”

Even Yichen looked surprised. That didn’t sound like Meilin at all. Meilin looked down at her drink and mumbled—

“I got tired waiting.”

The mood at the table softened. That sounded unexpectedly sincere. Xiaoran blinked.

“…That’s kinda romantic.”

“Hm.”

“What did you say exactly?”

Meilin immediately looked horrified.

“No.”

“PLEASE.”

“No.”

“MEILIN PLEASE I RAISED YOU.”

“You absolutely did not.”

Three against one was impossible. After several minutes of suffering, Meilin gave up.

“I said…” She paused briefly. “‘If you keep looking at me like that, eventually I’m going to misunderstand things.’”

Xiaoran slammed both hands on the table.

“THAT’S SO GOOD.”

Even Yichen looked impressed—one small nod, which from him was high praise. Meilin covered her face.

“I hate all of you.”

Yuhao looked deeply emotional.

“Why is everyone around me accidentally romantic.”

Meilin’s phone rang. [Shen Zixu calling] All three of them turned to look at her. Meilin stared back with visible regret.

“…Don’t make this weird.”

“No promises,” Xiaoran whispered immediately.

With the face of someone deeply unfortunate, Tang Meilin answered. And instantly, her voice softened. Just a little. But enough. Enough that Xiaoran gasped again.

“Oh my god she likes him FOR REAL.”

“XIAORAN.”

Beside her, Zhou Yichen laughed quietly into his drink while Xiaoran glowed with pure gossip happiness.

chapters.desc: A tiny studio in Shanghai, four flights of stairs, and Lin Xiaoran’s mother has questions for Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: Moving Day Comes With Parents
chapters.epigraph: “Check twice. She lies the first time.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had met Zhou Yichen’s parents three times. Zhou Yichen had met hers exactly once, for forty seconds, outside an exam gate, while holding a strawberry milk. Moving day was going to fix that whether anyone was ready or not.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was packed so full that Xiaoran rode the whole way to Shanghai with a lamp across her knees and a rice cooker wedged against her ankles. Her father drove. Her mother sat in the passenger seat with a printed list titled MOVING — XIAORAN, ticking things off whenever they passed a toll gate, as if the items might escape between cities.

“Bedding.”

“In the back.”

“Winter coat.”

“It’s August.”

“Winter coat.”

“…In the back.”

“Medicine box.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. Her mother turned around in her seat.

“I’ll buy medicine there,” Xiaoran said.

“You won’t. You never do.” Mrs. Lin turned back to the list and made a small, decisive mark. “There’s a box in the blue bag. Cold medicine, fever patches, stomach tablets. Don’t get sick. There’s nobody there to look after you.”

“Yichen’s there,” her father offered from the driver’s seat.

There was a short silence in the front of the car.

“Hm,” said her mother.

Xiaoran stared out of the window and decided not to think about what that hm meant.

✦ ✦ ✦

The apartment was a tiny studio ten minutes’ walk from campus, on the fourth floor of a building with a broken elevator. Her parents had rented it after a long, quiet argument about whether a girl who got lost walking to the bakery should be living somewhere with a kitchen. Her father had won, mostly by crying. Zhou Yichen was waiting at the bottom of the stairs. He’d moved into his own place across the road the week before, and he had clearly been standing there for a while, because there was a stack of flattened boxes by his feet and a roll of packing tape on his wrist like a bracelet. He was wearing a plain white T-shirt and, for the first time Xiaoran could remember, looked slightly nervous.

“Uncle. Auntie.” He bowed. “I can carry things.”

Her father beamed at him like a man meeting a long-lost son. Her mother looked him up and down once, the way she looked at a receipt that might contain an error.

“You’re the one with the taxi,” Mrs. Lin said.

“Yes, Auntie.”

“Thirty-one minutes.”

“Yes.”

“That’s dangerous driving.”

“…I didn’t drive, Auntie.”

“Hm,” said her mother, and handed him the heaviest box.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took two hours and eleven trips up four flights of stairs. Yichen carried the mattress, the desk, the bookshelf in pieces, and both suitcases, and assembled the bookshelf while her father read the instructions aloud in a dramatic voice and got every step slightly wrong. Xiaoran was put in charge of “arranging things,” which mostly meant sitting on the floor opening boxes and getting emotional about her old pencil case.

Her mother watched all of it from the doorway. She watched Yichen put the bookshelf together and then quietly redo one shelf her father had installed upside down, without saying anything about it. She watched him check the window locks. She watched him open the tiny fridge, look inside, close it, and leave—and come back fifteen minutes later with a bag from the convenience store downstairs: eggs, bread, bottled water, and six strawberry milks, which he lined up on the top shelf, labels facing out.

Mrs. Lin’s eyebrows went up by exactly one millimeter. Xiaoran saw it, and nearly dropped the pencil case.

✦ ✦ ✦

They took a break when the last box was in. Her father went to find the building manager about the elevator and came back forty minutes later having become best friends with him. Xiaoran’s cousin Lin Jun sent a message that just said is he there? is your mom interrogating him? send video, and Xiaoran turned her phone face down. Her mother sat on the only chair. Yichen sat on the floor because there was nowhere else. Xiaoran sat on the bed between them and wanted to evaporate.

“Do you cook?” Mrs. Lin asked.

“A little, Auntie.”

“She doesn’t.”

“I know.”

“MOM.”

“She’ll eat instant noodles for a week and call it independence.”

“I’ll make sure she doesn’t.”

“She’ll stay up until three and say she’s ‘nearly done.’”

“She does that now.”

“I’m RIGHT HERE,” Xiaoran said.

Her mother ignored her, which was a skill she had perfected over eighteen years. “Business,” she said to Yichen. “Not sports.”

He didn’t look surprised that she knew. “Business. I’ll still play.”

“Why business?”

Xiaoran held her breath. She knew why. She had been in the empty classroom where he’d explained it—the options that kept them in the same city, the future he’d refused to choose without her. If he said any of that to her mother, Mrs. Lin would decide he was either a saint or a lunatic, and Xiaoran honestly didn’t know which would be worse. Yichen thought about it for a moment.

“Because basketball is something I love,” he said. “I don’t want it to be the only thing I’m allowed to be.”

Her mother looked at him for a long second. Then she turned to Xiaoran.

“He talks better than you.”

“EVERYONE talks better than me, I’m in MEDIA, that’s why I’m STUDYING—”

Yichen ducked his head. Xiaoran was almost certain he was laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time her parents had to leave, the sun was going down over the roofs and the apartment looked like a place someone could actually live. Her old bunny sat on the bookshelf. The lamp from the car was on the desk. The strawberry milks were still lined up in the fridge like soldiers. Her father cried, as predicted. He hugged Xiaoran for a very long time and then, to everyone’s surprise, hugged Yichen too, and pressed a folded printout into his hand.

“Campus map,” he said thickly. “I highlighted the routes. She’ll lose her own copy.”

“I will NOT—”

“You lost the last three,” her mother said.

Her father went down to start the car, blowing his nose. Xiaoran stood in the doorway of her new apartment and felt, all at once, how far away home was going to be. Her mother picked up her handbag. At the top of the stairs she stopped, turned, and looked not at Xiaoran but at Yichen, who was standing a step behind her.

“She’ll tell you she’s fine,” Mrs. Lin said, “when she isn’t. Especially when she’s sick.”

Yichen straightened a little.

“She learned that from me,” her mother added. “It’s not a good habit.”

For a moment, nobody said anything. Xiaoran had never once heard her mother admit that anything about herself was not a good habit.

“I’ll check on her,” Yichen said.

“Check twice. She lies the first time.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

Her mother nodded, once, the way she approved a balanced account. Then she reached up and straightened Xiaoran’s collar—the same small, brisk movement from outside the exam gate—and went down the stairs without looking back, because Mrs. Lin did not do emotional goodbyes in stairwells. Xiaoran waited until she heard the car pull away. Then she turned around.

“What,” she said, “was THAT.”

Yichen was looking at the stairs with an expression she couldn’t quite read.

“I think,” he said slowly, “your mom likes me.”

“She called you dangerous.”

“And then she gave me instructions.” He looked down at the campus map in his hand, every route highlighted in her father’s careful yellow. “That’s what my mom did, too. With you.”

Xiaoran opened her mouth to argue, remembered Mrs. Zhou thanking her across a dinner table for making her son lighter, and closed it again. She went back inside, opened the fridge, and took out a strawberry milk. Then she took out a second one and handed it to him.

“Housewarming,” she said.

“It’s your housewarming. I bought these.”

“Then it’s a thank-you.”

He took it. They sat on the floor of her tiny apartment with their backs against the bed, drinking strawberry milk, while the city lit up outside a window that didn’t have curtains yet.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“If I get sick and say I’m fine—”

“I’ll check twice.”

She leaned her head against his shoulder.

“Okay,” she said. “Good.”

chapters.desc: Orientation day, a phone on silent, and the first time in months Zhou Yichen is genuinely angry.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Was Actually Angry
chapters.epigraph: “Calm people don’t worry less. They just hide it better.”
chapters.content:
University orientation should have been exciting. New campus. New people. New beginning. Instead, Lin Xiaoran accidentally made Zhou Yichen genuinely angry for the first time in months, and it was horrifying.

✦ ✦ ✦

Morning sunlight spilled across the enormous campus while freshmen flooded every path, clutching orientation folders and confusion. Excited voices. Club booths. Seniors aggressively recruiting. Lin Xiaoran clung to Zhou Yichen’s sleeve like a lost child in a shopping mall.

“This place is too big.”

“You said that six times already.”

“Because it keeps being true.”

Yichen looked down at her and straightened the strap of her bag. The business faculty was gathering in the central building. The Media and Communication hall was on the opposite side of campus. Very far. And Lin Xiaoran’s sense of direction was still catastrophic. So, naturally, he walked her there first.

“Your orientation starts earlier than mine anyway,” he said calmly.

Xiaoran looked pleased.

“You love me too much.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The media building was chaos: energetic seniors, cameras on display, posters everywhere, students already networking loudly thirty minutes into orientation. Xiaoran hid slightly behind Yichen, observing suspiciously.

“…Everyone here talks so much.”

“You’re literally majoring here.”

“That’s future Xiaoran’s problem.”

Yichen almost smiled. A male senior came up to them, all enthusiasm.

“Freshman?”

Xiaoran pointed at herself weakly.

“Unfortunately.”

The senior laughed. Friendly, tall, and far too socially confident for Xiaoran’s comfort.

“Well, welcome to Media! Orientation hall is upstairs.”

“Thank you,” Yichen said politely.

The senior glanced between them.

“Ohhh. Boyfriend?”

Before Xiaoran could answer, Yichen did.

“Yes.”

Just like that, so certain. It still made Xiaoran’s chest warm every time. After helping her find a seat, Yichen sighed.

“You’ll survive now.”

Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve tighter.

“No.”

“You have orientation.”

“You can skip.”

“I’m class representative.”

“Oh right. Tragic.”

Yichen laughed and flicked her forehead.

“Text me if you get lost.”

“I WILL.”

“Calm messages only.”

“No promises.”

Before he left, he leaned down. “Good luck, Xiaoran.” And, very naturally, he kissed her forehead. Quick and gentle. Then he walked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The problem started about two hours later, because Lin Xiaoran got bored. The speeches dragged on forever. The ice-breakers were humiliating. One girl had already introduced herself as “China’s next visionary director.” Terrifying. At the break, the same senior came over again.

“Lin Xiaoran, right?”

“Oh.”

“Having fun?”

“No.”

He laughed. “You’re honest.”

His name was Gu Ming, a third-year media student. Very outgoing. Very friendly. Very… media major. And he kept talking. Not flirting, exactly—just naturally social. Xiaoran, completely oblivious, complained about the orientation schedule.

“Wait,” Gu Ming laughed suddenly. “You’re actually funny.”

“Thank you. I’m suffering constantly.”

At that exact moment, someone said her name quietly behind her.

“Xiaoran.”

Silence. The second she heard that voice, her survival instincts kicked in. Zhou Yichen sounded much too calm. Xiaoran spun around. There he was, business faculty orientation tag still on, one hand in his pocket, expression unreadable. But his eyes were colder than usual. Uh oh. Xiaoran blinked.

“…Why are you here?”

“I texted you.”

Silence. Her phone was in her bag. On silent. Twenty-three unread messages. Oh no. Gu Ming smiled casually.

“Oh, boyfriend’s here.”

Yichen nodded politely, but his eyes were already back on Xiaoran. Focused. Much too quiet.

“I’ve been looking for you.”

Xiaoran’s stomach dropped. Zhou Yichen never sounded like this. Gu Ming finally noticed the atmosphere.

“…I should go.”

The second he was gone, the silence got heavy.

“Why didn’t you answer your phone.”

“I forgot—”

“You disappeared from your orientation group.”

“…Oh.”

“I checked the media hall. You weren’t there.”

Okay. Now she understood. Yichen thought she’d gotten lost. Again.

“I was just downstairs…”

“You couldn’t send one message?”

Silence. His voice stayed controlled. Not loud. Not harsh. Somehow that was worse. Zhou Yichen almost never got genuinely upset with her. Usually he sighed, teased her, gave in eventually. Now he looked actually frustrated.

“I was worried.”

The words hit hard, and suddenly Xiaoran felt guilty. The campus really was huge, and Yichen knew exactly how easily she got lost.

“…Sorry.”

But Yichen still looked upset. Not dramatic anger. Real anger, the kind that came from worry. Then he noticed something else.

“Who was that senior.”

“Oh, Gu Ming?”

“You seem comfortable with him already.”

Now Xiaoran realized something else too. Zhou Yichen was jealous. Just a little. But definitely. And that made it worse, because she suddenly saw it from his side: she’d ignored his messages while laughing downstairs with another guy. That looked terrible.

“He was just helping me earlier.”

Yichen didn’t say anything. Calm on the outside. But Xiaoran knew him well enough by now: his jaw tightened when he was holding something back. Right now, it was very tight.

“You could’ve told me first before disappearing.”

There it was again—anger that came from worry, from caring too much. The guilt stabbed harder.

“I’m sorry…”

But Yichen just sighed and looked away, and that small thing made her stomach drop. He was REALLY upset. Xiaoran grabbed his hand. Yichen looked back.

“I forgot because orientation was annoying,” she admitted weakly. “And he kept talking and I didn’t think properly. I didn’t mean to make you worried.”

The frustration drained out of Yichen at how small her voice had gone. He hated being upset with her, especially when she already looked so guilty.

“…You scared me.”

That broke whatever tension was left. Zhou Yichen almost never admitted to being vulnerable. But he sounded honest. Tired. And Xiaoran wanted to hug him. So she did, right there outside the media building. She wrapped her arms around him and buried her face in his chest.

“I’m sorry,” she mumbled again softly.

Yichen let out a breath above her head. Still a little upset. Mostly relieved. After a few seconds, his arms came around her waist. Then, into her hair—

“You’re exhausting.”

“I know.”

“You need a tracking device.”

“That sounds unethical.”

“Hm.”

Finally, Yichen smiled a little. Just enough. Xiaoran relaxed against him.

“You smiled,” she whispered. “That means you forgive me.”

“It means I’m slightly less mad.”

“Oh.”

“But mostly,” he admitted, smoothing down her messy hair, “I’m relieved you didn’t vanish into the media building forever.”

Then, after a pause, very quietly—

“And I didn’t like seeing another guy make you laugh that much.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“…Wait.”

Yichen looked away. Too late.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“What.”

“You were jealous.”

“No.”

Despite everything, Xiaoran smiled—brightly this time. Seeing calm, perfect Zhou Yichen get a little jealous over her was dangerously cute. She kept smiling at him like she’d won something, completely unaware. Zhou Yichen looked at her for a long second, then let out a breath, the last of the tension leaving his shoulders.

“…You really don’t get it.”

“Hm?” Xiaoran tilted her head.

That small sound, that innocent face—that was exactly the problem. Yichen looked away for a moment, like he was gathering something he usually kept locked away. Then he stepped closer. Not angry now. Just honest. His voice low.

“If you knew what I was actually thinking,” he said softly, “you wouldn’t be standing here smiling like that.”

Something shifted. Even the campus noise behind them seemed farther away. Xiaoran blinked.

“…What do you mean?”

Yichen looked at her again, and this time there was no teasing in it. Just something dangerously sincere.

“You think I was just worried about you getting lost. That’s not all.”

Xiaoran’s heart did something strange.

“…Then what else?”

For the first time, Yichen hesitated. Just for a second. Then he said it anyway—low, controlled, almost like admitting defeat.

“I’ve already become a bit obsessed with you.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…Huh?”

Yichen sighed faintly, almost like he regretted saying it out loud, but didn’t take it back.

“You talk too much. You disappear too easily. You smile at people too casually. And I don’t like it.”

Xiaoran stared at him, completely red now.

“Zhou Yichen…”

But he kept going, calmer now, heavier underneath.

“You think I get jealous easily? I’m just better at hiding it.”

Then he reached out and tapped her forehead, the way he always did. But his voice didn’t match.

“…So don’t act clueless. If you actually understood how I feel, it would scare you.”

Then he turned, like he meant to leave before he said anything worse. Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve. And this time, Zhou Yichen didn’t pull away.

chapters.desc: A new university, new friends, and one festival crowd that swallows Lin Xiaoran whole.
chapters.title: Lost Inside the Crowd
chapters.epigraph: “New places change a lot of things. Not who comes looking for you.”
chapters.content:
University changed things quietly. Not dramatically. Not painfully. Just differently. Tang Meilin was at another university across the city. Chen Yuhao had vanished into engineering somewhere else. And for the first time in years, Lin Xiaoran had to build a life without her usual people beside her. It felt strange.

✦ ✦ ✦

Luckily, media students were very social creatures. Within two weeks, Xiaoran had somehow made new friends: Luo Jiayi—talkative, fashion-obsessed, emotionally chaotic—and Sun Ning, quiet but secretly savage. The three of them got close fast, mostly because Xiaoran attracted extroverts like a confused stray cat. Right now, the three of them were wandering through the university cultural festival, crowds flooding every walkway—music, club booths, food stalls, people everywhere. An actual sea of humans. Xiaoran already looked overwhelmed.

“There are too many people.”

“You say that every five minutes,” Jiayi replied while drinking lemonade.

“Because humanity keeps increasing.”

Ning laughed quietly beside them. Then a dance club performance started nearby, and half the crowd surged forward. Within seconds, Xiaoran had lost both of her friends.

“Oh.”

She blinked, surrounded by strangers.

“…Oh no.”

This was Lin Xiaoran’s greatest weakness: crowds, directions, human traffic. A deadly combination. She grabbed her phone.

Xiaoran: Busy?

Yichen: In a meeting.

Yichen: What happened.

Of course he could tell something had happened.

Xiaoran: I got covered by humans.

Silence.

Yichen: …What?

Xiaoran: I lost Jiayi and Ning.

Yichen: Location.

Xiaoran: Emotionally uncertain.

Yichen: Lin Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Wait.

She looked around desperately. Food stalls. Stage lights. Far too many students. One terrifying mascot costume.

Xiaoran: There’s a giant dancing shrimp nearby.

Yichen: Stay there.

Two words, and her anxiety dropped a little.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across campus, Zhou Yichen closed his business project file. His groupmate frowned.

“Where are you going?”

“Emergency.”

“What kind of emergency.”

“Xiaoran got lost.”

Silence. Another groupmate blinked.

“…Again?”

Yichen grabbed his jacket.

“She’s surrounded by crowds.”

“Oh.”

Everyone close to Zhou Yichen already knew: Lin Xiaoran plus directions equaled disaster.

✦ ✦ ✦

Back at the festival, things got worse. The crowd pushed harder toward the stage. People squeezed past, voices too loud, movement everywhere. And Xiaoran was tiny. Completely swallowed by university students. Someone bumped her shoulder. Another group shoved past. And for the first time since university started, Xiaoran felt a little alone. A little overwhelmed. Meilin wasn’t here. Yuhao wasn’t nearby yelling nonsense. And Yichen belonged to another faculty now—different buildings, different schedules, a different university life. The realization landed strangely in her chest. Her fingers tightened around her phone.

Then a familiar hand caught her wrist. Warm. Steady. Instantly recognizable.

“You really survive university through pure luck.”

Relief crashed over her. She spun around so fast she nearly hit his chest.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Yichen looked down at her, still a little out of breath from crossing campus, his faculty ID hanging from his neck, hoodie sleeves pushed up. Seeing him appear out of the crowd like that was unfairly comforting. Without thinking, Xiaoran grabbed his arm with both hands. Yichen glanced down.

“Scared?”

“…A little.”

His face softened. Then he drew her closer to his side, shielding her from the people pushing past without even thinking about it. Xiaoran finally breathed properly again.

“My new friends disappeared.”

“I know.”

“You replied too fast.”

“You texted like you were in danger.”

“That’s because I WAS.”

Yichen almost smiled.

Then something occurred to Xiaoran, and she looked up at him.

“…Weren’t you busy?”

“I was.”

“You left because I got lost?”

“Hm.”

Silence.

“…Your meeting?”

“They’ll survive.”

Xiaoran stared at him—the boy who had walked out of a group meeting because she sounded overwhelmed over text—and her chest went painfully soft. University had changed a lot of things. New people. New schedules. New places. But Zhou Yichen still came first when she needed him.

“Your business friends probably think I’m ridiculous.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“You are ridiculous.”

“…Wow.”

“But,” he added, adjusting her grip on his sleeve so she wouldn’t get bumped, “they also know you matter to me.”

Somewhere nearby, Jiayi screamed—

“XIAORAN—”

A few seconds later, both girls pushed through the crowd.

“Oh thank god,” Jiayi gasped. “We lost you for ten minutes.”

“I entered survival mode,” Xiaoran replied seriously.

Then Jiayi noticed Zhou Yichen beside her, and understood everything.

“Ohhh.”

Ning looked deeply unsurprised.

“So this is the boyfriend.”

Yichen nodded politely once. Before Xiaoran could recover, Jiayi whispered loudly—

“He came all the way here because she got lost?”

Xiaoran’s ears went pink. Yichen stayed perfectly calm.

“She said she got covered by humans.”

Jiayi stared.

“…That’s the emergency text?”

“Yes.”

Instead of laughing, Jiayi suddenly looked moved.

“That’s actually really romantic.”

“It’s NOT,” Xiaoran protested immediately.

Nobody believed her—especially not when Zhou Yichen kept one hand around her wrist the entire walk afterward, like he had already decided this girl was absolutely not getting lost again today.

chapters.desc: Xiaoran insists on apologizing to Yichen’s study group—and learns a few things she was never supposed to know.
chapters.title: Lost Inside the Crowd (Part 2)
chapters.epigraph: “Everyone knew. She was the last to find out.”
chapters.content:
The moment Luo Jiayi realized Zhou Yichen had run across campus because Xiaoran got “covered by humans,” she decided two things. One: their relationship was disgustingly cute. Two: she and Sun Ning needed to disappear immediately.

✦ ✦ ✦

The four of them walked through the festival while Xiaoran stayed attached to Yichen’s sleeve like a traumatized child. Jiayi kept secretly watching them—the way Yichen slowed down for Xiaoran without thinking, the way she leaned toward him whenever the crowd got loud, the way his hand stayed around her wrist the whole time. Finally, Jiayi slapped Ning’s shoulder.

“Oh my god.”

Ning looked exhausted already. “What now.”

“I suddenly remembered we have somewhere to be.”

“We absolutely do not.”

“We do now.”

Xiaoran squinted at her.

“…What are you doing.”

“Leaving.”

“Huh?”

Jiayi grabbed Ning’s arm.

“You two should enjoy your accidental reunion date.”

“It’s NOT a date,” Xiaoran protested instantly.

Beside her, Yichen said calmly—

“It kind of is.”

Jiayi almost screamed. Ning looked like she wanted to applaud. Xiaoran went red.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Before she could recover—Jiayi was already waving.

“Okay bye! Don’t lose Xiaoran again!”

“Please take responsibility for her,” Ning added calmly.

Then both girls vanished into the crowd. Traitors.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran looked up at him accusingly.

“…You knew they were going to leave.”

“Hm.”

“And you allowed it.”

“I’m not seeing the problem.”

So the two of them kept walking through the festival, alone now. And everything felt softer. The evening light turning gold. Music drifting between the booths. Warm air full of food smells and laughter. A comfortable feeling settled between them, like this was a date that had happened without anyone planning it. Then Xiaoran stopped walking. Yichen looked down.

“What happened.”

She pointed.

“Strawberry tanghulu.”

Five minutes later, Xiaoran was happily eating tanghulu while Yichen carried both drinks, because apparently that was his fate in life. Halfway through a strawberry, she froze.

“…Wait. I ruined your meeting.”

Silence. Yichen knew exactly where this was going. Guilty Lin Xiaoran was stubborn Lin Xiaoran.

“You left your study group because of me.”

“You sounded distressed.”

“That’s not the point.”

“It is to me.”

Xiaoran looked even guiltier.

“I should apologize.”

“No.”

“I’m serious.”

Yichen sighed. Once she decided something, especially out of guilt, stopping her was impossible.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later, Lin Xiaoran was standing outside the business faculty study room holding apology drinks for people she had never met. A horrifying experience.

“I can still run away,” she whispered urgently.

Yichen looked calm.

“You dragged me here yourself.”

“I’ve changed my mind.”

“Too late.”

Before she could escape, Yichen opened the door. Several business students looked up, and the room went quiet. So this was THE Lin Xiaoran. The famous girlfriend. The one Zhou Yichen answered calls for during meetings, smiled at his phone for, walked out mid-discussion for. And she looked a lot softer and cuter than they’d expected. Xiaoran wanted to sink into the floor.

“…Hello.”

One groupmate blinked.

“…Oh.”

Another turned to Yichen.

“You actually brought her here.”

Yichen stayed calm.

“Hm.”

Xiaoran gave a quick little bow.

“I’m sorry for interrupting your meeting earlier.”

Silence. Then she held up the drinks like a peace offering.

“I made him leave in the middle of it. Because I got lost. In a crowd.”

One groupmate burst out laughing. Another covered his face. Yichen closed his eyes. The tension broke completely. Then another student grinned.

“So you’re the girlfriend.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…That sounds threatening.”

“No,” the girl laughed immediately. “It’s just funny hearing about you for weeks.”

Xiaoran’s eyes narrowed.

“…Hearing WHAT exactly.”

Yichen sensed danger. Too late. One of the guys answered at once—

“He talks about you constantly.”

Yichen went very still.

“…WHAT,” Xiaoran said.

Another groupmate nodded seriously.

“He leaves exactly at 5 PM because ‘Xiaoran gets hungry around this time.’”

Someone else added—

“And during presentations he checks his phone every ten minutes.”

“And he rejected dinner plans because you had a fever.”

“And he once went very quiet and scary because someone said media students were annoying.”

Xiaoran turned slowly to Yichen, who suddenly looked like he regretted bringing her here at all.

“…Zhou Yichen.”

“Hm.”

“You really are obsessed with me.”

Silence. One groupmate immediately whispered:

“She figured it out.”

Yichen sighed and rubbed between his brows.

“You already knew that.”

“No,” Xiaoran said seriously. “I suspected. That’s different.”

Several business students nearly choked laughing. And for the first time that evening, Yichen actually looked a little embarrassed. Just a little. But Xiaoran noticed, and that made the whole accidental date worth it.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen buys a car because of one joke. He is not sorry.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Started Looking Expensive
chapters.epigraph: “Some men hold grudges. He held them beautifully.”
chapters.content:
Everyone at university already knew Zhou Yichen came from money. Not in an annoying way. Just obviously. His watches looked expensive. His apartment near campus was suspiciously nice. His calm confidence practically said “raised with financial stability.” But he never acted flashy. Never bragged. Never showed off. Which was exactly why the whole campus nearly lost its mind the day he showed up in a new car.

✦ ✦ ✦

Monday morning, in the business faculty parking lot, half the students stopped walking. Pulling slowly onto campus was a matte black sports car so beautiful it looked unreal. Low engine rumble. Tinted windows. Clean, elegant lines. The kind of car people photographed secretly. Silence spread. Then someone whispered—

“…Whose car is THAT?”

Then the driver’s door opened, and Zhou Yichen stepped out. Black coat. Coffee in one hand. Keys spinning lazily around his fingers. For the first time ever, Zhou Yichen looked rich-rich. Not quietly rich. Not “well-off.” Financially offensive. His business faculty friends looked devastated.

“…You never told us you bought a supercar.”

Yichen shut the car door.

“It’s not a supercar.”

“That thing costs more than my future.”

Another friend narrowed his eyes.

“…Wait.”

“What.”

“You dressed to match the car.”

Silence. Black coat. Black watch. Black car. Oh no. Yichen just sipped his coffee.

“I dressed normally.”

Liar. Terrible liar.

✦ ✦ ✦

It got worse when Lin Xiaoran arrived, because she knew absolutely nothing. At first she only noticed the crowd around the parking lot. Then Luo Jiayi gasped beside her.

“Oh my god there’s a rich man vehicle.”

“University students become very weak around shiny objects,” Xiaoran muttered.

Then someone in the crowd said—

“Isn’t that Zhou Yichen?”

Silence. Xiaoran froze.

“…What.”

The crowd parted a little, and there he was, leaning against the black car, talking to friends, one hand in his coat pocket, morning sun on his profile. Completely calm. Completely handsome. Completely devastating. The car made it so much worse. He looked like a young CEO arriving for a revenge plot. Jiayi grabbed Xiaoran.

“YOUR boyfriend?!”

“I think so.”

“YOU THINK SO?!”

Xiaoran needed several business days to process this. Zhou Yichen looked different today. Not his personality—still calm, still composed, still soft-eyed the moment he noticed her. But there was something unfairly attractive about him standing next to that car. More mature. More intimidating. More… boyfriend-shaped. Then Yichen spotted her, and his expression softened.

“There you are.”

Oh. OH NO. Why did that sound hotter next to an expensive car? Xiaoran walked over weakly.

“…What is this.”

“My car.”

“That’s not a normal sentence.”

Yichen almost smiled.

“I picked it up yesterday.”

“YOU BOUGHT THIS YESTERDAY?!”

Nearby students listened harder. Naturally.

“Hm.”

“Hm?!” Xiaoran stared at him accusingly. “Why are you acting like you bought snacks?”

“It’s just a car.”

“No. This thing has economic influence.”

His friends nearly collapsed laughing. Xiaoran circled the car slowly, like she was investigating dangerous wildlife.

“…You look like a rich villain beside this.”

“That sounds rude.”

“It’s a compliment.”

Then she narrowed her eyes.

“Wait. Did you buy this to show off?”

His friends looked very interested. Zhou Yichen never showed off. Ever. So why now? Yichen looked at her calmly for a moment, then answered honestly—

“A little.”

Silence. Everyone froze, Xiaoran included.

“…WHAT.”

A business friend nearly screamed.

“HE ADMITTED IT.”

Yichen looked completely unashamed.

“You said last month that my old car looked too responsible.”

Xiaoran blinked. The memory came back. Oh no. She HAD said that. Specifically—

“You drive like a married businessman with two children.”

And apparently, Zhou Yichen had taken it personally.

“So you bought THIS because of ONE comment?”

“You said I lacked youthful energy.”

“I WAS JOKING.”

“Hm.”

“Oh my god.”

The students nearby were fully invested now. Watching calm, perfect Zhou Yichen buy a luxury sports car because his girlfriend called him boring was insane. Yichen opened the passenger door.

“Get in.”

“…Why.”

“I’ll drive you to class.”

“My building is five minutes away.”

“I know.”

Then Xiaoran understood. He really WAS showing off today. Not arrogantly. Just… specifically for her.

“You’re being very peacock-like today.”

“I learned from media students.”

“That’s discrimination.”

She still got in immediately.

✦ ✦ ✦

The inside was even more terrifying. Soft leather seats. Everything smelled expensive. Xiaoran sat frozen while Yichen drove calmly through campus.

“…You look happy,” Yichen said.

“I’m inside a billionaire dating drama.”

Yichen laughed softly.

“There it is.”

“There WHAT is.”

“You’ve been staring at me weirdly since the parking lot.”

“…Because you suddenly look like a CEO.”

“Hm.”

“You’re acting cool on purpose.”

“I’m driving.”

“You know EXACTLY what you’re doing.”

She was right. Every red light was dangerous—one hand resting lazily on the wheel, relaxed posture, quiet confidence. And the worst part was that he wasn’t even trying. Yichen pulled up outside the media building. Before Xiaoran could escape, he leaned a little closer, one arm resting casually behind her seat.

“So.”

Xiaoran’s heart malfunctioned.

“…So what.”

“Do I still look like a married businessman with two children?”

This man held grudges beautifully. Xiaoran looked at him—the expensive car, the calm, handsome face she already liked too much, the boyfriend looking unfairly pleased with himself—and finally, very honestly—

“…No.”

The corner of Yichen’s mouth curved. A tiny victory smile. Xiaoran covered her burning face.

“…You’re unbearable with money.”

That only made Zhou Yichen laugh again.

chapters.desc: A bored Zhou Yichen, a rainy café, and four traps Lin Xiaoran walks straight into.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Was a Psychological Threat at the Café
chapters.epigraph: “Never trust a calm man with nothing to do.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen was dangerous when he got bored, because a bored Zhou Yichen went looking for Lin Xiaoran. Today it happened in the university café.

✦ ✦ ✦

Rain tapped softly against the windows while students crowded around warm drinks and laptops. Xiaoran sat across from Yichen, suffering through media theory homework.

“…I hate this major.”

“You chose it yourself.”

“I was young.”

Zhou Yichen looked deeply relaxed. His business assignment was already finished, his coffee untouched, one hand propping up his chin while he watched her spiral.

“Xiaoran.”

“What.”

“Give me your hands.”

Immediate suspicion.

“…Why.”

“Experiment.”

“That sounds like a trick.”

“Hm.”

Curiosity remained Lin Xiaoran’s greatest weakness. So eventually she placed both hands together on the table. Yichen laid one hand lightly over both of hers—warm palm, long fingers, comfortable pressure—and Xiaoran forgot the original question entirely.

“Okay,” Yichen said. “Now try separating your hands.”

Xiaoran blinked. Then confidently pulled. Nothing happened.

“…Wait.”

She tried harder. Still nothing.

“What?” she muttered.

Yichen looked calm.

“See? You can’t.”

Xiaoran stared in disbelief while trying again.

“How are you doing this.”

“Physics.”

“That’s not a real explanation.”

At the next table, two business students had stopped typing to watch. Xiaoran kept struggling against absolutely nothing.

“Wait.”

She narrowed her eyes suspiciously.

“…You’re just holding my hands.”

“Hm.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

He laughed. First trap: successful.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, round two began. Yichen frowned down at his sleeve. Xiaoran noticed immediately.

“What happened.”

“My cologne smells strange today.”

“Oh.”

Yichen looked thoughtful.

“Can you check?”

And because Lin Xiaoran unfortunately trusted him too much—she leaned closer without hesitation. Very close. Close enough to smell his cologne properly. Warm, clean, familiar—and while she was busy concentrating on it, Yichen kissed the top of her head. Xiaoran froze instantly.

“…What was THAT.”

“You leaned too close.”

“That’s YOUR fault.”

“Hm.”

A girl at the counter was openly smiling at them now. Xiaoran covered her burning face.

“You’re abusing trust.”

“You smelled my shoulder voluntarily.”

“That sentence sounds bad.”

“It’s accurate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Round three happened during snack sharing. Xiaoran happily ate fries while scrolling her phone.

“Open your mouth.”

No suspicion. Critical mistake. She opened her mouth automatically expecting fries. Yichen placed an ice cube inside. Cold shock exploded. Xiaoran nearly screamed.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

And this criminal laughed so hard he actually had to look away. Actual visible laughter, from Zhou Yichen, in public.

“You’re EVIL.”

“You trusted me too easily.”

“I thought we had love.”

“We do.”

“THIS is your version of love?!”

“Hm.”

It was, honestly.

✦ ✦ ✦

But the worst one happened later. Much later. Because eventually Xiaoran grew smarter. More cautious. More prepared. At least—she THOUGHT so.

“Xiaoran.”

“What now.”

Yichen looked completely serious.

“Your eyelash.”

Immediate panic.

“What about it?”

“Something’s stuck there.”

“Oh no.”

“Stay still.”

And because she believed him—she stayed still obediently while Yichen leaned closer. Closer. Closer. Until suddenly—he kissed the corner of her eye instead—gentle, brief, completely unfair—and calmly leaned back like nothing had happened. Silence. Absolute silence. Xiaoran’s brain stopped working.

“…You LIED.”

“There was nothing on your eyelash.”

“I trusted you.”

“That was your mistake.”

“YOU’RE A MENACE.”

Yichen finally laughed again. That warm, quiet laugh that only ever showed up around her. Which made it worse, because now she couldn’t even stay angry properly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, Xiaoran decided to retaliate. She narrowed her eyes across the café table.

“Okay.”

Yichen looked calm.

“Okay what.”

“My turn.”

“Hm.”

Xiaoran grabbed his wrist. Yichen let her, naturally. She leaned in, close enough that several students nearby looked interested again. And proudly—

“You have something on your face.”

Yichen looked unsurprised already.

“Do I.”

“Yes.”

“Where.”

“Here.”

Then Xiaoran poked his cheek. Hard. Her oldest move. Silence. One nearby student actually wheezed laughing. Yichen stared at her for a long second.

“…That’s your revenge?”

Xiaoran froze.

“…Wait.”

Oh no. OH NO. That was actually terrible. Yichen leaned back, a slow smile appearing.

“Cute effort.”

“Don’t say it like that.”

“You need more practice.”

Humiliating. Yichen reached across the table. Grabbed her hand lightly. And before Xiaoran could react—he kissed her knuckles once, then calmly went back to his coffee. Xiaoran malfunctioned completely.

“…I hate you.”

“No you don’t.”

Which, unfortunately, was correct.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran hates exams. Then Zhou Yichen mentions pandas.
chapters.title: Pass Everything and I’ll Take You to Chengdu
chapters.epigraph: “Zhou Yichen never made promises carelessly.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated exam season. Not in a normal university-student way. No. She hated them the way a medieval peasant feared plague—emotionally, spiritually, academically.

✦ ✦ ✦

The media faculty library looked like a war zone: students asleep on desks, coffee everywhere, laptops dying. In the middle of it all, Lin Xiaoran stared at her notes like they had personally betrayed her.

“…I actually don’t think my brain is participating.”

Across from her, Zhou Yichen calmly flipped through business case studies. Completely relaxed. Completely unfair.

“You’ve said that four times.”

“Because it’s true.”

“You passed midterms.”

“By divine intervention.”

Yichen almost smiled. Almost. Xiaoran collapsed onto the table.

“Yichen, if I fail editing theory, bury me quietly.”

“You won’t fail.”

“How do you know.”

“You cry before every exam and still pass.”

“That’s because panic is my learning method.”

Several painful minutes later, she looked up.

“…Can I have motivation.”

Yichen glanced at her calmly.

“What kind.”

“Something life-changing.”

Silence.

“If you pass all your finals,” he said while turning a page lazily, “I’ll take you to Chengdu.”

Xiaoran blinked slowly.

“…What.”

“To see giant pandas.”

Dead silence. Lin Xiaoran sat upright so fast her chair nearly tipped over.

“REAL pandas?!”

“Hm.”

“CHENGDU pandas?”

“Yes.”

“The fat ones that roll down hills?”

Yichen laughed quietly under his breath.

“There are thin pandas?”

“Oh my god.”

Her entire personality changed. Lin Xiaoran loved pandas with concerning sincerity, and everyone knew it. Meilin once said Xiaoran herself was basically a spoiled panda. Not inaccurate.

“…Wait.”

Yichen looked calm.

“You’re bribing me.”

“I’m motivating you.”

“With pandas.”

“Hm.”

“You promise?”

Yichen looked at her for one second.

“I promise.”

That calm certainty hit harder than she expected, because Zhou Yichen never made promises carelessly. If he said it, it would happen. Xiaoran grabbed her notes.

“Move.”

Yichen blinked slightly.

“…What.”

“I suddenly love education.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next three weeks were horrifying, because for the first time in university history, Lin Xiaoran studied voluntarily. Even Yichen looked shocked.

“Why are you awake at 2 AM.”

“Pandas don’t sleep on dreams.”

“That sentence made no sense.”

“Neither does media theory.”

Xiaoran shoved a stack of flashcards at him.

“Quiz me.”

“You’re scary when motivated.”

“CHENGDU, YICHEN.”

“Yes, I know.”

Even Luo Jiayi was disturbed.

“You studied during lunch voluntarily.”

“I have goals now.”

“You rejected café gossip.”

“I have PANDA goals.”

Yichen watched the whole transformation with growing amusement. He had expected her to study harder. Not to become academically possessed.

One evening in his apartment, Xiaoran sat surrounded by notes, memorizing concepts out loud—hair messy, eyes tired, still stubbornly going.

“You can rest.”

“No.”

“You’ve been studying four hours.”

“I’m fighting for wildlife.”

Yichen laughed quietly again. He set a warm drink down beside her.

“Drink first.”

Xiaoran looked up immediately. Her expression softened. Through the entire exam season, Yichen had never pressured her, never mocked her, never compared her to anyone. He just stayed beside her, helping, the way he always did.

“…What if I still fail.”

Yichen looked down at her calmly.

“You won’t.”

“But what if.”

He crouched beside her chair and brushed a hand through her messy hair.

“Then I’ll still take you.”

Xiaoran froze instantly.

“…What.”

“I said I’ll still take you.”

“But the deal—”

“I know.”

“Then why.”

Yichen looked at her for a long second.

“Because you tried this hard.”

Somehow that was worse. Xiaoran stared at him.

“…You can’t say things like that during exam season.”

“Why not.”

“It makes me want to cry.”

Yichen smiled faintly and flicked her forehead.

“Study first, crybaby.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Exam week passed painfully: one paper good, one paper terrible, one paper a disaster. Results day arrived. Media students crowded every corner of the campus café, refreshing their portals, and Xiaoran sat frozen beside Yichen.

“…I can’t open it.”

“You absolutely can.”

“What if Chengdu disappears.”

“It’s not vanishing geographically.”

“My future might.”

With shaking fingers—she opened the portal.

“…WAIT.”

Yichen looked up immediately. Xiaoran stared at the screen blankly.

“…I passed everything. I PASSED EVERYTHING.”

Nearby students jumped.

Meanwhile Xiaoran turned toward Yichen with actual tears forming.

“THE PANDAS.”

Yichen laughed—warm, real laughter.

“There it is.”

“THEY’RE WAITING FOR ME.”

“I don’t think they know you exist.”

“They will soon.”

Xiaoran launched herself at him, arms around his neck, nearly wrecking the café atmosphere. Neither of them cared. Then against his shoulder—

“…Thank you.”

Yichen held her waist steadily while smiling softly near her hair.

“For what.”

“For believing I could do it.”

“I always do.”

And that made Lin Xiaoran happier than Chengdu itself.

chapters.desc: First winter break of university. The old noodle shop, a failed lab report, and Tang Meilin’s boyfriend walks in.
chapters.title: The Four of Us, One Winter Later
chapters.epigraph: “Same time next winter.”
chapters.content:
The noodle shop near their old high school hadn’t changed at all. Same fogged-up windows. Same plastic stools that wobbled if you leaned back. Same handwritten menu on the wall, with the price of beef noodles crossed out and rewritten so many times the paper had gone soft. Lin Xiaoran pushed open the door on the third day of winter break, and the smell of broth and chili hit her so hard she nearly cried in the doorway.

“You’re not crying,” Tang Meilin said behind her.

“I’m a little bit crying.”

“It’s a noodle shop.”

“It’s OUR noodle shop.”

The owner looked up from behind the counter, squinted at them, and then said, without any greeting at all, “Milk for the girl who can’t eat spice?”

Xiaoran turned to Meilin with wet eyes. “He remembers.”

“You sobbed into his chili oil for twenty minutes. Nobody would forget that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen and Chen Yuhao were already at the corner table, the one by the window where they used to sit after practice. Yichen had saved her the seat against the wall, the way he always did, so she wouldn’t get bumped by people coming in. Yuhao was lying face down on the table.

“What happened to him?” Xiaoran asked.

“Engineering,” Yichen said.

Yuhao lifted his head. He looked older. Not dramatically—he still had the same messy hair and the same hoodie with the faded team logo—but there were shadows under his eyes that hadn’t been there in summer, and he’d stopped bouncing his leg under the table, which Xiaoran found more alarming than anything.

“I failed a lab report,” he said. “I didn’t even know you could fail a report. I thought you just wrote it.”

“You can fail anything,” Meilin said, sitting down beside him. “I believe in you.”

“That’s not comforting.”

“It wasn’t meant to be.”

And just like that, it was summer again. Or last year. Or any of the hundred afternoons they’d spent at this table, arguing about nothing while the windows fogged up.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ordered too much, the way they always had. Yuhao ate like someone who had been living on vending machine food for four months, which he admitted he had. Meilin told a long, deadpan story about her roommate trying to keep a hamster in a dorm that didn’t allow pets, and how the hamster had escaped into the ventilation system and been missing for six days. Xiaoran laughed so hard her milk went up her nose.

At some point, Yichen slid the plate of dumplings closer to her without looking up from his phone, and moved the chili oil to the other end of the table. Yuhao watched this happen and put down his chopsticks.

“You know what the worst part of university is?”

“Labs,” Meilin said.

“Not having to watch this every day.” He pointed his chopsticks at Yichen, then Xiaoran. “I thought I’d be relieved. I was so ready to be free of it. And then one day I saw a couple in the canteen sharing an umbrella and I got homesick. For YOU two. Do you know how humiliating that is?”

Xiaoran put a hand on her heart. “Yuhao.”

“Don’t.”

“You missed us.”

“I missed being annoyed. It’s different.”

But his ears had gone pink, and Meilin patted his head like he was a dog, and he let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway through the second round of noodles, Xiaoran told them about Chengdu. She had been saving it. She had passed every single final, including editing theory, which had tried to kill her, and Zhou Yichen was taking her to see the pandas in the spring, and she explained all of this in one breath while Meilin stared at her.

“You studied voluntarily?”

“For three weeks.”

“She studied at two in the morning,” Yichen said. “I have screenshots.”

“That’s a bribe,” Meilin said. “He bribed you with pandas.”

“It was motivation.”

“It was a bribe, and it worked, and I want to write it down so I can use it on my brother.”

Yuhao shook his head slowly. “Lin Xiaoran passed everything. In university. I need to sit with this.”

“You failed a lab report,” Xiaoran reminded him.

He lay back down on the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

Shen Zixu showed up at eight, which was when Meilin went quiet.

Not unhappy quiet. A different kind. She checked her phone, put it face down, picked it up again, and then said, very casually, “He’s outside. He’s coming in. Nobody say anything.”

Xiaoran and Yuhao looked at each other.

“Nobody,” Meilin repeated.

The door opened. A tall boy with glasses came in, brushing snow off his shoulders, and looked around the shop until he found Meilin. Then he smiled, and Meilin—Tang Meilin, who had once told Xiaoran that crushes were “a waste of brain space”—smiled back so quickly and so softly that Xiaoran had to grip the edge of the table.

“Hi,” Shen Zixu said to the table in general. “Sorry I’m late. I’ve heard a lot about you.”

“Only good things,” Yuhao said immediately.

“Mostly about the chili oil,” Zixu said.

Xiaoran glared at Meilin. Meilin looked at the ceiling. He sat down in the chair Yichen pulled over for him, and for the first ten minutes everyone was painfully polite. Then Yuhao asked him what he studied, and he said architecture, and Yuhao said “so you also fail lab reports,” and Zixu said “we don’t have labs, we have all-nighters,” and the two of them started comparing how little they slept with a kind of competitive misery that Xiaoran recognized immediately as the beginning of a friendship.

Under the table, Meilin nudged Xiaoran’s foot.

“Well?” she said quietly.

Xiaoran looked at Shen Zixu, who had just noticed Meilin’s cup was empty and refilled it with tea without breaking his sentence. She thought about a boy in a convenience store, buying a strawberry milk she hadn’t asked for.

“I like him,” she whispered.

Meilin didn’t say anything. But she relaxed, all at once, like she’d been holding her shoulders up since the summer.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed until the owner started stacking stools on the empty tables around them. Outside, the snow had stopped, and the street was quiet and white under the orange streetlights. Zixu walked Meilin toward the bus stop. Yuhao said goodbye three separate times and kept turning back to add things.

“Group chat. Every week. I’m serious.”

“We have a group chat,” Meilin called.

“A group chat where people REPLY.”

Then he was gone too, and it was just the two of them, walking past the dark gates of their old high school. Xiaoran stopped in front of the bars and looked through. The courtyard. The steps where she’d waited for him after practice. The window of their old classroom on the third floor. It all looked smaller than she remembered, the way places do when you’ve left them.

“Do you think we’ll drift?” she asked.

Yichen stopped beside her. “Us?”

“Them. All of us.” She pulled her sleeves down over her hands. “Yuhao’s in another city. Meilin has a whole life now. We only see each other twice a year. I keep thinking—what if this is how it starts? You get busy, and then you’re people who used to be friends.”

He was quiet for a while. That was something she’d learned about him over the years: when she asked a real question, he didn’t answer right away. He actually thought about it.

“Yuhao missed us enough to get homesick over an umbrella,” he said eventually. “Meilin was nervous about whether you’d like her boyfriend. People who are drifting don’t care about that.”

Xiaoran thought about Meilin’s shoulders coming down under the table.

“I didn’t know she was nervous.”

“She checked her phone about ten times before he came in.”

Xiaoran hadn’t noticed a single one. He took her hand, sleeve and all, and turned her away from the gate. “We’ll see them in summer. And Yuhao will make us do a weekly group call, and you’ll be the only one who joins on time.”

“I’ll be the only one who joins at all.”

“Probably.”

She laughed, and her breath came out white in the cold, and she leaned into his arm as they walked home through the snow. Behind them, the noodle shop’s sign flickered off. In the group chat, Yuhao had already sent a photo of the four of them at the table that evening, slightly blurry, everyone laughing at something nobody would remember later. Under it, Meilin had written: Same time next winter.

Xiaoran saved the photo, and sent a heart.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran is clingy every day of the year—except the days she actually needs someone.
chapters.title: When Lin Xiaoran Gets Sick, She Stops Acting Like Herself
chapters.epigraph: “You let me spoil you every other day.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran was usually clingy. Professionally clingy. The type who leaned on Zhou Yichen at every meal, stole his sleeves constantly, and demanded attention every three business hours. So if she ever caught a cold, people expected her to become ten times worse. That never happened. Whenever Lin Xiaoran got sick, she stopped relying on anyone at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first sign appeared on Thursday morning. No dramatic good-morning messages. No memes. No complaints about university life. Just:

Xiaoran: I’m going to skip class today.

Yichen knew something was wrong. Lin Xiaoran skipped class under exactly three conditions: natural disaster, emotional disaster, or physical illness. So he called. No answer. He called again three minutes later. Still nothing. Xiaoran texted back.

Xiaoran: don’t call
my voice ugly right now

Yichen: Are you sick.

Long pause.

Xiaoran: tiny bit

Which obviously meant terribly sick.

✦ ✦ ✦

An hour later, Zhou Yichen was outside her door with medicine and food, and he sensed something strange right away. Usually the second Xiaoran saw him, she latched on. Now, when she opened the door a crack, she just stood there—hair messy, oversized hoodie, face pale, very obviously sick, and trying very hard to act normal.

“…Why are you here.”

“You’re sick.”

“I can survive independently.”

That alone confirmed she had a fever. Healthy Xiaoran would already have demanded forehead kisses. Then Yichen stepped inside calmly.

“How high.”

“I don’t know.”

“You didn’t check?”

“I drank water.”

“…That’s not medical treatment.”

Xiaoran slipped past him before he could fold up the blanket on the couch. Suspicious. Then he noticed something worse. The medicine was untouched. The food was untouched. And despite how exhausted she looked, the apartment was weirdly clean—like she had spent her energy tidying instead of resting.

“Xiaoran. Did you clean while sick?”

Silence.

“…Maybe.”

“Why.”

“I was already awake.”

Then he remembered her mother at the top of the stairs on moving day. She’ll tell you she’s fine when she isn’t. Especially when she’s sick. At the time, it had sounded like a warning about colds. It hadn’t been.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next hour was frustrating. Every time Yichen tried to help, Xiaoran quietly dodged it.

“I can get water myself.”

“I can take medicine alone.”

“You don’t need to cook.”

“I already ordered food.”

None of it sounded like her. Eventually Yichen stood in the kitchen doorway, watching her try to cut fruit with a visible fever.

“…Give me the knife.”

“I can do it.”

“You almost cut your finger.”

“I have survival instincts.”

“No you don’t.”

He took the knife out of her hands anyway, gently. Xiaoran looked upset. Not angry. Not bratty. Just quietly uncomfortable.

“I said I can do it.”

Yichen paused. Her voice sounded strange—smaller, somehow.

“Why are you acting like this.”

Silence. Xiaoran looked away, avoiding his eyes, and that worried him more than the fever. Then after a long moment—

“…I don’t like it.”

“What.”

“When people take care of me too much.”

Dead silence. Yichen leaned against the counter, watching her.

“Why.”

“Because I feel useless.”

She said it quietly, almost embarrassed. And suddenly everything made sense—the cleaning, the independence, the way she refused help on reflex. Lin Xiaoran, who clung to him every day without shame, turned defensive the moment she was actually vulnerable.

“You think being sick makes you a burden.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. Which was the answer.

“My mom used to say sick people become troublesome,” she admitted eventually. “So I just… got used to handling it myself.”

Something in Zhou Yichen’s chest tightened. This girl carried strange habits so quietly. He stepped closer. Xiaoran blinked.

“…What.”

Yichen touched her forehead. Still warm.

“You know what’s annoying? You act clingy every normal day.”

“…That sounds rude.”

“But the second you actually need someone,” he continued softly, “you suddenly try doing everything alone.”

Xiaoran stayed quiet.

“I don’t want to trouble you.”

That sentence genuinely upset him. Not angry-upset. Heart-hurting upset.

“Lin Xiaoran, you know what troubles me more?”

She looked up slowly.

“You being sick and pretending you don’t need me.”

Yichen sighed and brushed the messy hair away from her forehead.

“You let me spoil you every other day. So why can’t you let me take care of you too?”

Xiaoran’s throat tightened. The way he said it—calmly, naturally, as if caring for her wasn’t an obligation or a burden or a sacrifice, just something obvious—was too much.

“…I don’t know.”

Yichen looked at her for a second. Without asking, he pulled her into his arms, and her stubbornness gave way all at once. She was tired. Very tired. Then softly near her hair—

“You don’t have to act strong around me all the time.”

Very weakly—

“…Can I be clingy now.”

Yichen laughed softly.

“There she is.”

Lin Xiaoran wrapped her arms around his waist properly and buried her burning face against his chest. Like herself again.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen joins the university basketball team. Lin Xiaoran discovers he has fans.
chapters.title: Too Many Girls Know Zhou Yichen
chapters.epigraph: “Because when I play seriously, I want you there.”
chapters.content:
University life settled down slowly after the first few chaotic months. Classes became routine. Assignments became suffering. And somehow, Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran adapted surprisingly well: different majors, different schedules, different buildings, but still eating together, still walking each other home, still disgustingly in love. At least until Zhou Yichen made one important decision.

“I’m joining the university basketball team.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The café table went quiet. Xiaoran blinked slowly over her drink.

“…Seriously?”

Yichen nodded once.

“Hm.”

Across from them, Luo Jiayi gasped.

“Oh my god.”

Meanwhile Sun Ning looked unsurprised. Everyone had seen it coming. Zhou Yichen loved basketball too much to stay away, and after months of adjusting to university and business faculty pressure, he finally had time again. Xiaoran leaned across the table.

“You’ll become busier.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll have practice every day.”

“Probably.”

“…There’ll be female fans.”

Dead silence. That, Yichen knew, was the real concern.

“There are already female students.”

“That’s different.”

She was right. The second Zhou Yichen joined the team, campus life became deeply irritating—for her specifically.

✦ ✦ ✦

First practice day, university indoor court, and the atmosphere already looked dangerous. The team was competitive, fast, aggressive—serious basketball. And Zhou Yichen fit in too well. Too naturally. Too attractively. He stood by the court in black practice gear, taping his wrist, hair already damp, expression focused. Basketball Zhou Yichen felt different from everyday Zhou Yichen—more intense, more confident, more… boyfriend-threatening. Courtside, Xiaoran sat beside Luo Jiayi, suffering.

“…Why does he suddenly look like a drama poster?”

Jiayi stared openly.

“I understand women now.”

“Stop looking at him.”

“I physically can’t.”

A girl nearby whispered loudly:

“That’s Zhou Yichen from business faculty right?”

“He’s so handsome.”

“I heard he’s rich too.”

Xiaoran’s eye twitched. Then practice started, and Zhou Yichen became terrifyingly competitive. Sharp passes. Fast footwork. Completely focused. The kind of player people couldn’t stop watching. Even the coach looked impressed. One clean three-pointer dropped through the net, and the gym cheered—including several random girls. Unacceptable. Xiaoran sat there frozen.

“…Too many women know him.”

Jiayi nearly choked laughing.

“You sound like an emperor losing territory.”

“He belongs to ME.”

Across the court, Yichen glanced up and found Xiaoran pouting in the stands. The corner of his mouth curved—just for her. Unfortunately, that made the girls nearby scream harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Practice ended nearly two hours later. While the team stayed behind to talk through drills, Xiaoran waited outside, nursing her wounds. Finally Yichen came out, bag over one shoulder, hair damp, shirt clinging to him from practice. This was horrible. Several girls in the hallway turned to look. One whispered,

“He looks even better after practice.”

Xiaoran almost started a war. Yichen walked straight past them, stopped in front of her, and squeezed her cheek.

“There you are.”

Dead silence. The girls froze.

“…You did that on purpose.”

“Hm?”

“The cheek thing.”

“You were glaring at strangers.”

“I was protecting what’s mine.”

Yichen laughed softly. Then he took her bag off her shoulder without thinking, the way he always did, and that small, familiar thing soothed her jealousy a little. However much attention he got, he still treated her like she was special without even trying.

“…Are girls always this obsessed with basketball players.”

“Yes.”

“Oh.”

“Jealous?”

“Extremely.”

Yichen looked amused.

“You knew I played basketball already.”

“Not university-athlete basketball.”

“Difference?”

“You look better now. It’s annoying.”

Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“…You won’t forget me because of basketball right?”

Yichen looked at her calmly. And understood the real feeling underneath all that jealousy. Not insecurity, exactly. Just the fear of being left behind while he kept getting brighter.

“Come to practice tomorrow too.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Why.”

Yichen adjusted her grip on his sleeve.

“Because when I play seriously,” he admitted softly, “I want you there.”

Silence.

“You’re my girlfriend.”

He said it like it settled everything. All the irritation drained out of Xiaoran at once.

“…Fine.”

“Hm.”

“But if too many girls scream again,” she warned, “I’m starting a war.”

Yichen laughed under his breath. “Please don’t.”

He touched the back of her head briefly.

“Just support me normally.”

That alone made Lin Xiaoran feel embarrassingly proud.

chapters.desc: Three months, one passed exam season, and the first trip that’s just the two of them.
chapters.title: The Chengdu Promise Finally Happened
chapters.epigraph: “Giant pandas were only the second-best thing in Chengdu.”
chapters.content:
The problem with making promises to Lin Xiaoran—was that she remembered them forever. So from the moment Zhou Yichen casually said:

“If you pass all your finals, I’ll take you to Chengdu.”

She had been preparing for the trip ever since—including mentally greeting the pandas.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later, they were standing in Chengdu Tianfu Airport together. Alone. No friends, no classmates, no accidental third wheels. Just the two of them. It felt strange, because despite how long they had been together, most of their outings somehow involved other people. This was an actual couple trip. Xiaoran stood by the luggage carousel, practically vibrating.

“Yichen. We’re in panda territory.”

“You’ve said that six times.”

“This is the best place on earth.”

Yichen laughed quietly while pulling their suitcase down easily. Then he fixed her crooked scarf, the same way he used to fix her crooked hair ribbon.

“Cold?” he asked.

“A little.”

“Your hands?”

“Frozen.”

Yichen took them in his without another word, warm fingers wrapping around hers as easily as breathing, and somehow Chengdu already felt softer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first disaster happened thirty minutes later. Lin Xiaoran got distracted by street food immediately.

“Yichen LOOK.”

“Hm?”

“Bunny-shaped buns.”

“You already ate on the plane.”

“That was airplane food. It doesn’t count.”

Ten minutes later she was happily eating spicy noodles at a tiny restaurant while Yichen watched from across the table. At least—until Xiaoran suddenly stopped moving. Silence.

“…Yichen. My mouth hurts.”

There it was. The consequences. Lin Xiaoran loved spicy food in theory and handled it like a weak Victorian noblewoman. Whatever tolerance she had built during her chili-oil training had clearly expired. Chengdu showed no mercy. Then Yichen sighed softly.

“How much chili did you add.”

“…The auntie said ‘medium.’”

“You trusted local standards?”

“I was arrogant.”

Her eyes were already watering. Yichen pushed an iced soy milk toward her.

“Drink.”

Xiaoran grabbed it with both hands. The restaurant aunties were openly watching them. One said something in Sichuan dialect, smiling. Yichen understood enough to catch:

“Your girlfriend is cute.”

Xiaoran understood enough to be embarrassed.

“She’s making fun of me.”

“No.”

“What did she say.”

“That you’re cute.”

“…Oh.”

“She’s correct.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran kicked his shoe under the table.

“You can’t flirt while I’m dying from spice.”

“I’m multitasking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second disaster happened at the panda base. Lin Xiaoran forgot humans required rest. The moment she saw the first giant panda rolling down a hill, she lost all composure.

“YICHEN.”

“Hm.”

“LOOK AT HIM.”

“He’s eating bamboo.”

“HE’S PERFECT.”

She grabbed Yichen’s sleeve.

“Take photo.”

Five minutes later:

“Another one.”

Ten minutes later:

“Wait, this one is looking at me.”

Twenty minutes later:

“Yichen crouch lower the angle matters.”

Meanwhile Zhou Yichen—business student, basketball player, future corporate elite—spent the morning as a full-time panda photographer, without a single complaint, mostly because watching Xiaoran this happy was worth it. After roughly four hundred panda photos, Xiaoran turned around.

“Yichen, I understand life now.”

“Since when?”

“We should retire here.”

“To the panda base?”

“Yes.”

“You can’t survive without food delivery.”

“…The pandas will provide.”

While laughing at her nonsense—Yichen noticed how relaxed she looked here. No assignments. No stress. Just bright eyes and soft excitement every few minutes. He liked seeing this version of her too much.

“Yichen. Take a picture with me.”

Xiaoran usually hated asking strangers for couple photos. Today she looked determined. Of course Yichen agreed. A nearby tourist helped take the photo. And in the picture—Xiaoran smiled brightly while hugging his arm. Zhou Yichen was looking down at her instead of the camera—soft-eyed, completely gone. The tourist who took it laughed.

“Young man,” she teased, “you’re looking at your girlfriend too lovingly.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran nearly exploded. Yichen didn’t deny it at all—just took the phone back and said,

“Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night it started to rain while they were walking near Jinli Ancient Street. Warm lights reflected off the wet stone, the shops glowing, and Lin Xiaoran had, of course, forgotten that umbrellas existed.

“…We’re going to die.”

“We’re getting wet.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen pulled her under a shop awning—just like a closed bookstore, years ago, in another city—and suddenly they were very close. Xiaoran looked up at him. His hair was already damp. Dark coat. His hand still holding hers. Suddenly the whole trip felt different. At home, their relationship lived between class schedules and everyday routines. Out here, far from campus, it was obvious: they belonged in each other’s lives now.

“…Thank you for bringing me.”

Yichen looked down.

“For pandas?”

“For remembering.”

“You studied hard for them.”

“And?”

“I keep my promises.”

Hearing it here, in Chengdu, with the rain all around them, made Xiaoran’s heart ache a little. She leaned forward and rested against his chest, and Yichen wrapped an arm around her like instinct. Then softly above her head—

“Cold?”

“A little.”

He pulled her closer without a word. At that moment—Lin Xiaoran decided giant pandas were only the second-best thing in Chengdu.

chapters.desc: His first university tournament is four days away. Lin Xiaoran has discovered potassium.
chapters.title: The Week Lin Xiaoran Became a Sports Nutrition Expert
chapters.epigraph: “Your body belongs to university basketball now.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen’s first university basketball tournament was approaching. Lin Xiaoran took this development extremely seriously. Concerningly seriously.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started after one casual conversation.

“Coach said we need to stay in good condition this week,” Yichen mentioned while packing his bag after practice.

Xiaoran nodded absentmindedly.

“What kind of condition.”

“Physical.”

“What does that include.”

“Sleep. Food. Training.”

Silence. Lin Xiaoran opened her phone, and Yichen immediately sensed future problems.

“…What are you searching.”

“Nutritional support for athletes.”

“There it is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning—Yichen received twelve messages before 8 AM.

Xiaoran: athletes need protein

Xiaoran: also potassium

Xiaoran: why do bananas sound medically important

Xiaoran: DO NOT EAT INSTANT NOODLES THIS WEEK

Yichen sat in business statistics, staring at his phone with exhausted amusement. Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: i made meal schedule

Yichen: Why.

Xiaoran: because your body belongs to university basketball now

Yichen: That sounds concerning.

Xiaoran: and to me emotionally

✦ ✦ ✦

Things escalated quickly. By Wednesday, Lin Xiaoran had become a full-time sports mom. She brought homemade fruit containers to practice. She sent hydration reminders every hour. She downloaded articles with titles like Foods That Improve Athletic Performance. The basketball team watched it all in disbelief. At the practice break, Xiaoran stood courtside holding a thermal lunch bag.

“Yichen.”

One teammate blinked slowly.

“…Did your girlfriend pack your lunch.”

Yichen took the bag calmly.

“Hm.”

Another player looked devastated.

“My girlfriend forgot my birthday.”

Xiaoran ignored everyone and opened the containers.

“Eat this first.”

Yichen looked down: chicken, vegetables, rice. Actually balanced. Suspiciously balanced.

“…You made this?”

“Hm.”

“Without burning the kitchen?”

“Rude.”

In fairness, the last time she had cooked for him, she’d nearly set his kitchen on fire first. Then another teammate whispered:

“She’s actually taking this seriously.”

No one understood how seriously. The night before, Lin Xiaoran had spent three hours researching whether walnuts improved concentration in sports. Three hours.

“Also,” Xiaoran added seriously, “you cannot drink iced coffee this week.”

Dead silence. Yichen blinked.

“…Excuse me.”

“It affects your body.”

“My body survived finals week.”

“This is DIFFERENT.”

Then she narrowed her eyes suspiciously.

“How many coffees today.”

Silence.

“…Yichen.”

“One.”

“You’re lying.”

“…Two.”

The basketball team nearly collapsed laughing. Xiaoran looked genuinely disappointed.

“Your tournament is in four days.”

“It’s just coffee.”

“Michael Jordan probably drank water.”

“Michael Jordan absolutely drank coffee.”

“That’s not the point.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The funniest part was that Zhou Yichen actually listened. Mostly. Enough to shock everyone around him. One teammate stared in disbelief during lunch.

“You stopped drinking energy drinks?”

Yichen looked calm.

“She’ll lecture me.”

“…You’re scared of your girlfriend?”

“No.”

Pause.

“…A little.”

Lin Xiaoran’s disappointed face was a terrifying weapon.

That evening, Yichen arrived at Xiaoran’s apartment to find another disaster: the kitchen, covered in ingredients, and in the middle of it, Lin Xiaoran in an apron, watching a recipe video with deadly focus. Yichen stopped in the doorway.

“…What’s happening.”

“Recovery soup.”

“Is that safe?”

“I researched.”

That made it worse. Xiaoran held up a spoon.

“Taste.”

Yichen tasted it carefully. It was good. Shockingly good. He blinked once.

“…This is edible.”

“EXCUSE ME.”

“I meant good.”

“Hm.”

Then proudly—

“It has nutrients.”

“Everything has nutrients.”

“This one has athlete nutrients.”

While she went back to stirring, Yichen leaned against the counter and watched her—hair tied up messily, sleeves rolled, muttering nutritional facts to herself—and it felt strangely warm. This girl, who regularly forgot her own umbrella, was trying this hard for him.

“You don’t actually need to do all this.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“I know.”

“Then why.”

“Because you care about basketball a lot.”

She looked away and pretended to focus on the soup. But Yichen understood. This was how she supported him—not loudly, not dramatically, just by trying hard in small ways. He came up behind her, wrapped one arm loosely around her waist, and rested his chin on her shoulder. The kitchen went quiet. Then softly near her ear—

“Thank you.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…For soup?”

“For caring this much.”

“…You better win now.”

Yichen laughed quietly against her hair.

“No pressure.”

“I researched potassium for you. Also, I packed bananas for tomorrow.”

“There it is.”

chapters.desc: Number eleven, a stadium full of fans, and a final minute Lin Xiaoran will scream through.
chapters.title: The First Tournament Was Very Bad for Lin Xiaoran’s Heart
chapters.epigraph: “You know what I kept thinking during the game? That you were watching.”
chapters.content:
By the time Zhou Yichen’s first university tournament arrived—Lin Xiaoran had become half girlfriend, half team manager. She monitored his sleep. She threatened teammates who gave him iced drinks. She packed fruit containers like it was war. She even made him eat walnuts because, apparently,

“Your brain also plays basketball.”

The team found the whole thing hilarious. They had also started calling Yichen “Captain Zhou” within a week of him joining—half a joke about his high school title, half because the seniors had already started listening to him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday morning. Tournament day. The university stadium was already packed, the atmosphere loud and competitive and, unfortunately, very full of women.

“Why are there THIS many girls.”

Luo Jiayi looked around calmly.

“Basketball tournament.”

“No. This feels hormonal.”

The moment the team walked out for warm-ups, the noise doubled. And at the center of the problem, of course, was Zhou Yichen. Black warm-up jacket, tall frame, focused expression, a basketball spinning lazily in one hand. Tournament Zhou Yichen looked even more dangerous than practice Zhou Yichen—colder, sharper, his usual softness replaced by pure competition. Lin Xiaoran stared.

“…Oh no.”

Jiayi looked amused already.

“What.”

“He became 100 times more handsome.”

“Correct.”

“This is horrible.”

Things became worse once the game actually started. Zhou Yichen played terrifyingly well—fast, precise, every motion clean and confident. And unlike in everyday life, he barely smiled on court, which somehow made him even more attractive. Unfair. One clean steal. Fast break. Score. The stadium exploded, very much including the female students. Behind Xiaoran, a row of girls was whispering.

“Number eleven is INSANE.”

“He’s so handsome.”

“Who is he?”

“He’s from business faculty.”

“Does he have a girlfriend?”

Dead silence. Xiaoran turned around. Very slowly.

“…Yes.”

The girls froze immediately. Then awkwardly—

“Oh.”

“Very much yes,” Xiaoran added calmly.

During a timeout, Yichen glanced up at the stands and found her right away—still pouting, still clutching his water bottle like it was hers. His expression softened. A tiny change, barely noticeable, except Xiaoran noticed. Competitive Zhou Yichen looking only at her in a stadium full of people was deeply dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦
