By halftime, the university team led comfortably and looked ready to collapse. Xiaoran stood by the bench with snacks and drinks like a one-woman support staff. One teammate blinked slowly.

“…Did she prepare all this herself.”

Another grabbed banana slices immediately.

“Captain Zhou’s girlfriend is basically our nutrition department.”

Yichen sat drinking water, his hair dark with sweat. Xiaoran approached carefully.

“…You okay?”

“Hm.”

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Do you need sugar.”

“You sound like a worried auntie.”

“Because you’re sweating like crazy.”

One teammate nearby suddenly whispered:

“He listens to her differently.”

Another nodded seriously.

“Scary honestly.”

It was true. However focused he was on the game, the second Xiaoran spoke to him, his whole expression relaxed. Xiaoran noticed a small red scrape on his arm. Immediate panic.

“What happened there.”

Yichen glanced down casually.

“Nothing.”

“YOU’RE BLEEDING.”

“It’s tiny.”

“That’s still your BODY.”

The whole bench watched in silence while Xiaoran inspected his arm like he had come back from a war.

“Does it hurt?”

Yichen looked at her for one second.

“Not really.”

The way she was looking at him—worried, protective, trying so hard to take care of him—made every exhausting minute worth it. Then before the second half started—Xiaoran caught his sleeve. Yichen looked down.

“…Hm?”

“Win properly.”

Just two words, but her eyes were so sincere—so trusting, so proud already—that something in Zhou Yichen tightened. He really wanted to win now. Not just for the team. For her, too.

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Final quarter. Close score. The other team caught up and pressed hard, the noise became overwhelming, and on court, Zhou Yichen became terrifying—focused eyes, quick decisions, sharp, aggressive plays. Even his teammates started relying on him without thinking. Last minute. Tie score. A fast break—and Yichen scored. The stadium exploded. The university team had won, and his teammates mobbed him. In the stands, Lin Xiaoran stood frozen. Seeing Zhou Yichen like this felt unreal: breathing hard, hair a mess, a victory smile finally breaking through after a whole game of serious focus. He looked brightest exactly here, on court, doing what he loved. Through the whole crowd, Yichen looked up and searched for her first. Not his teammates. Not the coach. Her.

When their eyes met, he smiled properly—warm, real, nothing like the competitive face from earlier—and it hit harder than the win itself. Jiayi grabbed her by both shoulders.

“GO DOWN THERE.”

“Huh?”

“YOUR BOYFRIEND LOOKS LIKE A SPORTS DRAMA MALE LEAD.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A few minutes later, Xiaoran finally reached him by the sideline. The team was still celebrating nearby; Yichen had stepped slightly apart to drink water, still flushed from the game, still unfairly handsome.

“You won.”

“Hm.”

Xiaoran looked up at him and said, very sincerely—

“…You looked really cool.”

Dead silence. Compliments from Lin Xiaoran usually sounded chaotic. This one sounded honest. Soft. Almost shy. Yichen laughed quietly under his breath.

“Only cool?”

“Hm?”

“You screamed my name three times during fourth quarter.”

“…YOU HEARD THAT?”

“The whole stadium heard that.”

His teammates started laughing. Xiaoran covered her face in horror.

“No one told you to become that handsome while playing.”

Yichen stepped closer, close enough that only she could hear.

“You know what I kept thinking during the game?”

“…What.”

“That you were watching. So I wanted to play well.”

Lin Xiaoran almost forgot how breathing worked after that.

chapters.desc: The team wants to celebrate. Lin Xiaoran plans to slip away. Zhou Yichen has other plans.
chapters.title: “You’re Coming With Me.”
chapters.epigraph: “So why are you acting like you don’t belong beside me?”
chapters.content:
After winning their first university tournament—the basketball team became completely unbearable. Loud. Overexcited. Sweaty. Half the team was crowded around Zhou Yichen, shouting about where to celebrate.

“Hotpot.”

“No, barbecue.”

“Private room karaoke.”

“Captain Zhou decides.”

Lin Xiaoran stood a little behind the group, holding Yichen’s jacket and water bottle like temporary storage staff. She was already planning to leave. The tournament was over. He’d won. Mission complete. This was team territory now, not girlfriend territory. One teammate threw an arm around Yichen.

“Captain Zhou, bring your girlfriend tonight.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran waved both hands.

“Oh no no no.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“She’s coming.”

“…Excuse me?”

Another teammate grinned.

“YES bring her.”

“Our team nutritionist deserves celebration too.”

“That was ONE banana container,” Xiaoran protested.

“It changed my life,” someone said.

Everyone agreed, which somehow made Xiaoran more uncomfortable, not less. She was dating Yichen, but she still felt a little awkward around his basketball world. The team knew her. Liked her, even. She still felt like an outsider standing next to something important to him.

“You go,” she whispered to Yichen. “I’ll head home.”

Yichen looked at her once.

“No.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“You should celebrate with your teammates.”

“I am.”

“…Without me.”

Yichen looked genuinely confused.

“Why without you.”

To him, the question made no sense. Xiaoran lowered her voice.

“Because I’m not part of the team.”

Dead silence. Yichen’s expression changed. Not angry. Not cold. Just sharper.

“Who said that.”

“No one.”

“Then why are you thinking it.”

Xiaoran looked away. Said out loud, it sounded childish. But still—this win belonged to them. The players. The coach. Not her. She didn’t want anyone thinking, Why is the captain’s clingy girlfriend here?

“I don’t want to bother everyone.”

That sentence always bothered Zhou Yichen more than anything. Without another word, he took his jacket out of her hands and put it around her shoulders instead, still warm from him.

“Come with me.”

“…Yichen.”

“Xiaoran.”

“That’s your team celebration.”

“And you supported me this entire month.”

Silence.

“You think I don’t know how much effort you put in?”

Suddenly she remembered all of it—the nutrition schedules, waiting through practices, researching athlete meals at 2 AM, packing snacks, cheering louder than anyone. Then Yichen continued softly—

“You stayed up helping me review game footage before qualifiers.”

“…You were stressed.”

“You came to every practice.”

“That’s normal.”

“You worried more about my sleep schedule than I did.”

A few teammates had overheard, and immediately looked emotional. One whispered,

“Captain Zhou’s girlfriend is actually amazing.”

Another nodded seriously.

“She takes this more seriously than Coach.”

Xiaoran grew more embarrassed by the second.

“That’s because I’m your girlfriend.”

Yichen looked down at her calmly.

“Yes.”

One word, but the way he said it made it heavier, like it already explained everything that mattered.

“So why are you acting like you don’t belong beside me?”

“I just…” Xiaoran admitted quietly, “didn’t want people to think I was forcing myself into your space.”

For one second—Yichen looked stunned. Then he laughed softly—not mocking, just helpless, hopelessly fond—and reached up to fix her messy hair.

“Lin Xiaoran, you know what the team calls you?”

“…What.”

“Our unofficial manager.”

“…WHAT?”

“You boss everyone around. You scolded Zhang Rui for buying iced cola before practice.”

The teammates nearby burst out laughing.

“She scolded us like a disappointed mother.”

“She told Fang Ze sleep matters more than male ego.”

“Honestly she’s terrifying.”

Xiaoran covered her face. Yichen looked more and more amused.

“No one thinks you’re bothering us. They’re happy you’re here.”

Hearing that from him mattered more than hearing it from anyone else.

“…Really?”

Yichen looked at her like the answer was obvious.

“Hm.”

He laced their fingers together—warm, steady, certain—and her nervousness eased. Then one teammate shouted,

“CAPTAIN ZHOU STOP FLIRTING AND COME EAT.”

Another pointed accusingly.

“He goes soft around her!”

Yichen ignored them completely. Then calmly to Xiaoran—

“You’re coming.”

“…Do I have a choice.”

“No.”

A small smile finally appeared.

“Besides,” he added quietly, “I want you there.”

That alone would have made Lin Xiaoran follow him anywhere.

chapters.desc: Hotpot, three victory speeches, and a quiet walk home under the streetlights.
chapters.title: After the Celebration, Zhou Yichen Became Too Gentle
chapters.epigraph: “When we won, I searched for you first.”
chapters.content:
The basketball team celebration lasted way too long. Hotpot. Shouting. Three separate victory speeches nobody asked for. Somehow every teammate got more emotional the more he ate—especially Zhang Rui.

“I LOVE THIS TEAM.”

“You cried because the beef finished.”

“THAT WAS SYMBOLIC.”

Lin Xiaoran sat beside Zhou Yichen watching the team spiral into post-victory chaos, and it felt strangely nice. Earlier she had worried she wouldn’t belong. Now everyone included her without thinking—they were even calling her “team manager,” unironically. Terrifying. Fang Ze pointed across the table.

“Captain Zhou.”

Yichen looked up calmly.

“You smiled seventy percent more tonight because your girlfriend came.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran choked on her drink. Yichen stayed completely calm.

“…Only seventy?”

The entire table exploded screaming.

“OH MY GOD.”

“THAT’S DISGUSTING.”

“WHY IS HE FLIRTING NATURALLY.”

Xiaoran stared at him in horror.

“You can’t say things like that publicly.”

“You survived.”

“No, I did not.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time dinner ended, the city had gone quiet—late-night lights along the campus streets, a cold wind, the warmth of the celebration still lingering. Now it was only Yichen and Xiaoran, walking slowly toward her apartment. Alone for the first time all day.

“…Your teammates are fun.”

“Hm.”

“They’re also very noisy.”

“Correct.”

Xiaoran kicked a pebble along the sidewalk.

“…I’m glad I went.”

Yichen glanced at her. That sentence mattered more than she realized.

“I told you. You belong there.”

Xiaoran looked away.

“…I still felt nervous.”

“Why.”

“Because you looked so… different today.”

Yichen blinked.

“Different?”

“You looked really cool.”

Dead silence. That compliment again—soft, sincere, dangerous for his heart.

“Everyone likes you there.”

“That worries you?”

“A little.”

A very Lin Xiaoran answer.

“You shine a lot when you play basketball.”

Silence.

“And?”

“And I don’t know.” She frowned lightly. “It just suddenly feels like a lot of people can see how good you are now.”

Ah. There it was. Not jealousy, exactly. Not insecurity. Just that strange fear of falling too far behind someone you love.

“Xiaoran, you know what I wanted after the game?”

“…What?”

Yichen kept his eyes on the road ahead.

“You, beside me at the celebration. When we won, I looked for you first.”

She remembered. She remembered that moment exactly—the crowd screaming, his teammates all around him, and him still looking for her first.

“You really like me a lot huh.”

Yichen laughed quietly.

“There it is.”

“What.”

“You acting surprised every time.”

“Well you hide it calmly.”

Xiaoran suddenly stopped walking. Yichen turned.

“…What happened.”

But instead of answering—she just looked at him under the streetlights. He looked unfair tonight—relaxed after the win, hair still messy from the game, hands in his jacket pockets, tired eyes on nobody but her.

“…You’re too handsome lately.”

Yichen actually smiled this time—a real one, the dangerous kind.

Xiaoran stepped in and hugged him tightly. Warm hoodie, familiar comfort, all at once. And quietly against his chest—

“…I’m proud of you.”

That hit harder than the entire tournament. Yichen wrapped both arms around her properly and held her close, carefully, like something precious. Then softly above her head—

“Say that again.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“You’ll become arrogant.”

Too late. Zhou Yichen’s heart was already beating embarrassingly fast. He lowered his head and pressed one slow kiss to her forehead—gentle, lingering, more affectionate than teasing.

“Thank you for supporting me.”

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened in his hoodie. Hearing him say it so softly was unfair.

“…You’re suddenly too gentle.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“No.”

“No?”

“You just finally stopped running away every time I say something honest.”

Xiaoran buried her face deeper in his chest.

“Stop talking.”

“There she is.”

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran’s first field assignment. Zhou Yichen moves his schedule to hold her iced tea.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Was Completely Useless During the Assignment
chapters.epigraph: “If you got nervous, I wanted to be there already.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran’s first major media faculty assignment sounded very serious academically. A campus documentary project. Students had to go off campus, interview small local business owners, record footage and atmosphere shots, and edit it all into a short visual story. Very professional. Very independent. Very “real university student.” Xiaoran was handling it surprisingly well, which should have been the end of the story. Unfortunately, Zhou Yichen decided he needed to come anyway, despite being completely irrelevant to media production.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You do realize I can survive outside alone.”

Yichen nodded calmly while walking beside her.

“Hm.”

“Then why are you here.”

“You said the filming location is far.”

“It’s literally two subway stations away.”

“And?”

“And you have business faculty group discussion later.”

“I moved it.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran stopped walking.

“…You moved your schedule?”

“Hm.”

“FOR THIS?”

Yichen looked genuinely confused by her reaction.

“You sounded nervous yesterday.”

Because yes, she had been nervous yesterday—not because she couldn’t do the assignment, but because it was her first time doing field interviews alone. New place, new people, equipment she was responsible for. And somehow Yichen had noticed without her saying a word.

“…I didn’t ask you to come.”

“You didn’t need to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The funniest part was that Zhou Yichen contributed absolutely nothing academically. Nothing. Xiaoran interviewed a bakery owner, holding the camera carefully, while Yichen sat in the corner with her spare tote bag and iced tea like emotionally supportive furniture. The bakery auntie kept glancing at him curiously.

“That’s your boyfriend right?”

Dead silence. Xiaoran nearly dropped the microphone.

“…Yes.”

“He’s been staring at you the entire time.”

Across the shop, Yichen looked up, not even embarrassed. The auntie laughed.

“He looks more nervous than you.”

She was right. Despite acting calm, Yichen had spent the last hour silently monitoring everything. Was the road crowded? Had she eaten lunch? Was the equipment too heavy? Would strangers bother her? Entirely unnecessary concerns. Still there. Afterward, reviewing footage outside the café, Xiaoran finally turned to him.

“…You’re weird today.”

“Hm?”

“You keep following me.”

“I’m walking normally.”

“No, you are not.”

Every time she moved locations, Yichen followed—holding umbrellas, carrying equipment, opening doors, standing nearby during interviews while contributing zero information. A male student came over.

“Excuse me,” he asked Xiaoran, “are you filming for media faculty?”

“Ah, yes.”

“I’m from journalism. If you need help with editing software—”

“No need.”

Dead silence. The poor student blinked. Zhou Yichen had answered before Xiaoran could even open her mouth—calmly, naturally, possessively. Xiaoran stared at him.

“…Why did YOU answer.”

Yichen looked calm.

“You already know editing.”

“That’s not the point.”

The journalism student quietly escaped. Smart man. Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“…Were you jealous?”

“No.”

“You interrupted him.”

“He was staring at you too long.”

“There it is.”

Yichen said nothing, which was confirmation. Xiaoran grinned.

“You followed me around all day because of jealousy?”

“I followed you because you get lost.”

“That’s also true.”

By sunset, the assignment was done. Xiaoran was tired and hungry, and genuinely happy. She had done well today. The interviews went smoothly, the footage looked good, and for the first time since starting university she felt capable at this.

“…I think I’m getting better at this. I wasn’t even that nervous by the end.”

Yichen looked at her.

“You did well.”

Calm, simple praise—but compliments from him always felt more serious.

“Thank you for coming with me.”

“You really didn’t need to.”

“I know,” he said quietly.

Xiaoran blinked. Then Yichen continued calmly—

“You’re capable of handling things yourself.”

“Then why come?”

For one second—he looked thoughtful, like he was trying to explain something difficult simply.

“Because I wanted to see you doing what you like. And if you got nervous,” he admitted softly, “I wanted to be there already.”

The evening suddenly felt warmer, and Lin Xiaoran’s heart went soft. He really did treat her like someone precious, all the time.

“…You know you didn’t help at all, right? You contributed nothing.”

Yichen laughed.

“I carried bags.”

“You held iced tea.”

“Important support role.”

Xiaoran stepped closer, smiling, and hooked both arms around his waist. Then quietly against his chest—

“…Still liked having you there though.”

That small, honest confession hit Zhou Yichen harder than he expected. Then softly above her head—

“Good.”

Then he kissed her forehead, like he’d been wanting to all day.

chapters.desc: A national media strategy competition, a month of 2 AM study sessions, and something Lin Xiaoran wants to prove.
chapters.title: Lin Xiaoran’s First Win
chapters.epigraph: “I want to know I can be good at something difficult too.”
chapters.content:
Nobody expected Lin Xiaoran to voluntarily join an academic competition. Including Lin Xiaoran herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s not academic-academic,” she defended weakly while waving the registration poster at Zhou Yichen.

He looked down calmly. National University Creative Media Strategy Competition. Project-based, presentation-based, research-based. Very brain-based. Yichen looked back up slowly.

“…This looks deeply academic.”

“It’s media.”

“There are charts.”

“Creative charts.”

The competition involved far more than creativity. Students had to build a full media campaign proposal—research, audience analysis, branding strategy, content planning—and then defend it in front of judges. Weeks of thinking. Tragic news for Lin Xiaoran, who was creative but hated structured intellectual suffering. So why join? Because at university, for the first time, she wanted to prove something—not to teachers or classmates, just to herself. That she wasn’t only “cute.” Wasn’t only “Yichen’s girlfriend.” Wasn’t only emotional chaos in human form. That maybe she could actually make something good.

✦ ✦ ✦

The month of preparation was horrifying, because Lin Xiaoran briefly turned into a serious person. Very briefly. 2 AM, the business faculty study room, and Xiaoran sat buried in papers, muttering at her laptop.

“…Why are statistics shaped like this.”

Across from her, Yichen was reviewing her slides.

“You wrote this chart wrong.”

“I hate graphs.”

“You labeled the age demographic backwards.”

“Oh my god.”

A few business students at the next table were watching with fascination: the famous basketball player Zhou Yichen, spending his nights patiently helping his girlfriend organize competition data. Without complaint. Xiaoran collapsed across the table.

“Yichen. My brain feels boiled.”

“You’ve said that every night this week.”

“Because it’s true.”

But for all the complaining, she worked hard. Harder than Yichen had ever seen. She watched research videos during meals, practiced her presentation alone, and redid entire sections because “it doesn’t feel smart enough.” She even woke up early voluntarily, which genuinely scared him. One night, while fixing her presentation notes, Yichen asked quietly,

“Why are you pushing yourself this hard.”

Then Xiaoran answered softly without looking up—

“…Because I want to win something myself.”

Dead silence. Something in him softened. She sounded sincere. Not bratty, not dramatic. Just honest.

“You already do a lot well.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“That sounds like comfort.”

“It’s true.”

“No. I want proof. I want to know I can actually be good at something difficult too.”

The room went quiet. Yichen reached over and squeezed the back of her neck gently.

“You are.”

Like he had never once doubted it. Somehow, that made her work even harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Competition day came too fast. A university auditorium. Several schools. Formal clothes. Actual judges. Lin Xiaoran wanted to disappear.

“This was a terrible decision.”

Beside her, Yichen straightened the sleeve of her blazer.

“You practiced enough.”

“What if my voice dies.”

“Then I’ll answer questions.”

“You’re not allowed to.”

“I’ll do it anyway.”

Yichen was not technically part of the competition. Not even remotely. He had come simply because “you’ll be nervous.” Correct. Right before they went into the hall, Xiaoran grabbed his wrist.

“…Do I look stupid.”

Dead silence. That question alone showed how nervous she was. Yichen looked at her carefully. Professional outfit. Hair tied neatly. Presentation folder clutched tight. Trying so hard not to panic. She looked beautiful—but more than that, she looked serious. Determined. Like someone slowly growing into herself.

“You look cool.”

Silence.

“And smart.”

That one hit harder. Much harder. People complimented her looks all the time. But Zhou Yichen—someone genuinely brilliant—calling her smart?

“…Don’t say things that affect my heart before presentations.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The presentation itself felt surreal. At first her hands shook, her voice was nervous, her breathing uneven. Then, somewhere in the middle, she relaxed—because she realized she actually understood her project, deeply. Every late night, every revision, every practice run was inside her now. Slowly, her confidence showed: clear explanations, sharp ideas, unexpectedly strong answers when the judges questioned her. Even the audience looked impressed. From the back row, Zhou Yichen couldn’t stop staring. Not because she looked cute, or because she was his girlfriend, but because she looked capable. Bright. Passionate. Like someone standing properly in her own world. It made his chest tighten. Lin Xiaoran had grown so much without even noticing.

Results. Third place. Second place. And then—

“First place…”

“…Lin Xiaoran’s team from the Media Faculty.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…What.”

Her teammates screamed first. Someone grabbed her. The auditorium broke into applause, and Lin Xiaoran stood on stage holding her certificate, completely stunned. She genuinely hadn’t expected to win. Not really. Her eyes went straight to the audience. There—Yichen, standing near the back, smiling. Not surprised. Like he had known all along. Somehow that nearly made her cry harder than the award.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the auditorium, Xiaoran ran straight to him, still clutching the trophy awkwardly, eyes bright, cheeks pink. And before Yichen could even speak—

“I WON.”

“Hm.”

“I ACTUALLY WON.”

“I know.”

“You knew?!”

Yichen laughed and steadied her before she tripped.

“You worked hard enough.”

“No but—”

Xiaoran stopped talking, because looking at him, she realized something embarrassing: the person who had believed in her first was always Zhou Yichen. Even before she believed in herself.

“…I think I’m really happy.”

Yichen looked down at her softly.

“I know.”

He reached over and fixed her messy hair.

“You looked really cool up there.”

Somehow, hearing that from him felt even better than winning first place.

chapters.desc: A livestream assignment, thirty identical bottles, and eyeliner—the destroyer of relationships.
chapters.title: Can My Boyfriend Do My Makeup?
chapters.epigraph: “Why is this harder than free throws?”
chapters.content:
The assignment sounded simple. Too simple. Which should have been the first warning sign. As part of her media production course, Lin Xiaoran had to run a livestream: audience interaction, an engagement challenge, real-time content, something entertaining. Then her professor added one more requirement.

“It has to be authentic.”

The moment Xiaoran heard that word—she knew exactly who her victim would be.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later, Zhou Yichen received a message.

Xiaoran: Need your help.

Yichen: Okay.

Xiaoran: For an assignment.

Yichen: Okay.

Xiaoran: You have to do my makeup live on camera.

Yichen: …

Yichen: What?

✦ ✦ ✦

The livestream was titled Can My Boyfriend Do My Makeup? A terrible idea. An excellent idea. A very successful idea, mostly because Zhou Yichen looked like he wanted to flee the country.

✦ ✦ ✦

The livestream started at 7 PM. Within ten minutes, several hundred viewers had joined: mostly university students, some of Xiaoran’s classmates, a suspicious number of basketball team members, and, unfortunately, Chen Yuhao. The comments exploded right away.

“IS THIS THE BASKETBALL GUY?”

“WHY DOES HE LOOK SO NERVOUS”

“HE LOOKS LIKE HE’S ABOUT TO TAKE AN EXAM”

“HE LOOKS TOO HANDSOME FOR THIS”

Zhou Yichen stared at the products spread across the table—foundation, concealer, primer, powder, blush, contour, bronzer, highlighter—and went very still.

“Why are there so many.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“That’s your problem.”

“This is unreasonable.”

“You survived business school.”

“Business school never gave me thirty identical bottles.”

The chat lost it.

“HE’S RIGHT”

“THIRTY IDENTICAL BOTTLES”

“I’M CRYING”

Yichen picked up a tube.

“What is this.”

“Primer.”

“What does it do.”

“I don’t know.”

“You don’t know?”

“I just use it.”

Dead silence. Yichen looked genuinely betrayed.

“YOU DON’T KNOW?”

“NO.”

The audience couldn’t stop laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, the challenge began, and Xiaoran fully expected disaster. Zhou Yichen’s hands weren’t exactly made for makeup. Basketball, weight training—his hands were large, rough, strong. Not the kind anyone associated with delicate beauty routines. But the moment he actually started, something changed. Zhou Yichen took the task seriously. Far too seriously, like everything else. He leaned in, studying her face, wearing the same focused expression he had before tournaments. The comments changed.

“WAIT”

“WHY IS HE TRYING SO HARD”

“THIS IS CUTE”

“HE LOOKS MORE NERVOUS THAN SHE DOES”

He was. Terrified—not of embarrassing himself, but of hurting her. The makeup sponge hovered uncertainly near her face.

“Am I pressing too hard?”

“No.”

“This?”

“No.”

“This?”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“What.”

“You’ve blended the same spot for a full minute.”

“I want consistency.”

The comments exploded again. Yichen kept concentrating. The closer he got, the more nervous he became. Makeup apparently required precision, and Xiaoran’s skin looked so soft. The opposite of basketball. One wrong move and he’d ruin everything.

Then came eyeliner. The final boss. The destroyer of relationships. The chat noticed immediately.

“OH NO”

“GOOD LUCK BRO”

“HE’S FINISHED”

Even Xiaoran got nervous. Eyeliner. Yichen stared at the tiny brush. Then at her eye. Then at the brush again.

“Why is this harder than free throws.”

“Because if you miss, it’s my face.”

Very gently, he lifted her chin—one hand supporting her face, the other holding the eyeliner—and the room went quiet. Even the comments slowed down. Everything felt softer. Closer. His concentration was absolute. His thumb rested lightly against her cheek.

“Don’t move.”

“I’m not moving.”

“Good.”

For several seconds, neither of them spoke. He was just trying his best—not to mess up, not to poke her eye, not to ruin her assignment.

“Your eyelashes are really long.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran blinked. The chat exploded.

“HE’S GONE”

“IT’S OVER”

“THAT WAS NOT NECESSARY”

“WHY WAS THAT SO SWEET”

Yichen looked confused.

“What.”

“You just complimented my eyelashes.”

“…I was making an observation.”

The audience refused to believe him. Correctly.

✦ ✦ ✦

After nearly an hour, it was finished. Xiaoran looked in the mirror and blinked. Then blinked again.

“…Wait.”

Yichen looked worried.

“What happened.”

“It’s good.”

“What.”

“It’s actually good.”

Dead silence. Nobody had expected that. Not even him. The blush placement worked. The foundation matched. The eyeliner had survived. Not professional—but pretty. Very pretty. Then the comments poured in.

“HE COOKED”

“HOW DID HE WIN”

“BEGINNER’S LUCK”

“I’M SHOWING THIS TO MY BOYFRIEND”

Yichen looked like he had just finished a final exam.

“Good.”

Xiaoran looked at him—really looked. The tired eyes. The careful attention he’d put into every tiny detail. And suddenly she understood: the makeup wasn’t the important part. The important part was that he had cared about every brush stroke, because it was her face. Before the stream ended, she leaned over and kissed his cheek. Quick. Unexpected. The comments descended into chaos. Zhou Yichen froze. After surviving foundation, blush, eyeliner, and public humiliation, the hardest part of the evening was still Lin Xiaoran. Very on brand.

chapters.desc: Four hours of silence, one genuinely angry boyfriend, and a stuffed panda deployed as a weapon.
chapters.title: The Selfie That Made Zhou Yichen Forget Why He Was Angry
chapters.epigraph: “You cannot send selfies during arguments.”
chapters.content:
There was a very important rule in Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran’s relationship. If Zhou Yichen became genuinely angry, Lin Xiaoran usually went quiet right away, because for all her spoiled behavior, she hated disappointing him. Today was different. Today she decided to fight back with selfies.

✦ ✦ ✦

The argument itself wasn’t even dramatic. It started because Xiaoran forgot something important. Again. She forgot to tell Yichen she’d be staying late with her media project group. Normally not a big deal—except she disappeared for almost four hours with her phone nearly dead. No messages. No updates. Zhou Yichen spent those four hours getting irritated, then worried, then irritated again because he was worried. A terrible combination—especially since this wasn’t the first time. Orientation day had gone almost exactly like this, minus the media senior.

By the time she finally called him, his mood was terrible.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Hello?”

“Yichen.”

Nothing on the other end. Just silence.

“Oh no.”

Zhou Yichen almost never gave the silent treatment. This was serious.

“Where are you.”

“…Media building.”

“You remembered your phone exists.”

“That’s a little aggressive.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

Uh oh. Boyfriend genuinely angry.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thirty minutes later, they met outside her apartment building, and Yichen was still angry. Not loud angry. Not dramatic angry. Much worse: calm angry. The terrifying version. They sat on a bench, Yichen talking and Xiaoran listening like a student being disciplined.

“You couldn’t send one message?”

“I forgot.”

“You couldn’t borrow a phone? You couldn’t tell me beforehand?”

Xiaoran had no answer.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down guiltily, because he was right. Completely right.

“I was busy.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you angry?”

Dead silence. Wrong question. Very wrong question. Yichen finally looked at her, and that made her feel worse—not because he looked angry, but because he looked worried. Actually worried.

“I thought something happened.”

Silence.

“I called twelve times.”

Silence.

“You weren’t answering.”

The argument stopped feeling funny. This wasn’t about control, or checking up on her, or being possessive. He had been scared.

“…Sorry.”

Yichen sighed, long and tired, and stood up.

“I’m going back.”

“…Still angry?”

“Hm.”

“…How angry.”

Yichen looked at her once.

“…Very.” Then he walked away.

Uh oh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours later, Zhou Yichen was still angry. Not furious. Just stubbornly annoyed, which honestly lasted longer. He sat in his apartment reviewing notes, trying to focus, mostly failing, because his phone kept lighting up.

Xiaoran: Are you still angry

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: How much

Yichen: Enough.

Xiaoran: That doesn’t explain anything

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: You’re being mean.

No response. Two minutes later—another message.

Xiaoran: :(

Ignored. Thirty seconds later—

Xiaoran: I apologised already

Ignored. Five minutes of silence. Finally. Peace. Then his phone vibrated again. Yichen opened it without thinking—and froze. Lin Xiaoran had sent a selfie.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t even a special selfie. That was the worst part. Just her, sitting on her bed in oversized pajamas, hair messy from the shower, holding a stuffed panda against her cheek and pouting. Caption: still angry? This girl. This absolutely shameless girl.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen stared at the picture. Then stared longer. Then rubbed his forehead, because his anger was suddenly much harder to hold on to. Unfortunately, Xiaoran knew him too well. Another photo arrived. Different angle. Same pout. Caption: i think this face deserves forgiveness

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Liar.

Yichen: Not lying.

Xiaoran: Then why did you save the photo

She had somehow noticed. Terrifying woman.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across campus, Xiaoran grinned victoriously from her bed. She knew exactly what she was doing. Then another message.

Xiaoran: Look

Attached: another selfie. This time hugging the panda. Caption: this girl misses her boyfriend

Yichen: That girl is irresponsible.

Xiaoran: But cute.

Yichen: That’s not relevant.

Xiaoran: It feels relevant.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: You’re smiling.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: You are.

Yichen: Go to sleep.

Xiaoran: HAHA

Caught. Completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

The worst part was that she wasn’t even apologizing properly anymore. Now she was teasing him. Deliberately. Weaponizing cuteness. Another photo arrived. Yichen groaned, because somehow she looked even cuter in this one. Caption: boyfriend still angry :( Then another. Caption: he doesn’t love me anymore :( Then another. Caption: single woman era begins. Yichen called her. Immediately, before she could send any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second she answered, Xiaoran started laughing.

“You’re impossible.”

“There he is.”

“Lin Xiaoran, you cannot send selfies during arguments.”

“Why.”

“Because it’s cheating.”

“I learned from experts.”

“You are the expert.”

Then a short silence. A comfortable one. The anger was finally fading.

“…Are you still angry?”

This time it sounded sincere. Not teasing. Just soft. Yichen sighed. He wasn’t angry anymore. Not really. Annoyed? A little. Worried? Still. But angry? Impossible—not after hearing her voice, not after those stupid photos, not after knowing she was safe.

“A little.”

“Liar.”

“Hm.”

“You forgave me already.”

Then Yichen admitted quietly—

“…Mostly.”

Victory. Xiaoran smiled brightly.

“I’ll message next time.”

“You said that at orientation.”

“I mean it this time.”

“I know.”

“…Send me the third photo.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing so hard she nearly dropped her phone.

“YOU SAVED THEM.”

“No.”

“YOU DID.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The silence confirmed everything. Somewhere in his apartment, Zhou Yichen realized he had lost the argument completely. Again. Lin Xiaoran could beat him with nothing but a messy selfie and a stuffed panda—a strategy he considered deeply unfair.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran posts three photos for the first time in months. Zhou Yichen makes the mistake of scrolling down.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Read the Comments
chapters.epigraph: “I just didn’t like everyone else liking them too.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran rarely posted on social media. Mostly because she forgot it existed. Her entire account was one photo of a cake, two photos of a panda, one blurry sunset, and a picture of Zhou Yichen’s sleeve from two years ago. That was it. So when she suddenly posted after almost three months of silence, the whole friend group noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cause was stupid, as most important Xiaoran events were. Earlier that week, her faculty had finished a photography workshop—portraits, lighting, composition, editing, all the artsy things media students loved. Xiaoran hadn’t cared much, until her classmates showed her the final photos. She looked amazing. Not because the photos were revealing—they weren’t—but because for the first time she looked mature. Elegant. Confident. Different from her usual cute, chaotic self. Even she was surprised.

“That’s me?”

Her classmate laughed.

“Who else would it be?”

“No, seriously.”

She stared at the photo again: a long black dress, soft lighting, hair falling over one shoulder, looking straight into the camera. For once she didn’t look like someone about to ask a capybara-related question. She looked pretty. Very pretty. Her classmates encouraged her.

“Post it.”

“No.”

“Post it.”

“No.”

“POST IT.”

Peer pressure won.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Xiaoran uploaded three photos. Caption: Media assignment finally finished ✨ Nothing dramatic. Nothing suggestive. Just beautiful photos. Unfortunately, the internet suddenly remembered she existed.

✦ ✦ ✦

By midnight the post had exploded, far beyond her usual engagement. Classmates. Seniors. Friends. People she barely knew. Pretty. Gorgeous. Stunning. Beautiful.

Then came the problem: male comments. Lots of male comments.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran woke up to dozens of notifications. Elsewhere on campus, Zhou Yichen discovered the post.

✦ ✦ ✦

At first he just smiled. The photos looked incredible. He stared for several seconds. Then longer. Then saved one, for completely reasonable boyfriend reasons. Then he opened the comments. Mistake. Huge mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Senior, you’re beautiful.”

“Can I get to know you?”

“Media faculty goddess.”

“Whoever dates her is lucky.”

“Marry me.”

Dead silence. Zhou Yichen stared. Then stared harder. Then kept scrolling, which made everything worse, because the comments kept going. And going.

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunchtime, Chen Yuhao had already received a message.

Yichen: People are annoying.

Yuhao: What happened?

Yichen: Read Xiaoran’s comments.

Five minutes later—

Yuhao: HAHAHAHAHAHA

Yuhao: You’re jealous.

Yichen: No.

Yuhao: You’re definitely jealous.

Yichen: No.

Yuhao: You sent me fourteen screenshots.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran remained completely unaware, sitting outside the media building eating snacks in peace—until Yichen appeared and sat down beside her. Very calmly. Too calmly. Xiaoran became suspicious.

“…Why do you look like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re plotting.”

“I’m not.”

Liar. Very obvious liar. Yichen held out his phone. Her post.

“…Oh.”

Silence.

“Oh.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“You read the comments.”

“Hm.”

“And?”

Another silence.

“A lot of people seem interested.”

Zhou Yichen only sounded this calm when he was actively trying not to be unreasonable. Xiaoran blinked.

“…Are you jealous?”

“No.”

Too fast. She grinned.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen looked away, which confirmed everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The funny part was that Xiaoran didn’t feel annoyed. She felt delighted. Zhou Yichen was usually ridiculously secure—calm, confident, unbothered. So every time this tiny bit of jealousy showed up—at orientation, with the journalism student, and now here—it delighted her all over again. She scooted closer.

“…Do you know why I posted them?”

Yichen looked at her.

“No.”

“Because I liked how I looked. I thought maybe I’d gotten a little prettier.”

Silence. Yichen laughed—one quiet, helpless laugh. After all this, that was her reason? Not attention. Not validation. Just simple happiness.

“You did.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

“You looked beautiful.”

That compliment mattered more than every comment combined.

“I liked the photos.”

“…Really?”

“Hm.”

Another pause.

“I just didn’t like everyone else liking them too.”

There it was. Actual honesty. Xiaoran burst out laughing—hard—until Yichen caught her wrist.

“Stop laughing.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“This is adorable.”

She leaned in, eyes sparkling.

“Too bad.”

“…What.”

“I’m posting more photos eventually.”

Yichen sighed deeply, like a man accepting fate. He wasn’t upset that she’d posted, or that she looked beautiful. If anything, he liked seeing her confident. The problem was simply that everyone else noticed too. A deeply inconvenient development. Xiaoran rested her head against his shoulder, still smiling.

“Don’t worry. No matter how many comments I get…”

She squeezed his hand lightly.

“…I’m still your girlfriend.”

The last trace of jealousy disappeared, because that was the only thing he actually cared about.

chapters.desc: Finals week, a stress habit nobody noticed, and Zhou Yichen at the campus pharmacy with enough supplies for a minor apocalypse.
chapters.title: Stop Biting Your Lip
chapters.epigraph: “Because you take care of everyone except yourself.”
chapters.content:
There was something very important everyone knew about Lin Xiaoran. She looked delicate. Soft voice, pretty face, cute habits—the kind of girl who looked like she belonged in a romance drama. Reality was different. Lin Xiaoran had the pain tolerance of a construction worker. The problem started during finals month. Specifically, the week from hell: a media project deadline, two presentations, three exams, one group assignment, and approximately zero remaining brain cells.

For seven straight days, Xiaoran survived almost entirely on coffee, snacks, and academic suffering, and Zhou Yichen grew more and more concerned. Something felt off.

“Eat properly.”

“I am.”

“Cookies don’t count.”

“They count.”

“No.”

Then later—

“Sleep.”

“I’m editing.”

“It’s two in the morning.”

“I’m almost done.”

“You said that yesterday.”

And the day before. And the day before that. The worst part was that Xiaoran didn’t notice anything wrong herself. Until one afternoon. Media building. Group project meeting. Everyone exhausted, everyone academically dying. Xiaoran sat reviewing footage, absentmindedly chewing her lower lip—a bad habit when she was stressed. She had been doing it all week without realizing. One teammate froze.

“…Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Your mouth.”

“My mouth what?”

“You are literally bleeding.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran blinked. She touched her lower lip. Red. Actual blood.

“…Oh.”

“Oh?!”

Between dehydration, stress, and constant lip-biting, the skin had finally cracked badly. Xiaoran looked completely unconcerned.

“It doesn’t hurt.”

“THAT IS NOT THE POINT.”

Someone made the mistake of telling Luo Jiayi, and Luo Jiayi made the mistake of texting Zhou Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later, the meeting room door opened and Zhou Yichen walked in. The whole group recognized him, mostly because he was impossible not to recognize: university basketball team, business faculty, and—unfortunately for Xiaoran—her boyfriend. One teammate whispered,

“Oh no.”

Another nodded.

“She’s getting parented.”

Yichen walked straight to her, stopped, looked down, and frowned. It looked worse than he had expected—a visible crack in her lower lip, slightly swollen, still red. Xiaoran smiled innocently.

“Hi.”

No response.

“How long.”

“…What?”

“How long has this been happening.”

“…Today?”

A lie. A terrible one. One teammate betrayed her immediately.

“Three days.”

“QIN LU.”

Yichen closed his eyes briefly, like a man asking heaven for patience.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, Xiaoran was sitting in the campus pharmacy against her will while Yichen bought medicine.

“It doesn’t even hurt.”

“Hm.”

“You’re overreacting.”

“Hm.”

“Yichen.”

“Hm.”

The one-syllable answers meant danger. Finally he sat down beside her with lip balm, healing ointment, water, and enough supplies to survive a minor apocalypse.

“This is ridiculous.”

Yichen looked at her. He tilted her chin up, very gently, to look, and his mood got worse. She kept saying it wasn’t serious, but it looked painful.

“Stop biting them.”

“I don’t do it on purpose.”

“I know. But you still do it.”

Silence. Because he was right. Again. Annoyingly right.

Then came the embarrassing part: Yichen decided to apply the medicine himself. In public. At the pharmacy. While people watched.

“Open your mouth.”

“What.”

“Medicine.”

“I can do it.”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“No.”

Dead silence. He was stubborn today. Eventually, Xiaoran surrendered, for survival purposes. Behind the counter, the pharmacist watched the whole thing with open amusement while Yichen applied the medicine extremely carefully, like she was made of glass.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

A lie. It did hurt a little now, but admitting that felt inconvenient. Yichen narrowed his eyes.

“You just flinched.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

Caught. Again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward, they walked back toward campus on a quiet afternoon, students everywhere, until Yichen finally spoke.

“You’ve been stressed.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“A little.”

There it was. The truth.

“I’m okay.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you worried?”

Yichen stopped walking and looked at her—really looked. Tired eyes. Messy hair. An exhausted expression she thought nobody noticed.

“Because you take care of everyone except yourself. You’ll spend three hours helping teammates. You’ll remember my practice schedule. You’ll remind other people to sleep. But you won’t take care of yourself.”

For once, Lin Xiaoran had no argument, because he was completely right. Again.

“…Sorry.”

Yichen sighed—long, helpless, fond. The sigh of a man who had been dating Lin Xiaoran for years. He reached over and pinched her cheek.

“Stop apologizing.”

“What then?”

“Take care of yourself.”

“I’ll try.”

“You will.”

“I said I’ll try.”

“You will.”

There it was: the Zhou Yichen certainty, absolutely impossible to argue with.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, she got a message.

Yichen: Did you apply the medicine?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Photo.

Xiaoran: WHAT

Yichen: Evidence.

Xiaoran: You’re insane.

Yichen: Photo.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, she sent a selfie: lip balm visible, pouting. Caption: medical patient suffering A minute later, his reply came.

Yichen: Cute.

This man had spent the whole afternoon worrying himself sick, and still found her cute. Absolutely hopeless boyfriend.

chapters.desc: Three years together, and Lin Xiaoran has never once seen Zhou Yichen watch basketball. Until 8 AM on a Saturday.
chapters.title: The Terrifying Discovery That Zhou Yichen Was a Nerd
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not nerd things. It’s an organized binder.”
chapters.content:
For almost three years, Lin Xiaoran believed she understood Zhou Yichen completely. Basketball. Business major. Good grades. Annoyingly handsome. Secret softie. Simple. Reasonable. Normal. Then one Saturday morning, she discovered a side of him that genuinely frightened her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It began because Xiaoran was bored. She had claimed one corner of Yichen’s sofa at eight in the morning, supposedly to study, and was mostly drawing pandas in the margins of her media theory notes. Yichen sat at the other end with his laptop. Peaceful. Normal. Then the laptop let out a roar—a full arena of people screaming at once. Xiaoran looked up.

“…What was that?”

“Hm?”

“That.”

Yichen glanced at the screen. “Oh. The game started.”

“What game? It’s eight in the morning.”

“It’s eight in the evening in New York.”

She stared at him. “You get up at eight on a Saturday to watch basketball?”

“Sometimes seven.”

“You never told me.”

“You never asked.”

Fair. Annoyingly fair. She already knew he loved basketball. Everyone knew. She had watched him play for three years, held his jacket through tournaments, researched potassium for him. But she had never once seen him watch it. So she climbed across the sofa and sat beside him, curious. That was her first mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the screen, players ran up and down a court under blinding lights while two commentators talked very fast. Xiaoran understood the basics: ball, hoop, tall men. Then she noticed something horrifying. Yichen was paying attention. Not casual attention, not background-noise attention. The kind of focus he usually reserved for his own games, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole court instead of following the ball. One play ended in a missed shot. Immediately—

“He should have switched.”

Xiaoran turned slowly. “…What?”

“The big man stayed in drop coverage. That gave the guard the whole pull-up.”

“What.”

“And the weak-side help was late, so the corner was open anyway.”

“What.”

“They’ve been doing it all quarter. His shooting numbers off the dribble are the best in the league this month.”

“WHAT.”

Yichen finally looked at her, and paused, because she was staring at him like he had grown a second head.

“…You know what all of that means?” she asked.

“Hm.”

“ALL of it?”

“Hm.”

She grabbed both his shoulders. “WHO ARE YOU?”

✦ ✦ ✦

It got worse, because once she started asking questions, he answered them.

“How do you know they’ll lose?”

“They’re losing the possession battle. Too many turnovers.”

“The what battle?”

“And their spacing is terrible. Look—four guys on one side of the floor.”

“Yichen, you’re speaking wizard.”

“It’s basketball.”

“It is NOT the basketball I know. The basketball I know is you running around looking handsome and me screaming.”

“That’s also basketball.”

The terrifying part was that he wasn’t even trying. It just came out of him, the way math did, the way finding her in a crowd did. Then, during a commercial break, Xiaoran discovered the bookshelf. Huge mistake. Behind the business textbooks, filling an entire shelf, was a row of thick notebooks with years written on the spines in his neat handwriting, starting from when he was thirteen. She pulled one out. Inside were hand-drawn diagrams—circles and arrows and dotted lines—with notes in the margins. Backdoor cut works if the wing over-helps. Try in practice. Dad says I always pass too early.

Under the notebooks was a shoebox full of ticket stubs from city league games, a dog-eared book called Spacing, Tempo and the Modern Offense, and a binder of printed shot charts with colored highlighter on every page. She held up the binder like evidence in a courtroom.

“What is THIS.”

Yichen glanced over. “Shot charts.”

“You PRINTED them. And HIGHLIGHTED them.”

“It’s easier to see on paper.”

“You did this for FUN?”

“Hm.”

Silence. Her boyfriend was a nerd. An actual nerd. Not a basketball player who happened to be smart—a basketball nerd, with a filing system. Yichen looked confused by her reaction. To him this was obviously normal.

“My dad used to watch games with me,” he said, by way of explanation. “He’d pause the replay and ask what I would’ve done.”

“THAT DOESN’T EXPLAIN THE HIGHLIGHTER.”

He looked at the binder, then at her, then back at the binder, genuinely puzzled about where the problem was.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the game came back, the calm, composed Zhou Yichen disappeared entirely.

“Why would you take that shot? No. NO. There’s twenty seconds on the clock.”

“They just threw the game away.”

Xiaoran stared at him. This man was emotionally invested. Deeply, aggressively invested in a team on the other side of the planet that did not know he existed. Then, in the last minute, one player made a cut so clean the defense didn’t even turn around in time, caught the pass in stride, and laid it in. Yichen sat bolt upright.

“THAT was beautiful.”

Xiaoran had never heard him call anything beautiful except a basketball play of his own, and her. Apparently, now there were three things.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rest of the morning became educational suffering, because every time she asked one question, he answered with a lecture.

“What’s a pick-and-roll?”

Twenty minutes.

“What’s drop coverage?”

Fifteen minutes, with diagrams on the back of her media theory notes.

“Why does everyone keep yelling about spacing?”

Thirty minutes. She regretted that one deeply. When the game finally ended, Xiaoran sat slumped against the cushions, mentally exhausted. Yichen looked perfectly happy.

“…You really love this,” she said.

“Hm.”

Simple answer. But it landed differently, because she rarely saw him like this. Not competitive. Not responsible. Not quietly taking care of everyone around him. Just excited, the way a kid gets excited. A little nerdy.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“Know what?”

“That you could talk this much.”

He laughed—properly laughed.

“You asked questions.”

“YOU HAD ANSWERS READY. You had DIAGRAMS.”

She leaned against his shoulder anyway, warm and comfortable.

“It’s cute,” she said.

“What is?”

“You. Getting this excited about nerd things.”

“It’s not nerd things.”

“You have a binder.”

“It’s an organized binder.”

“SEE.”

He laughed again, helplessly, and put an arm around her waist. Xiaoran smiled into his shoulder. Three years, and she was still finding new parts of him—especially the parts nobody else got to see.

“Want to watch the game tomorrow?” he asked.

She looked up, suspicious. “Are you trying to convert me?”

“Maybe.”

“Will there be another lecture?”

“Probably.”

“Then no.”

“Understandable.”

But for the rest of the week, Lin Xiaoran kept asking—completely out of nowhere, in the middle of lunch, in the library, once during a movie—“What’s drop coverage again?”

Just to watch Zhou Yichen accidentally turn into a basketball nerd all over again.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen says he doesn’t need anything for his birthday. Lin Xiaoran remembers one sentence from three months ago.
chapters.title: Two Tickets to the Garden
chapters.epigraph: “Of course I remembered.”
chapters.content:
For most people, buying Zhou Yichen a birthday gift was difficult, because he already had everything. A family with money. Good grades. Basketball. Expensive watches, expensive shoes, expensive everything. Whenever his birthday came around, he said the same thing.

“I don’t need anything.”

Annoying answer. Especially for Lin Xiaoran, because this year she wanted the gift to matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months before his birthday, she found out what it should be. It was another early weekend morning on his sofa. Since discovering that her boyfriend was secretly a basketball nerd, Xiaoran had become very slightly interested in watching games—not much, just enough to understand when he started speaking wizard. She was eating crackers. He was explaining things nobody had asked about. Normal relationship activities. Then the broadcast cut to a wide shot of the arena: an enormous round ceiling, a sea of people, the court glowing in the middle like a stage.

“That’s the Garden,” Yichen said.

“Hm?”

“Madison Square Garden. New York.” He was quiet for a second. “One day I want to watch a game there.”

Xiaoran looked over, because Zhou Yichen almost never said things like that. He was still watching the screen, completely casual, as if he hadn’t just told her a dream.

“Really?”

“Hm.”

“Why that one?”

“It’s the Garden.”

“That explains nothing.”

He laughed quietly. “The history. The building. The way the crowd sounds.” Then, after a moment, more quietly: “Dad and I used to say we’d go. When I was a kid. He never had the time.”

“Why not now?”

He shrugged. “Season’s during school. Tickets. Flights. Planning.” He said it lightly. “Maybe someday.”

Then he went back to explaining spacing, like the conversation had never happened. Lin Xiaoran remembered every word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later, his birthday arrived. Yichen expected something small. A handmade gift, maybe. Clothes. One of Xiaoran’s chaotic, sincere little presents with a card covered in stickers. Instead she handed him an envelope.

“What is this?”

“Open it.”

He was immediately suspicious, because she looked far too excited. Inside were two tickets. For several seconds, Zhou Yichen’s brain stopped working. He read them, then read them again, then a third time, as if they might rearrange themselves into something more reasonable. New York. Madison Square Garden. A Saturday night in January, during winter break. Two seats, very high up, in a section number that began with a two.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing. He was staring at the tickets like they might disappear.

“What is this,” he finally said, very quietly.

Xiaoran blinked. “…Your birthday gift?”

“No.”

“What do you mean, no?”

“No.” He sounded genuinely stunned. A rare event. “Xiaoran. These are tickets to the Garden.”

“I know.”

“I can read.”

“Good.”

“LIN XIAORAN.”

She started laughing, because he looked so shocked, and the famous calm Zhou Yichen had apparently stopped functioning entirely.

“How,” he said.

So she explained. The prize money from the competition. The freelance video jobs she’d taken on weekends, editing a bakery’s promotional clips and a classmate’s cousin’s wedding. Three months of birthday budget. Learning far more about game schedules and seat maps than she had ever wanted to. Waking up at four in the morning to buy them the minute they went on sale. All because of one sentence on a Saturday morning.

“I wanted to surprise you,” she said.

He didn’t say anything. Suddenly Xiaoran felt nervous. Maybe it was too much. Maybe the seats were too high, or January was a bad time, or he’d rather go with his father, or—Yichen stood up. He walked around the table, pulled her to her feet, and hugged her. Hard. So suddenly that she almost squeaked.

“Yichen?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t let go, either.

“…Are you okay?”

Then he laughed—soft, disbelieving, almost helpless—against her hair.

“You’re insane.”

“I know.”

“You’re actually insane.”

But he still wasn’t letting go, and that told her everything. Zhou Yichen wasn’t a dramatic person. He didn’t get emotional easily or react loudly. Right now, he looked completely overwhelmed.

“You remembered,” he said quietly.

“Hm?”

“The Garden thing.”

And suddenly she understood. It wasn’t really about the tickets, or New York, or even basketball. It was that she had listened. One random morning, one casual sentence, one small dream he’d said out loud and then put away—and she had remembered.

“Of course I remembered,” she said.

He looked down at her, and for once his calm expression was nowhere to be found. The girl he loved had spent three months working and saving for this, just to make him happy. How was anyone supposed to stay calm after that?

“If someone asked me,” he said, “what the best birthday gift I’ve ever gotten was—”

His hand found hers.

“It would be this.”

Xiaoran looked extremely pleased.

“Better than your car?”

“Yes.”

“Better than your watch?”

“Yes.”

“Better than—”

“Stop comparing yourself to objects.”

She laughed. Then a thought hit her.

“Wait. You’re taking me, right? I bought two.”

He finally smiled—the real one, the one that only showed up for her.

“Obviously.”

He laced his fingers through hers.

“You bought the tickets. The least I can do is take the girl I love to New York to use them.”

For the next three days, Chen Yuhao became extremely tired of hearing Zhou Yichen talk about Madison Square Garden over the phone. This was impressive, because normally talking too much was Xiaoran’s job.

chapters.desc: Snow, a pretzel the size of her head, and an envelope that makes Lin Xiaoran shout in a Chinatown noodle shop.
chapters.title: New York Before Tip-Off
chapters.epigraph: “The gift was never the money.”
chapters.content:
The day before the game, Lin Xiaoran discovered two things. First, New York was absurdly big. Second, Zhou Yichen was richer than she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The moment they stepped out of the hotel, Xiaoran stopped walking. Completely. It had snowed overnight. The street was a canyon of buildings so tall she had to tip her head all the way back to see where they ended. Yellow taxis honked at nothing. Steam rose out of a grate in the road like the city was breathing. A man walked past carrying a Christmas tree, three weeks after Christmas, as if that were normal.

“…Xiaoran?”

She pointed at everything at once.

“It looks fake.”

“It’s a city.”

“No.” She pointed again, at a building with a gold roof. “It looks like someone built a movie set and forgot to take it down.”

Yichen smiled quietly. Watching her see New York, he decided, was better than seeing it himself. Every five minutes she discovered something new. Every ten minutes she took another photo. Every fifteen minutes she stopped dead in the middle of the sidewalk to stare up at something and got gently steered aside by a New Yorker who did not have time for this. They walked until their faces went numb. They watched skaters go around the rink under a giant gold statue. They shared a hot pretzel the size of Xiaoran’s head, which she declared “a little disappointing but still important.” They got lost twice—once in Central Park, once inside a single department store.

By evening they were sitting in a tiny noodle place in Chinatown, because a long flight and one hotel breakfast had already made Xiaoran homesick for broth, and the conversation finally turned to tomorrow. The game. The reason they had flown halfway around the world.

“I’m excited,” Xiaoran said. “Even though I still only understand half of what’s happening.”

“Hm.”

“You’ll explain.”

“Hm.”

“No lectures longer than ten minutes.”

“…Hm.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Why are you so happy?”

Yichen looked away. Which was already suspicious.

“There’s something I need to tell you.”

Uh oh.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“That sounds like something happened.”

“Not really.”

Then he slid an envelope across the table.

“…What is this.”

“Open it.”

Now it was her turn to be suspicious. Inside were documents. New tickets. Not their tickets—their tickets were safely in her bag, in a plastic sleeve, because she had checked them every hour since Shanghai. These had different section numbers. A lot lower. The row said A. Xiaoran read them twice.

“…Yichen.”

“Hm.”

“These are not our tickets.”

“Hm.”

“These say courtside.”

“Hm.”

She looked up, very slowly.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

There it was—the tone that meant I know exactly what you’ve done. He stayed calm, mostly because he had known this was coming.

“You upgraded them.”

“Hm.”

“You upgraded EVERYTHING.” She flipped through the rest. Courtside seats. A pregame arena tour. Access to watch the teams warm up from the tunnel. “Yichen, I know how much these cost.”

“Hm.”

“I WORKED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

“I SAVED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

The noodle shop owner glanced over from behind the counter. Two tables away, an elderly couple had stopped eating to watch. Then Xiaoran found the actual crime, tucked at the very back: a bank transfer receipt for exactly the amount she had paid for the original tickets. Silence.

“…No.”

Yichen sighed. Yes. This part. Always this part.

“No?”

“No.” She folded her arms. “Absolutely not.”

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

“Listen first.”

“No.”

He reached across the table and took her hand.

“You gave me the best birthday gift I’ve ever had,” he said. “You worked weekends for it. You saved your competition money. You got up at four in the morning to buy those tickets.”

She stayed quiet.

“And because I know how hard you worked,” he went on, thumb moving over her knuckles, “the last thing I want is for you to spend everything you saved on me.”

That made the argument harder. Much harder.

“The gift was never the money,” he said. “It was that you remembered. That you wanted me here.”

It was exactly the kind of answer Xiaoran couldn’t fight, because he wasn’t brushing her effort aside or replacing it. He understood what it had meant.

“You don’t get it,” she said, quieter.

“Then explain.”

She looked away. “…I wanted to give you something myself.”

There it was. Not the money. The feeling. Yichen lifted her hand and pressed a kiss to her fingers, right there in the noodle shop, in front of the elderly couple, who looked thrilled.

“You did,” he said. “The moment you bought those first tickets, you already did.”

Xiaoran felt her heart give way a little. Then she pointed at him across the noodles.

“You still upgraded everything.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“I wanted to.”

“Show-off.”

“Hm.”

At least he admitted it. She kept the original tickets anyway. She wasn’t going to use them, but she folded them carefully back into their plastic sleeve and put them in the inside pocket of her coat, where they stayed for the rest of the trip.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, on the arena tour, they walked out of the tunnel onto the empty court. The ceiling rose above them, enormous and round, rows and rows of empty seats climbing toward it in every direction. A lone janitor was polishing the floor. Their guide was saying something about history and famous nights. Xiaoran forgot she was annoyed. Beside her, Zhou Yichen stood at the edge of the court with his hands in his coat pockets, very still, looking like the happiest man on Earth.

Actually—no. The happiest man on Earth wasn’t looking at the court. He wasn’t looking at the ceiling or the banners or the famous floor. He was looking at her. Because somehow, the best part of the whole trip wasn’t the Garden. It was watching Lin Xiaoran see it with him.

chapters.desc: Game day at Madison Square Garden. But first, a fashion crisis on Fifth Avenue.
chapters.title: The Day Lin Xiaoran Wanted to Look Grown-Up
chapters.epigraph: “Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful.”
chapters.content:
Game day. Saturday. The day the whole trip had been building toward. The day Lin Xiaoran discovered a completely unexpected crisis. The crisis was not basketball. It wasn’t New York, or the fact that she still understood about forty-seven percent of what Yichen said about defensive schemes. The crisis was fashion.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started at breakfast, in a café on Fifth Avenue, where Xiaoran made the mistake of looking out of the window. Every woman who walked past looked effortless. Long wool coats. Leather gloves. Scarves wrapped like they’d been styled for a magazine. Sleek hair, good boots, the kind of confidence that made a gray sidewalk look like a runway. Then Xiaoran looked down at herself. Puffy white jacket. Comfortable jeans. Sneakers. A small panda keychain hanging from her bag.

She looked like a university student. Because she was a university student. But today, for some reason, she suddenly felt very young. Across the table, Yichen looked up from his coffee and noticed her face immediately.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran pointed at a woman outside the window. “Look.”

He looked. “…Okay.”

“She looks like an adult.”

He looked at the woman, then at Xiaoran, then at the woman again.

“I don’t understand the problem.”

“I look like someone’s daughter.”

Yichen nearly laughed. “Xiaoran.”

“No, seriously. Look at her.” Another woman passed—camel coat, red lipstick, coffee in one gloved hand. “She looks sophisticated. I look like I got lost on a school trip.”

That was when he did laugh—a real one—which only made her more offended.

“THIS IS SERIOUS.”

“It isn’t.”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. The idea of Lin Xiaoran having an identity crisis on Fifth Avenue was, to him, extremely funny.

Unfortunately, once she decided something, she was impossible. Thirty minutes later they were shopping—not because Yichen suggested it, but because Xiaoran had announced, “I am becoming elegant today,” and apparently this was non-negotiable.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next three hours were chaos. The first dress was too mature. The second was too fancy. The third made her look, in her own words, like she was attending someone’s divorce. The fourth almost worked, except for the sleeves, which had opinions. Yichen followed behind, carrying more and more shopping bags. Patient. Hopelessly supportive.

At one point, a saleswoman smiled at Xiaoran and said, “Your husband is very patient.”

Xiaoran nearly choked. Yichen looked suspiciously pleased. Neither of them corrected her. Then Xiaoran found it. Not too glamorous. Not too grown-up. A soft burgundy knit dress with a simple neckline and long sleeves, warm enough for January, and a long camel coat to wear over it. Feminine without trying too hard. When she looked in the mirror, she paused.

“…Oh.”

The saleswoman smiled. “There you go.”

Even Xiaoran couldn’t argue. She looked older, somehow. Softer. More sure of herself. Still herself—just slightly different. Then she looked over at Yichen. Big mistake. He had gone completely silent.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing.

“Yichen?”

The saleswoman smiled knowingly. “Oh.”

Finally he cleared his throat. “…It looks good.”

Short answer. Too short. Which told Xiaoran everything, because Zhou Yichen only got this brief when he was completely compromised. She smiled in triumph. Success. Unfortunately, the next problem appeared at the register. Yichen paying. Again.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Yichen.”

“Xiaoran.” Then he made his winning argument. “You bought me the Garden. Let me buy you a dress. You got up at four in the morning for those tickets. Let me win one argument this trip.”

Deeply annoying. But sensible. So the dress became Yichen’s purchase, a fact he looked suspiciously happy about for the rest of the afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, they took a yellow cab to the arena, and the city outside the window was all lights. Inside, the Garden was nothing like the empty building from the tour. It was full and loud and alive, twenty thousand people under that enormous round ceiling, music thumping, the court shining like it was lit from underneath. Their seats were so close to the floor that Xiaoran could hear the players’ sneakers squeak during warm-ups and see the sweat on the referees’ foreheads.

She stood by her seat in the burgundy dress and the new coat, holding her phone, not even taking photos, just looking. Then she caught her reflection in the glass of the scorer’s table. The dress. The coat. Her hair, which she had spent forty minutes on in the hotel bathroom. For once, she didn’t see a girl who had gotten lost on a school trip. She saw a woman.

It felt nice. Then she noticed Yichen looking at her. Again.

“…What.”

Nothing.

“Yichen. What.”

He looked away. Then, quietly—

“You look beautiful.”

Somehow, after years together, it still worked on her every single time. And this time, the way he said it felt different. Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful. The word stayed with her. Then the lights went down, the crowd roared, and the game began, and the atmosphere changed completely. Even Xiaoran felt it—the pressure, the speed, how much every possession seemed to matter. And beside her, Yichen changed too. He leaned forward, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole floor at once, tracking every screen and rotation the way he did on the sofa at eight in the morning, except now it was right in front of him. Every time a play worked exactly the way he had explained it on the back of her notes, he made a small sound under his breath, like a man watching a magic trick he already knew the secret to and loved anyway.

He looked ridiculously handsome. Xiaoran decided basketball was dangerous. Not playing it—watching someone you love fall in love with it all over again, three feet from the court. Late in the fourth quarter, a player went flying out of bounds after a loose ball and landed in the second row, two seats down. The whole crowd gasped. Yichen shot to his feet with everyone else. Xiaoran wasn’t watching the player.

She was watching him. He looked happier than she had seen him all year. Without thinking, she slipped her hand into his. He glanced down, surprised for half a second. Then he laced their fingers together and turned back to the game, and didn’t let go. The final minutes went by in a roar. The buzzer sounded. Confetti didn’t fall, because it was a regular season game in January, but it felt like it should have.

And standing there together, in the loudest building Xiaoran had ever been in, both of them quietly realized the same thing. Years from now, when they remembered New York, they probably wouldn’t remember the final score. Or who made which shot, or the defensive schemes, or the forty-seven percent. They would remember this. Her first grown-up dress. His inability to stop looking at her. The noise, the lights, the snow waiting outside.

And the hand he didn’t let go of the whole way home.

chapters.desc: A few comments read at 2 AM, two weeks of skipped meals, and a date that ends in a quiet café.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting
chapters.epigraph: “Who told you that you needed to change?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen worried about. Basketball injuries. Exams. Career plans. Whether Xiaoran remembered her student card. Normal, reasonable concerns. One concern had never crossed his mind, because it sounded impossible: Lin Xiaoran dieting. The girl who once ate three desserts on a single date. The girl who considered bubble tea a personality trait. The girl who treated snacks as emotional support. Dieting? Impossible. Which was exactly why he didn’t notice at first.

It started with social media. Again. Always social media.

✦ ✦ ✦

A month earlier, Xiaoran had posted photos from New York: the burgundy dress, the city lights, a version of herself that looked a little more woman than girl. The response was overwhelmingly positive. Some of it wasn’t. Nothing cruel. Nothing dramatic. Just enough.

“She’s pretty but she’d look even better if she lost a little weight.”

“Her face is beautiful.”

“A slimmer figure would be perfect.”

Stupid, unimportant comments—the kind most people would ignore. Except Xiaoran read them at 2 AM, scientifically the worst time to read anything. And somehow they stayed with her. Not because she hated herself. She didn’t. But for the first time, she started wondering: what if? So Lin Xiaoran made a terrible decision. She started dieting, secretly. Not healthy dieting. Not reasonable dieting. Skipping breakfast, tiny lunches, coffee instead of food, water whenever she was hungry—the kind of diet guaranteed to make everyone miserable, especially her.

The strange part was that nobody noticed right away. Xiaoran acted mostly normal, and university was busy—deadlines, projects, practices, exams, life. Even Zhou Yichen missed it, for almost two weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came Saturday. Date day. The plan was simple: lunch, shopping, walking around the city, dinner. Xiaoran woke up feeling awful. Her stomach had spent two weeks surviving on disappointment and caffeine, and it was finally protesting. Violently. She still said nothing, because she didn’t want Yichen to worry. Terrible decision.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the stomachache was worse. Walking hurt. Standing hurt. Existing hurt. Somehow she kept smiling—until Yichen stopped walking.

“Xiaoran, what’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

A terrible lie. She looked pale—very pale—and Zhou Yichen knew her too well.

“No.”

“What?”

“Something hurts.”

Dead silence. Caught. Again.

“…My stomach.”

Everything changed, because Zhou Yichen’s expression changed. Not panic. Not anger. Worry. Always worry first.

“When did it start?”

“A little while ago.”

“How long.”

She hesitated.

“Xiaoran.”

“…This morning.”

The truth, finally. She’d been hiding it all morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ten minutes later they were sitting in a quiet café. A warm drink in front of her. Food in front of her. Food she wasn’t touching. And finally, Yichen actually noticed.

“…Why aren’t you eating.”

Silence. Then more silence.

“…I’m not hungry.”

Wrong answer. Very wrong answer. Suddenly the pieces connected: the smaller meals, the constant coffee, the weight she’d lost, how tired she’d been. Everything. Dead silence.

“Have you been dieting?”

Uh oh. Xiaoran looked away. The universal sign of guilt. Zhou Yichen became angry. Not loud. Not shouting. The worst kind: quiet angry.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She winced. He had used her full name. Maximum danger.

“Answer me.”

“…A little.”

“A little.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“You’ve barely been eating for two weeks.”

Oops. Of course he knew. Nothing stayed hidden from him forever.

“Why.”

Suddenly Xiaoran felt stupid. The comments sounded ridiculous now. Embarrassing. Small.

“…I wanted to look prettier.”

The anger disappeared. Completely. That answer hurt worse. Much worse.

“Xiaoran.”

She didn’t look up. Couldn’t. A hand touched her forehead, warm. Then a kiss—right on her forehead, soft and lingering. Xiaoran blinked, confused. She had expected a lecture. Not that.

“Look at me.”

She did. Big mistake. His eyes looked sad. Actually sad. Somehow that was worse than anger.

“Who told you that you needed to change?”

Xiaoran shook her head.

“Don’t do that.”

Another kiss to her forehead, gentle and patient.

“Who.”

“…Nobody.”

A lie. But he let it go. That wasn’t the point. Then another kiss against her forehead. And another. Each one impossibly gentle.

“What am I supposed to do with you?”

His voice sounded helpless.

“Yichen—“

Another kiss.

“You skip meals.”

Kiss.

“You drink coffee instead.”

Kiss.

“You get sick.”

Kiss.

“And somehow you’re surprised your stomach hurts.”

By now, Xiaoran’s ears were red. Being scolded while being repeatedly kissed was very confusing.

“I just wanted to look prettier.”

Then Yichen laughed. His hand moved to hold her cheek, gently.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You took me to New York. You worked for months to buy those tickets. You won competitions. You make everyone around you happier. And somehow the thing you’re worried about is losing weight?”

She looked down, because it sounded ridiculous when he said it.

“I just…”

Nothing came out. She didn’t even know anymore. Yichen sighed—the sigh he saved for her alone—and pushed the food toward her.

“Eat.”

Xiaoran didn’t move.

“Eat. Or I’m carrying you home.”

He sounded completely serious, which made it believable.

“You won’t think I’m ugly?”

Yichen leaned forward and kissed her forehead again, longer this time, then whispered,

“You’re beautiful when you’re eating. You’re beautiful when you’re studying. You’re beautiful when you’re talking too much. You’re beautiful when you’re annoying.”

“That’s rude.”

“Accurate.”

Then, more seriously: “If comments like that get in your head again, tell me. Don’t fix it by not eating.”

A tiny smile appeared. There she was—the real Xiaoran. Watching her finally pick up her fork made Zhou Yichen more relieved than winning a basketball game. He still spent the rest of the date kissing her forehead every twenty minutes, just to make sure she remembered. And every single time, he quietly added:

“Eat your food.”

Which was considerably less romantic.

chapters.desc: A thirteen-day family vacation. Lin Xiaoran is a mature adult. Day Three is concerning.
chapters.title: Two Weeks Was Apparently Too Long
chapters.epigraph: “I hate family vacations.”
chapters.content:
When Zhou Yichen announced he was leaving on a thirteen-day family vacation, Lin Xiaoran laughed. Actually laughed.

“That’s fine.”

“Hm.”

“I’m a mature adult.”

“Hm.”

“I can survive two weeks.”

“Hm.”

Tang Meilin, who had been there for the One-Week Clingy Disaster of high school, looked deeply suspicious. Whenever Xiaoran claimed she was emotionally stable, disaster usually followed. Day One wasn’t bad at all. Yichen left in the morning. Xiaoran went to class, worked on assignments, had dinner with friends. Perfectly normal. At 10 PM she called him, for three hours. Still normal. Probably. Day Two was manageable. She sent him pictures of lunch, of campus, of a cat near the media building. Then another cat. Then another. Then a cloud that vaguely resembled a cat. Yichen replied: You sent me six cats today.

Xiaoran: You’re welcome.

Day Three was concerning, because after class she walked toward the business building out of habit—then remembered Yichen wasn’t there. He was several countries away. It hit surprisingly hard.

“…Oh.”

For the first time, campus felt a little bigger. A little emptier. Which was ridiculous, because she had survived sixteen whole years before meeting him. Yet somehow the place felt wrong without him. Day Four, things escalated.

“You’re staring at your phone.”
