One of her classmates pointed it out.

“I’m not.”

“You checked it six times.”

“I received messages.”

“Not from him.”

Xiaoran had no answer.

Caught. Yichen, meanwhile, appeared to be having the time of his life. At least, that’s what his photos suggested: beaches, resorts, family dinners, mountain views. Every picture looked amazing, which only made Xiaoran more annoyed. How dare he enjoy himself while she suffered? A completely unreasonable thought. But still. Day Five, she stole one of his hoodies. Again. Not because she missed him. Obviously. It just happened to smell faintly like his cologne, which was entirely unrelated.

Day Six, the video calls got longer. Day Seven, even longer. At one point, Mrs. Zhou wandered into the background and laughed.

“Still talking?”

Dead silence. They had been talking for two hours.

“Mom.”

“What?”

Mrs. Zhou looked delighted. She waved at Xiaoran.

“He’s been carrying his phone around all day waiting for your messages.”

Dead silence. Yichen looked horrified.

“Mom. Please leave.”

Xiaoran was trying very hard not to smile. That information was valuable. Very valuable. Day Eight, the suffering peaked. Not dramatically. Quietly.

That afternoon, Xiaoran won a small media competition. Normally Yichen was the first person she’d tell—not because she had to, but because she wanted to. But it was the middle of the night where he was. Suddenly the win felt slightly incomplete, which surprised her. Later that night, his reply arrived. Three words. Proud of you. She stared at them for five minutes. Day Nine, Chen Yuhao called.

“Are you alive?”

“Barely.”

“It’s been nine days.”

“Feels like nine years.”

“You’re impossible.”

“Correct.”

Day Ten, she started counting. Three days left. Then two. Then one. Every conversation somehow included, “When are you coming back?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, even Yichen noticed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You asked me that six times.”

“I’m just checking.”

“Xiaoran.”

“…Fine. I miss you.”

Silence.

“I know.”

Simple and soft, the kind of answer that made missing him worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final day arrived. Thirteen days. Long enough for Xiaoran to decide she hated extended vacations. The airport felt familiar now—she had done this once before, in high school, for one single week. This time she wasn’t dramatic. Not visibly. No clinging, no pouting, no speeches. Just waiting. Patiently. Okay—not patiently. She checked the arrival board twelve times. Finally the doors opened, and there he was. Black shirt. Travel backpack. Slightly messy hair. The same Zhou Yichen—and somehow not, because after almost two weeks, seeing him in person felt strangely unreal.

Then he spotted her and smiled, and just like that, everything felt normal again. Yichen walked toward her.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran threw herself at him. Not gracefully. Not elegantly. Just immediately—hard enough that Yichen took a step back catching her. Her arms tightened, and for a while neither of them said anything. Thirteen days wasn’t forever. But it had been long enough for Xiaoran to realize something: she didn’t just like spending time with Zhou Yichen. He had quietly become part of what made ordinary days feel complete. Finally she muttered into his shoulder,

“I hate family vacations.”

Yichen laughed softly—the familiar laugh, the one she had missed most.

“I noticed.”

His arms tightened around her. Warm. Safe. Home. After a pause, near her ear, he whispered,

“You know… I missed you too.”

Xiaoran hugged him even tighter, which made Zhou Yichen laugh again. Apparently two weeks apart had only made his girlfriend clingier—an outcome that surprised absolutely nobody.

chapters.desc: A lost French couple, a café near campus, and a language Lin Xiaoran forgot to mention.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Discovered His Girlfriend Secretly Spoke French
chapters.epigraph: “The same thing she’d been telling him all along—just in a different language.”
chapters.content:
There were many surprising things about Lin Xiaoran. Some were expected: her ability to get lost in places she’d visited twenty times, her talent for creating problems out of nothing, her habit of asking questions like:

“Would you still love me if I became a refrigerator?”

A follow-up, apparently, to the capybara question. Normal Xiaoran behavior. What Zhou Yichen didn’t expect—was discovering she spoke French. Not badly, either. Fluently enough to make people stare. And she had apparently been practicing for months without telling him. The betrayal was unbelievable. It started on a random Saturday. They were having lunch at a café near campus. Nothing unusual. Just a quiet date—until Xiaoran froze.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked up.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened, and she sat up straighter. Very suspicious. Across the café, a middle-aged French couple stood looking lost—the man holding a map, the woman holding a phone. Xiaoran stood up.

“I’m back in a minute.”

And walked toward them. Yichen blinked. Okay. Probably helping with directions. Then Xiaoran opened her mouth. French came out. Perfect French. Not textbook French, not app French—real, conversational French. Dead silence. Because WHAT. The French couple immediately brightened. A full conversation followed—questions, answers, directions, recommendations, laughing. Zhou Yichen sat there, staring. Who was this woman? That was his girlfriend. Supposedly. Yet somehow she had unlocked an entire language pack without informing him.

The conversation continued for several minutes. Then Xiaoran smiled, said goodbye, came back, sat down, and went straight back to her juice. Like nothing had happened. Dead silence.

Finally Yichen spoke.

“What.”

“What?”

“You speak French.”

“Oh.”

OH? That was the response?

“Since when?”

“Recently.”

“Recently enough to have a whole conversation?”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Caught. A guilty smile appeared.

“A few months.”

Dead silence.

“A FEW MONTHS?”

She had hidden an entire language. Like a criminal.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Xiaoran looked genuinely confused.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

Mission accomplished. Yichen was absolutely surprised. Then suspicious.

“When did you learn?”

“Every night.”

“Every night.”

“Mhm.”

“You already have assignments. And competitions.”

“Mhm.”

“You already watch random documentaries about things nobody cares about.”

“Mhm.”

“So when exactly did you have time?”

Xiaoran proudly pointed at herself.

“I am gifted.”

“No.”

“Okay maybe I sacrificed sleep.”

“There it is.”

The truth. It was always sleep deprivation.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually the story came out. Months ago, Xiaoran had watched a French film for one of her media courses. Then another. Then another. Then she had become obsessed, which was very on-brand: when Xiaoran liked something, she liked it aggressively. Normal people watched movies. Xiaoran accidentally learned a language. Then Yichen had an idea. His eyes narrowed.

“Say something.”

“What.”

“In French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Embarrassing.”

“You were just speaking confidently.”

“That was practical French.”

“This is boyfriend French.”

Yichen refused to let it go. For twenty whole minutes. Until Xiaoran surrendered.

“Fine.”

Very quietly, she said something in French—soft, fast, beautiful, and completely incomprehensible to him.

“What did you say?”

Xiaoran looked away. Very suspicious.

“Nothing.”

“That’s a lie.”

“It’s not important.”

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

Now he was definitely curious. If she refused to translate, it meant something. After several more minutes of interrogation, she gave up.

“…I said you’re handsome.”

Yichen smiled. Not a big smile. The dangerous one—the one that always caused problems.

“Oh. That’s all?”

“Yes.”

“Only handsome?”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. Xiaoran secretly learning French and then using it to compliment him was absurdly adorable. Then he leaned closer.

“Teach me.”

“What?”

“French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Because you’ll immediately use it against me.”

Correct. His face confirmed it immediately.

Three weeks later, he had learned enough French to recognize one specific phrase—one Xiaoran muttered while studying, thinking he wasn’t paying attention. Thinking he couldn’t understand. A terrible mistake. He heard it perfectly, and this time he understood.

“Je t’aime.”

I love you. Simple. Soft. Unconscious. The kind of thing she probably didn’t realize she’d said out loud. Then Yichen closed his textbook.

“What.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“What?”

“You love me?”

Xiaoran froze. No. NO. He wasn’t supposed to understand that yet. Yichen looked unbearably pleased. From that day on, whenever Xiaoran forgot herself and slipped into French, Yichen paid very close attention. His girlfriend had spent months on French, and the first important thing she had learned to say was the same thing she had been telling him all along. Just in a different language.

chapters.desc: A peaceful Saturday at the Zhou house, until Mrs. Zhou’s best friend’s daughter walks in calling him “ge.”
chapters.title: The Worst Visitor in Zhou Family History
chapters.epigraph: “The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s own imagination.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran wasn’t nervous. She had visited the Zhou family house several times already. Mrs. Zhou liked her. Mr. Zhou liked her. Even the neighbors’ cat that slept on the Zhou family wall liked her. Everything was fine. Then Jiang Meimei arrived, and nothing was fine anymore. The disaster started on a Saturday afternoon. Xiaoran was curled up beside Zhou Yichen on the living room sofa, stealing his snacks. Mrs. Zhou was chatting happily, Mr. Zhou was reading, and Yichen was pretending to study. Life was peaceful.

Then the front door opened. Mrs. Zhou brightened at once.

“Oh! Meimei is here!”

Dead silence. Who? The answer appeared five seconds later. A girl walked into the living room—beautiful, elegant, perfect posture, perfect makeup, perfect smile. The kind of woman who had clearly never tripped over her own feet. Unlike Xiaoran, who had once gotten lost inside a shopping mall. Twice.

“Hello Auntie.”

The girl smiled sweetly. Mrs. Zhou immediately hugged her.

“Meimei!”

Uh oh. Xiaoran’s instincts went off like an alarm.

Then came the fatal sentence.

“Xiaoran, this is Jiang Meimei,” Mrs. Zhou said with a smile. “She’s my best friend’s daughter.”

Dead silence. BEST FRIEND’S DAUGHTER? That phrase alone carried terrifying power.

“Meimei practically grew up with Yichen.”

Dead silence. WHAT. Xiaoran slowly turned toward her boyfriend. Yichen looked completely normal, which made it worse. He clearly wasn’t surprised. Meaning he already knew her. Meaning they had history. Meaning—

“Yichen ge.”

Jiang Meimei smiled. Ge. The dreaded honorific.

Meanwhile Yichen simply nodded.

“Meimei.”

HE KNEW HER NAME. Xiaoran sat up straighter. This was serious. Then the conversation started, and somehow everything got worse.

“Oh, Yichen ge, are you still playing basketball?”

“Yes.”

“I saw your tournament photos.”

“Mm.”

“I showed them to my parents.”

“Mm.”

Their families were connected. Xiaoran hated everything. Jiang Meimei sat elegantly across from them, perfect in every way. The killing blow. Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“You know, when they were children, everyone thought Meimei and Yichen would become a couple.”

Xiaoran nearly inhaled a potato chip wrong. Jiang Meimei laughed politely. Mrs. Zhou laughed. Mr. Zhou laughed. Even the cat on the wall looked suspicious. Only Yichen looked exhausted—he had clearly heard this story a thousand times. Xiaoran had not, and now she was suffering. Greatly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next hour was torture—not because Jiang Meimei did anything wrong. That was the problem. She was nice. Kind, polite, friendly, impossible to dislike. Which made Xiaoran dislike the situation even more. Then, over tea, Jiang Meimei casually mentioned—

“I still have the birthday gift Yichen gave me years ago.”

A birthday gift. HE BOUGHT HER GIFTS. Xiaoran was spiraling. Internally. Externally she was smiling—a very normal smile. Definitely not dying. A hand landed on her knee—warm, steady. Yichen. Without even looking at her, he squeezed once. A warning. He could apparently feel the jealousy radiating off her. Traitor. The real disaster happened later. Mrs. Zhou asked Yichen to help carry something upstairs, and Xiaoran was left alone with Jiang Meimei.

The moment he was gone, panic set in. Now they would have to talk. Woman to woman. Nightmare. Jiang Meimei smiled. Xiaoran prepared for battle. Then, unexpectedly, Meimei laughed.

“You look terrified.”

“…What?”

“You’ve been staring at me for two hours.”

Caught. Immediately. Meimei smiled again, genuinely amused.

“You’re much cuter than I expected.”

“…Expected?”

“Mrs. Zhou talks about you constantly.”

“She does?”

“All the time.”

Then Meimei leaned closer.

“And honestly, I understand now.”

Xiaoran blinked. What was happening? Meimei laughed again.

“You know, Yichen ge never liked any girls growing up. Never.”

“…Really?”

“Really.”

Then she pointed upstairs.

“The fact he looks at you the way he does is honestly shocking.”

Now Xiaoran wanted details. Many details.

“What way?”

Meimei stared at her, then burst out laughing.

“Oh my God.”

“What?”

“You don’t know.”

Know what? Before Xiaoran could ask, footsteps sounded on the stairs. Yichen was back, and both girls immediately looked at him—one amused, one confused. Yichen looked instantly suspicious.

“…What happened?”

“Nothing,” Jiang Meimei said.

“Nothing,” Xiaoran said, in exactly the same tone. Very dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, after Jiang Meimei finally left, Xiaoran cornered her boyfriend.

“What way?”

Yichen blinked.

“What.”

“Jiang Meimei said you look at me differently.”

Realization, followed immediately by annoyance. Meimei had started problems on her way out. Wonderful. Yichen sighed.

“Forget it.”

“No.”

“Please.”

“NO.”

Several minutes of relentless pestering later, he finally surrendered.

“The way someone looks at the person they love.”

Direct hit. Xiaoran froze completely. Yichen looked away, slightly embarrassed. Xiaoran scooted closer. Then closer. Then rested her head on his shoulder, smiling.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“I’ve decided.”

“What.”

“I don’t hate Jiang Meimei anymore.”

“…You hated her?”

“Briefly.”

“Why.”

“She was too pretty.”

Yichen laughed. And just like that—the greatest threat in Lin Xiaoran’s imagination was over—mostly because Jiang Meimei had never been a rival at all. The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s imagination, which, unfortunately for everyone involved, was far more dangerous.

chapters.desc: Lunar New Year at her grandparents’ house, and one uncle with opinions about why she’s dating Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: The One Thing Lin Xiaoran Could Never Tolerate
chapters.epigraph: “I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”
chapters.content:
There were many things Lin Xiaoran disliked. Early classes. Group projects. Spicy food stronger than her tolerance, which was most spicy food. People who walked slowly in crowded places. But there was one thing she genuinely hated: gold diggers. Not because she was rich. She wasn’t. Her family lived comfortably—her mother an accountant, her father an engineer—not wealthy, not poor. Enough for food, for school, to get through a month without worrying. Nothing more, nothing less.

So it always made Xiaoran uncomfortable when people assumed she was dating Zhou Yichen for his money—especially since she had liked him long before she knew how wealthy his family actually was. Not everyone understood that. Including Uncle Deng: a distant relative from another city, the kind who appeared once every few years and somehow had opinions about everyone’s lives. It happened at Lunar New Year, at her grandparents’ house. Lots of relatives, lots of food, lots of noise, lots of gossip. A normal family gathering—until someone mentioned Zhou Yichen.

Everyone became very interested.

“That’s the boyfriend in the business program at Huaining University, right?”

“Very handsome.”

“Excellent grades.”

“Good family.”

It was harmless—until Uncle Deng laughed and said, casually,

“Well, Xiaoran certainly found herself a rich boyfriend.”

The room quieted slightly. Xiaoran paused.

“Smart girl,” Uncle Deng went on. “Nowadays girls know how to choose.”

Dead silence. No. Not that. Not that. Across the table, her mother frowned and set down her cup with a small, sharp click. Uncle Deng didn’t notice. Or didn’t care.

“Honestly, if I were young again, I’d choose someone wealthy too.”

A few relatives looked uncomfortable. The implication was very obvious. Xiaoran hated it. Not because it embarrassed her—because it insulted everything she felt for Yichen. Every late-night study session, every tournament, every argument, every moment, reduced to money. Xiaoran put down her chopsticks. Quietly.

“Uncle, if Yichen wasn’t rich, I’d still date him.”

The room went silent. Everyone knew that tone. The dangerous Xiaoran tone. Uncle Deng laughed.

“Of course you’d say that.”

Xiaoran smiled. It was not a friendly smile.

“Actually, when we started dating, I didn’t know his family was wealthy.”

Silence.

“He was just annoying.”

Several cousins burst out laughing. Accurate.

“He studied with me. He helped me. He listened to me complain. He stayed beside me when I failed things. He celebrated when I succeeded.”

Then she looked directly at Uncle Deng.

“So no. I didn’t choose him because he’s rich.”

The room got quieter. Nobody was joking anymore.

“I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”

Dead silence. Even her grandmother looked moved. Uncle Deng looked a little embarrassed, but still tried to defend himself.

“I wasn’t criticizing you.”

“Maybe not,” Xiaoran replied. “But it sounded like you were criticizing him.”

That surprised everyone. Most people would have defended themselves first. Xiaoran defended Yichen first. Always. Without thinking.

“You know what bothers me?”

Nobody answered.

“People think money is why someone stays.”

Her fingers tightened slightly around her teacup.

“But I’ve seen people with money treat others terribly. And I’ve seen people with nothing give everything.”

Then she smiled. A small smile. The real one this time.

“Yichen just happens to have both.”

Her grandmother laughed first.

“That’s a good answer.”

The tension broke. Conversation resumed, food returned, and the family gossip moved on.

Later that evening, as Xiaoran walked home, her phone rang. Yichen.

“Hm?”

“Lin Jun told me what happened.”

Family networks were terrifying.

“What part?”

“The part where you defended my honor.”

Then she heard him laughing softly.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“No, tell me.”

“I just think it’s nice.”

Xiaoran rolled her eyes.

“It wasn’t nice.”

“It was.”

“He was being annoying.”

“And?”

“And nobody gets to talk about you like that.”

A softer silence, the kind Yichen only ever had around her.

“So if I lost everything tomorrow…”

“No.”

“What?”

“No hypothetical questions.”

“Answer.”

She sighed. Then finally said:

“If you lost everything tomorrow, I’d still be there.”

Then she added:

“Unfortunately.”

Yichen laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved most. Somehow it felt worth more than all the money in the world.

chapters.desc: Grandma Lin wants to see the boy up close. Uncle Deng will be there. So will the dumplings.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Meets the Relatives
chapters.epigraph: “That one’s acceptable.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came from her grandmother, which meant nobody could refuse it.

Three days after Uncle Deng’s comment at New Year dinner, Grandma Lin called Xiaoran’s mother, and Xiaoran’s mother called Xiaoran into the kitchen, and said, without turning around from the sink, “Your grandmother wants the boy at dinner on the fifth.”

Xiaoran froze with a mandarin halfway to her mouth.

“…The boy?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Why?”

“She says if you’re going to defend someone in front of the whole family like that, she wants to see what he looks like up close.” Her mother turned off the tap. “Your uncle will be there.”

“Uncle Deng?”

“He’s staying until the seventh.”

Xiaoran put the mandarin down. “Mom. That’s a trap.”

“It’s dinner,” said Mrs. Lin, which in her language meant yes, and you’re both walking into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen arrived at five, exactly on time, which Xiaoran had known he would. What she hadn’t expected was how he arrived. No black car. He came up the lane from the bus stop on foot, in a plain dark coat, carrying a fruit basket in one hand and a paper bag in the other. Inside the bag were a tin of good tea for her grandfather, a box of pastries from the old bakery near their high school, and a small pot of narcissus for her grandmother, because Xiaoran had once mentioned, months ago and only once, that her grandmother liked them.

She met him at the gate.

“You took the bus.”

“Hm.”

“You never take the bus.”

He looked at the house—the red couplets on the door, the paper lanterns, the sound of a dozen relatives talking over a television—and then back at her.

“Your uncle thinks I’m a rich boyfriend,” he said. “I didn’t want to give him a parking space to prove it.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she reached up and fixed the collar of his coat, which didn’t need fixing, mostly so she’d have something to do with her hands.

“You’re nervous,” she said.

“Very.”

That surprised her so much she forgot to be nervous herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, it was exactly as bad as she’d feared and also completely different. Her grandmother took one look at the narcissus and said “Hm,” in a tone Xiaoran had only ever heard her use for very good melons. Her father shook Yichen’s hand for too long and then had to go stand in the kitchen for a minute. Lin Jun, lounging on the sofa with a beer, raised it in Yichen’s direction like they were old war buddies, which, after the day he’d “stolen” him, they sort of were.

Then the questions started. The aunties wanted to know his height, his major, his grades, and whether he could cook. The uncles wanted to know what business he planned to go into and whether he’d thought about the civil service. Two small cousins wanted to know if he could dunk, and when he said yes, they wanted proof, immediately, in the courtyard, and had to be held back by the hoods of their jackets.

Yichen answered all of it. Calmly. Politely. Without once mentioning his family’s company, or his car, or anything he owned. When one auntie asked what his parents did, he said “My father runs a business, and my mother keeps him from working too much,” and the auntie laughed and moved on. Across the room, Uncle Deng watched all of this over his teacup and didn’t say anything. Xiaoran watched Uncle Deng.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened at the dumpling table. Every year on the fifth, the whole family folded dumplings together, and every year it was a competition nobody admitted was a competition. Grandma Lin sat at the head of the table, folding perfect pleated dumplings at terrifying speed. Xiaoran’s were lopsided but sealed. Lin Jun’s were somehow perfect, which was annoying. Yichen’s were a disaster. He held the wrapper like it was an exam question. He put in too much filling. He pinched the edges with enormous concentration, and the dumpling burst at the seam and lay there on the board, looking injured.

One of the little cousins burst out laughing. So did Grandma Lin.

“Again,” she said, and pushed another wrapper toward him.

He tried again. It was worse.

“You’re better at basketball,” Xiaoran told him.

“I’m better at everything than this.”

Uncle Deng put down his teacup.

“Must be strange,” he said, “doing things with your own hands for once.”

The table didn’t go silent, exactly. But it got quieter. Xiaoran felt her mother go still beside her. She opened her mouth.

Under the table, Yichen’s knee touched hers. Wait. He picked up a third wrapper.

“It is,” he said. “My dad says money is the easiest thing to have and the easiest thing to lose. He made me work in one of his warehouses the summer I was fifteen so I’d understand that.” He spooned in less filling this time. “I was bad at that too. For the first week.”

Uncle Deng raised his eyebrows.

“And,” Yichen added, still looking at the dumpling, “Xiaoran told me what she said to you at New Year.”

Now the table really did go quiet.

“I’m not sure I’ve earned all of it yet,” he said. “But I’m trying to.”

He pinched the edges closed. It held. Grandma Lin picked it up, turned it over, and put it on the tray with her own.

“That one’s acceptable,” she announced.

Across the table, Uncle Deng looked at Yichen for a long moment. Then he picked up his teacup again, and said, gruffly, to nobody in particular, “Too much filling’s a common mistake.”

It was the closest thing to an apology anyone in the family had ever heard from him.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, the cousins dragged everyone out into the courtyard for sparklers. The air smelled like gunpowder and cold. Somewhere down the lane, someone was setting off firecrackers, and the little cousins screamed and ran in circles, writing their names in light. Xiaoran stood by the door with Yichen, holding a sparkler she’d forgotten to light.

“You didn’t have to say that,” she said. “About earning it.”

“I meant it.”

“I know. That’s why you didn’t have to say it.”

He didn’t answer. He just took her sparkler, lit it from his own, and handed it back. Behind them, the door opened. Xiaoran’s mother came out, wrapped in her coat, holding something red. She walked straight up to Yichen and held out an envelope. He looked at it. Then at Xiaoran. Then back at the envelope, completely lost.

“Auntie, I can’t—”

“Take it,” said Mrs. Lin. “It’s New Year.”

He took it with both hands, the way you were supposed to, and bowed. Mrs. Lin nodded once, brisk as always, and went back inside without another word. Yichen stared at the red envelope in his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm.”

“What does it mean? When the parents give it to—” He stopped.

Xiaoran looked at the door her mother had just closed, at the warm light behind the paper lanterns, at the shape of her grandmother at the window pretending not to watch. She knew exactly what it meant. In her family, the first red envelope from her mother didn’t go to friends, or classmates, or a boy someone was dating for now. It went to someone they expected to see at this table next year. And the year after that.

“It means,” she said, and her voice wobbled, “you have to come back next year and fold better dumplings.”

He looked at her for a long time in the flickering light. Then he tucked the envelope carefully into the inside pocket of his coat, over his heart, and didn’t say anything at all. He didn’t have to.

chapters.desc: A weekly viewing report, eleven hours of dramas, and the most dangerous thing Zhou Yichen has ever done: change a password.
chapters.title: Netflix vs Zhou Yichen
chapters.epigraph: “You violated my human rights.”
chapters.content:
There were many ways to start a relationship conflict. Jealousy. Miscommunication. Trust issues. Different life goals. Lin Xiaoran and Zhou Yichen managed to have one over Netflix—specifically, because Zhou Yichen accidentally found out how much Netflix Xiaoran watched in a single day. The discovery happened on a Tuesday. Yichen paid for the subscription. Not because Xiaoran couldn’t—because he’d insisted.

“Just use mine.”

At the time, Xiaoran thought that was sweet. A mistake.

One afternoon, Yichen got a notification: weekly viewing activity. Normally he ignored those. This time, he opened it—and froze.

“…What?”

The watch history went on. And on. Episodes one through seven of one show. Then another show. Then another. Dead silence. According to Netflix, Lin Xiaoran had spent almost eleven hours watching dramas on Sunday. Eleven. Hours. Yichen messaged her.

Yichen: How many hours were you on Netflix Sunday?

Seen. Typing. Stopped typing. Typing again.

Xiaoran: Why.

Yichen: Answer the question.

Xiaoran: Approximately.

Yichen: How many.

Xiaoran: The number isn’t important.

The number was important.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: …

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: Maybe?

Xiaoran: Nine?

Yichen: The report says eleven.

Dead silence. She had forgotten Netflix tracked things. Traitors, all of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen showed up at her apartment holding groceries, concern, and judgment.

“Eleven hours?”

“It was a weekend.”

“Eleven hours.”

“It sounds worse when you say it.”

“Because it is worse.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“It was educational.”

“What was educational?”

“The romance.”

“No.”

“The character development.”

“No.”

“The cinematography.”

“No.”

Dead silence. Then Yichen opened her refrigerator and discovered she had skipped lunch. The atmosphere got much worse. After the diet incident, skipped meals were the one thing he never joked about.

“Xiaoran. You skipped meals.”

“I forgot.”

“You remembered fourteen episodes.”

Xiaoran had nothing to say to that.

Then came the betrayal. The greatest betrayal.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Netflix logged her out. Because what? WHAT? She tried again. Nothing. Again. Nothing. Then her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Temporary restriction.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: You did WHAT?

Yichen: One week.

Xiaoran: ONE WEEK?

Yichen: You need sunlight.

Xiaoran: I HAVE SUNLIGHT.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: I SAW SUNLIGHT THROUGH THE WINDOW.

Yichen: That’s not the same thing.

The war began. For the first time in months, Lin Xiaoran ignored Zhou Yichen completely. No messages. No calls. No random photos. No good morning, no good night. Nothing. Yichen lasted exactly six hours before he got uncomfortable. Normally his phone held three cat photos, two random observations, one complaint, five unrelated thoughts, and at least one look at this cloud. Today: nothing. The silence was deeply unsettling. Evening came. Still nothing. The next day, nothing. Day three, nothing. By then, even Chen Yuhao had noticed.

“What did you do?”

“I blocked Netflix.”

“You idiot.”

“She watched eleven hours.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what’s the point?”

“You touched her freedom.”

Yuhao shook his head.

“She’s going to hold this grudge forever.”

A terrifying possibility.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen found Xiaoran in the media building working on an assignment. She looked up, saw him, and looked straight back down. The audacity.

“Xiaoran.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

Nothing. Finally Yichen sat down beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Still ignored. Five minutes passed. Then ten. Finally, Yichen sighed.

“Are you done?”

“No.”

Her first words in three days. Progress.

“You’re really angry.”

“Correct.”

“It was for your health.”

“You violated my rights.”

Her rights. Netflix had apparently become a legal issue. Then Xiaoran turned—actually turned—and pointed at him.

“I was three episodes away from the confession.”

“The confession?”

“Three episodes.”

The heartbreak in her voice almost made him laugh. Almost. Yichen rubbed his forehead. The whole argument was ridiculous.

“I was worried.”

Her anger wavered. That tone was unfair—the genuine one, the honest one.

“You skipped meals. You slept at three.”

More silence.

“You watched until your eyes hurt.”

Xiaoran looked away. Caught. Again.

“I know.”

The fight lost all momentum. The truth was, she knew. And Yichen knew she knew. After a moment, he took out his phone, opened Netflix, changed the password, and handed it over.

“…Really?”

“Really.”

Her anger vanished. Completely. Like magic. Traitorous woman. She grabbed his sleeve—the universal sign of peace.

“Thank you.”

“Conditions.”

“What.”

“No eleven-hour marathons.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“Xiaoran.”

“Ten?”

“No.”

“Nine?”

“No.”

“Eight?”

“No.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder. The ultimate negotiating strategy, and unfortunately the most effective one, because Zhou Yichen immediately knew he had already lost. Just like every other argument with Lin Xiaoran.

“Six hours maximum,” he said.

Xiaoran gasped.

“Victory.”

“That’s not a victory.”

“It is to me.”

Then she smiled—the bright one, the one that made Yichen forgive things far too easily. As she happily logged back into Netflix, Yichen realized blocking her had been a mistake. Not because she was angry—because a drama-deprived Lin Xiaoran was much harder to handle than a drama-addicted one. A lesson he never repeated.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran is “extremely busy.” Her lie lasts approximately three minutes.
chapters.title: The World’s Worst Liar
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran was many things. Cute. Dramatic. Smart. Chaotic. A good liar was not one of them. The problem wasn’t that she couldn’t make up stories. She absolutely could. The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her far too well, which was why her latest lie lasted approximately three minutes. A personal record. The disaster started on a Wednesday afternoon. Yichen had practice. Normally Xiaoran waited for him afterward. Today she wasn’t there. Instead, he got a message.

Xiaoran: I’m busy.

Dead silence. The message already looked suspicious. Not busy with what. Not talk later. Just: I’m busy. Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: Extremely busy.

Yichen smiled. Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.

An hour later, he found her at the campus café, looking very guilty. The moment she saw him, she sat up straight. Too quickly. Like a criminal.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

Silence. Yichen sat down across from her—calm, patient—and waited. Eventually, Lin Xiaoran always confessed. She simply couldn’t help herself. And right on schedule, she started talking.

“Today was productive.”

“Oh?”

“Very productive.”

“Hm.”

“I was studying.”

The first lie. Tiny, harmless. But Yichen noticed—not because of the words, but because she tugged her sleeves down over her hands, the way she had for years whenever she was nervous.

“Very serious studying.”

“Hm.”

“Educational.”

“Hm.”

“Academic.”

“Hm.”

Yichen’s mouth twitched. Now she was overexplaining. Another sign. Xiaoran kept talking, and the more she talked, the worse it got.

“I definitely wasn’t doing anything strange.”

There it was: the self-report. Nobody had accused her of anything, and she was already defending herself. Yichen was enjoying himself enormously. Watching Xiaoran lie was one of life’s simplest pleasures—not because she was convincing, but because she wasn’t. At all.

“I spent the entire afternoon being responsible.”

“Responsible.”

“Very.”

“Hm.”

“I would never waste time.”

Now Yichen had to look away, because his smile was becoming noticeable. Xiaoran noticed anyway. Uh oh. She knew that smile—the one that appeared whenever he caught her doing something ridiculous. And suddenly she was flustered. Not because she’d been caught. Because he looked unfairly handsome. There was something deeply dangerous about Zhou Yichen when he knew something she didn’t know he knew. Relaxed, confident, amused—the slight smile, the calm eyes, the feeling that he was letting her dig her own grave and enjoying every second. A disaster.

Yichen leaned back, comfortable, watching.

“So. What exactly were you studying?”

Dead silence. Details. The enemy of every liar. Xiaoran panicked.

“Media.”

“What part?”

“…Media media.”

Yichen’s smile widened, just slightly, and somehow that made her heart beat faster. Not because of the interrogation. Because he looked ridiculously attractive. This was terrible.

“Which assignment?”

“The assignment.”

“Which one?”

“The… important one.”

“Hm.”

The smile grew, slowly, until Xiaoran wanted to hide under the table. Not from embarrassment. From him. Why was he looking at her like that? Yichen folded his arms, still smiling, still patient, very obviously entertained.

“Xiaoran.”

“What.”

“Look at me.”

“No.”

Yichen laughed, which made things worse. He leaned forward, close enough that she could see the amusement in his eyes.

“Why not?”

“Reasons.”

“What reasons?”

“Personal reasons.”

“Such as?”

He was enjoying this far too much. Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Stop smiling.”

“What smile?”

THAT smile. The teasing one, the one that showed up whenever he felt completely in control. Which was unfortunately right now. Yichen tilted his head, still smiling, still impossible, and asked quietly,

“How long were you watching dramas?”

Direct hit. There it was. The truth. And the worst part? He had known from the very first sentence. The entire conversation had been a trap. A cruel, cruel trap. Xiaoran covered her face, defeated.

“Four hours.”

“Hm.”

“Maybe five.”

“Hm.”

“…Six.”

Exactly the six-hour limit from the Netflix treaty. Technically she hadn’t even broken the rule. She had just lied about getting close to it, which was somehow more embarrassing. There it was. The confession. As always. Yichen laughed softly—victorious, annoyingly handsome—and Xiaoran peeked through her fingers, only to regret it immediately. He was still smiling at her like that. Still far too attractive for someone who had just interrogated her.

He reached over and gently moved her hands away from her face.

“There she is.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“I don’t like you.”

“Liar.”

The worst part was that he was right about that, too.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has discovered a new research topic. It has categories, lists, and ratings. Zhou Yichen would like it to stop.
chapters.title: The Internet Was a Mistake
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know how dangerous you are?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen feared. Basketball injuries. Losing important tournaments. Lin Xiaoran attempting to cook without supervision. But one thing caused problems more consistently than all of them: the internet. Every time Xiaoran discovered a new interest online, everyone suffered. This week’s victim was Zhou Yichen. It started on a Thursday evening. Yichen was studying. Peacefully. Productively. A rare event. Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Question.

Every message that started with “Question” was dangerous.

Yichen: What.

Xiaoran: Did you know there are different types of kisses?

Dead silence.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: There are SO MANY.

Yichen: Why are you researching this.

Seen. No reply. Which was somehow more alarming.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next day, Yichen found out why. Xiaoran showed up outside his lecture hall carrying a notebook. Not suspicious normally. Extremely suspicious when carried by Lin Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I have information.”

“About?”

“Kisses.”

Dead silence. Several students nearby walked away. Smart people. Xiaoran opened the notebook. It had notes. NOTES.

“Look.”

Yichen looked, and immediately regretted it. She had clearly spent hours on this. There were categories. Lists. Observations. Ratings.

“Why.”

“Educational purposes.”

“No.”

“Fine. Curiosity.”

At least that was honest. Xiaoran pointed at the page.

“Apparently there are forehead kisses.”

“You know that.”

“You do those.”

“Correct.”

“Cheek kisses.”

“You know that too.”

“Hand kisses.”

Yichen didn’t answer.

“Eskimo kisses.”

Then she flipped another page.

“And French kisses.”

Dead silence. There it was. The real reason. Yichen understood everything. He closed the notebook, slowly.

“No.”

“What.”

“No.”

“You haven’t even heard my proposal.”

“I don’t need to. I know exactly where this conversation is going.”

He was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours later, in a quiet corner of the campus garden, Xiaoran was still talking about it. Relentlessly.

“Why does it have that name?”

“I don’t know.”

“Who invented it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Why is it famous?”

“Xiaoran. Please stop interviewing me.”

She pouted. It had absolutely no effect. Mostly. She rested her chin on his shoulder, thinking. Dangerous.

“I think couples probably try different things naturally.”

Yichen sensed disaster approaching. Rapidly. Xiaoran looked up—curious, innocent, hopelessly unaware.

“…Do you?”

Sometimes Yichen wondered how one person could be so smart and so clueless at the same time. She could analyze media campaigns, win competitions, research anything—and still completely fail to understand the effect she had on him. Very softly, Yichen sighed.

“Xiaoran, do you have any idea what you do to me?”

“What does that mean?”

Exactly. She didn’t know. Not even slightly. He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear—a familiar gesture that made her smile right away.

“There.”

“There what?”

“That smile.”

“…What about it?”

“You do things like that. You ask questions. You get curious. Then you look at me like everything is simple.”

Xiaoran blinked, completely confused. Yichen laughed quietly. Of course she was. Then he leaned in and kissed her forehead—gentle, warm, familiar. The kiss he always gave her, the one that calmed her down every time.

“There.”

“What was that for?”

“Because I like that one.”

Xiaoran smiled again.

“So that’s a no?”

“Absolutely.”

“This relationship has no freedom.”

Yichen actually laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved hearing. Xiaoran leaned against him, happy. The internet might have introduced her to dozens of kinds of kisses, but her favorite was still the simplest: Zhou Yichen looking at her like she was the best thing that had ever happened to him, and kissing her forehead like he was quietly reminding himself she was real. Even if she occasionally came up with terrifying research topics.

chapters.desc: In his dream, Lin Xiaoran is a famous idol who has never met him. He does not take it well.
chapters.title: The Dream That Made Zhou Yichen Hug Xiaoran at 3 AM
chapters.epigraph: “The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen rarely remembered his dreams. Most disappeared the moment he woke up. This one didn’t. Unfortunately. The dream started normally. At least—normal by dream standards. He was on campus. Walking toward the media building. Looking for Xiaoran. People started screaming. Not scared screaming. Excited screaming. The kind of screaming usually reserved for celebrities. Yichen stopped. Confused. Then he heard it.

“XIAORAN!”

“LIN XIAORAN!”

“SHE’S HERE!”

Dead silence. Because what? A black van pulled up. Security appeared. Cameras. Hundreds of fans. And out stepped—Lin Xiaoran. Except not his Xiaoran. Well—still his Xiaoran. Different. Much different. Her hair was longer and perfectly styled, her makeup flawless, her clothes designer. Beautiful. Actually breathtaking—the kind of beautiful that made entire crowds stop moving. And apparently—In this dream—she was a famous idol. Dead silence. Dream Yichen was just as confused as real Yichen.

Then Xiaoran smiled. The crowd lost their minds. People screamed louder. Phones everywhere. Security closed in around her. A terrifying realization appeared. Nobody was acting strange. Meaning this was normal. For her. Then Xiaoran walked past him. Completely past him—without stopping, without smiling, without even looking. Like he didn’t exist. Dead silence. That felt awful. Then Yichen followed. Because apparently dream logic said that was acceptable. The next several days became increasingly horrifying.

Because Dream Xiaoran genuinely didn’t know him. Not as a boyfriend, not as a friend, not at all. Meanwhile, Yichen was still himself—still a university student, still a basketball player, still hopelessly in love with her. Only now his girlfriend was an international celebrity who had never met him. Worst dream ever.

Then came the truly evil part. The fan meeting. Because somehow—dream Yichen ended up there. Standing in line like everyone else. Holding merchandise like everyone else. Waiting his turn like everyone else. The humiliation was unbelievable. He reached the table. And there she was. Beautiful, smiling, perfect—and completely unfamiliar.

“Hello.”

Her idol smile appeared—professional, warm, practiced. The one she gave thousands of people. Not the real one. Not his. Somehow that hurt. Then she looked up.

“What’s your name?”

What kind of nightmare was this?

“My…”

His voice actually failed. Dream Xiaoran waited politely. Completely unaware she was destroying him.

“Zhou Yichen.”

She smiled.

“Nice to meet you.”

And that was somehow worse. Much worse. Because no. No it wasn’t. She was supposed to know him. She was supposed to steal his hoodies, send him forty messages a day, hug him out of nowhere while he studied. Not this. Never this. Then Dream Xiaoran signed his album.

“Thank you for supporting me.”

Support. Not boyfriend. Not Yichen. Not idiot. Not mine. Support. The dream became increasingly absurd afterward. Yichen somehow went to her concerts. Watched her interviews. Watched her get more famous, watched millions of people love her—and every single time, she looked right through him like a stranger. Then one day in the dream—things became unbearable. Because an interviewer asked:

“What kind of man is your ideal type?”

Dream Yichen paid very close attention. Obviously. And Xiaoran thought carefully. Then smiled.

“I think someone gentle.”

Good.

“Someone patient.”

Good.

“Someone who makes me feel safe.”

Excellent. Then she laughed.

“I don’t know though. I’ve never met someone like that.”

Dream Yichen almost had a breakdown. WHAT DO YOU MEAN. HE WAS RIGHT THERE. The dream jumped again. Now he stood backstage after a concert. Watching her from a distance. Dream Xiaoran turned. Actually turned. Their eyes met, for the first time. She walked toward him. Closer. Closer. Until she was standing right in front of him. Finally.

“Do I know you?”

The world exploded. Zhou Yichen woke up immediately. 3:17 AM. Dark room. Heart pounding. Genuine irritation. That dream had been cruel. Then he felt something warm and heavy against his side. Lin Xiaoran. They had both fallen asleep on his sofa halfway through a movie, under the same blanket, and she was still there—completely real. Not an idol. Not famous. Not unreachable. Just Xiaoran. His Xiaoran, drooling slightly on his shoulder. Very glamorous.

Yichen stared at her for several seconds. He wrapped both arms around her, tight enough that she made a confused, sleepy noise.

“Hm?”

Half asleep. Barely conscious.

“What happened?”

Nothing. How was he supposed to explain? Sorry, I had a dream where you were a celebrity and didn’t know me, so now I’m emotionally damaged. Impossible. Then Xiaoran opened one eye.

“…Yichen?”

He was still hugging her. Not letting go.

“You okay?”

“…Bad dream.”

Her sleepy expression softened.

“Oh.”

Without even waking up properly, she wrapped her arms around him too.

“There.”

“What.”

“Better.”

Half asleep, and completely unaware she had just fixed everything. Then she yawned. And added:

“You’re my favorite person.”

Sleepy Xiaoran was dangerous. Two seconds later, she was asleep again. Zhou Yichen lay staring at the ceiling, his heart finally calming down. The dream version had been beautiful. World-famous. Perfect. But he preferred this one—the clingy one, the dramatic one, the one who stole his hoodies and never stopped talking. The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was. Before falling asleep again, he tightened his arms around her, just to make sure. In case Dream Xiaoran got any more ideas.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lin Xiaoran is loud, dramatic, cries easily, and can get lost walking somewhere she’s been twenty times. Zhou Yichen is calm, patient, and very hard not to notice. He fell for her almost right away, and he has been spoiling her ever since.

From their last years of high school to university in Shanghai, The Softest Kind of Love follows the two of them through first dates and bad fights, exams and families, and the slow work of growing up without growing apart.

Main chapters tell the story in order. Side stories are small moments you can read whenever you like.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a gentle romance, but a few chapters include:

• A crude, sexualized remark made about Xiaoran by a classmate (The One Time Zhou Yichen Lost His Temper)

• A physical fight between students (Xiaoran, Don’t Fight)

• A sports injury with some blood and a hospital visit (Don’t Scare Me Like That Again, Don’t Limp. I’ll Cry Again.)

• Hurtful rumors and a brief break-up scare (Should We Break Up?)

• Dieting and skipped meals after hurtful online comments (The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting)

• Mild language and lots of crying

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I wanted to write the kind of love story I like to read before bed: no cheating, no misunderstanding that drags on for twenty chapters, nobody secretly dying. Just two people who like each other a lot and keep choosing each other, even on the days one of them is being impossible.

Xiaoran is a bit of everyone who has cried over a math test or sulked because their boyfriend was too popular. Yichen is the person a lot of us wish we had, or wish we were—someone who notices when you’ve gone quiet.

Some chapters are silly. Some are soft. A couple of them made me cry a little while writing. Thank you for reading any of them at all.

— 甜慕
